Add expiry: a link that stops working after 30 days (store the deadline in the value)
Serve it for real with http.server: GET /<code> replies with a 301 redirect

blocks.title: shortener
blocks.prompt: Using the provided KV (with set, get and a disk you can pass to KV(disk) to recover after a restart), write a Shortener class: Shortener(kv), shorten(url) returns a new code (base 62 of a counter starting at 1: "1", "2", … "z", "A", … "Z", "10", …) and stores code → url; resolve(code) returns the url or None. Store the counter in the KV too (under the key "#next") so a restarted Shortener keeps counting instead of reusing codes.
blocks.tests:
kv = KV()
s = Shortener(kv)
a = s.shorten("https://example.org/a")
b = s.shorten("https://example.org/b")
assert (a, b) == ("1", "2"), f"codes count up from 1 in base 62; got {a}, {b}"
assert s.resolve(a) == "https://example.org/a", "resolve returns the stored url"
assert s.resolve("zzz") is None, "an unknown code resolves to None"
for i in range(59):
    last = s.shorten(f"https://example.org/{i}")
assert last == "Z", f"the 61st link gets code 'Z' (61 is the last base-62 digit); got {last}"
assert s.shorten("https://example.org/next") == "10", "after Z comes 10, like after 9 in decimal"
s2 = Shortener(KV(kv.disk))            # restart: memory is gone, the log is replayed
assert s2.resolve("2") == "https://example.org/b", "links survive a restart"
assert s2.shorten("https://new.example") == "11", "after a restart the counter continues; it must not reuse code 1"
hints: Base 62 is like converting to decimal digits: n, r = divmod(n, 62) gives the last digit DIGITS[r]; repeat until n is 0.
In shorten, read the counter with int(self.kv.get("#next") or 1), use it, and set it back to n + 1. Because it lives in the log, replay restores it.

blocks.title: bitcask_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write a class Store over a bytearray log with set(key, value), get(key) (via an in-memory index of (offset, length), returning None if missing), delete(key) (appends a tombstone key\n), and a constructor Store(disk=None) that rebuilds the index by replaying an existing log. Records are key\tvalue\n.
blocks.tests:
s = Store()
s.set("a", "1"); s.set("b", "2"); s.set("a", "3")
assert s.get("a") == "3" and s.get("b") == "2", "the newest value wins"
s.delete("b")
assert s.get("b") is None, "a deleted key is gone"
assert bytes(s.disk).endswith(b"b\n"), "delete appends a tombstone, it doesn't erase"
r = Store(s.disk)
assert r.get("a") == "3" and r.get("b") is None, "replaying the log after a crash rebuilds the same index, tombstones included"
assert r.index["a"] == s.index["a"], "replay points at the same offsets"
hints: Replay walks the records in order with a running offset; each line is len(line) + 1 bytes long (the newline).

blocks.q: In a Bitcask-style store, what is on disk, what is in memory, and why can you lose the memory part safely?
blocks.a: On disk: an append-only log of records (newest version wins, tombstones for deletes), split into segments that compaction rewrites to drop dead records. In memory: a hash index from each key to the byte offset (and length) of its newest record, so a read is one lookup plus one small disk read. The index is only a cache of where things are: after a crash you rebuild it by replaying the log from the start, and checksums let you detect and cut off a torn final write.

chapters.title: A tiny SQL database
chapters.tagline: A B-tree keeps rows sorted on disk, a parser reads SQL, and an index turns a full scan into four page reads
goals: Explain why databases store tables in B-trees rather than lists or hash tables
Search a B-tree and count the pages it touches
Split a full node and explain why the tree only grows at the root
Parse a small SELECT … FROM … WHERE … query
Answer range queries with an in-order walk, and say when an index helps

sections.title: What happens when you type SELECT

blocks.html:
SQLite is a single C file that runs on billions of phones. Underneath the SQL, its job is simple to say and hard to do well: keep rows on disk so that finding one, or a range of them, takes as few disk reads as possible.

The trick is the B-tree. Disks (and SSDs) read whole pages, typically 4 KB at a time. A B-tree packs hundreds of sorted keys into each page-sized node, so the tree is very short and very wide. Grow one yourself.

blocks.name: bx-btree
blocks.title: Grow a B-tree, then search it
blocks.goal: Insert rows until the tree is 3 levels tall, then Search for a key that's in it.
blocks.intro: Each block is a key; keys side by side are one node (one disk page, here with room for only 3 keys). Insert and watch nodes split.

blocks.q: How does a B-tree get taller?

opts.t: A new level is added under the leaves when they're full
The root splits: its middle key becomes a new root above it, so every leaf moves down one level together
Each insert adds one level
It never gets taller; it only gets wider

blocks.why: Growing at the top is the whole secret of B-tree balance. Every path from root to leaf always has the same length, so the worst-case lookup is always the height: a few page reads, however unlucky the insert order.

sections.title: Why not a list, or a hash table?

blocks.html:
• A sorted list gives fast lookups (binary search) but inserting in the middle shifts everything after it, and on disk that means rewriting pages.
  • A hash table (chapter 6) finds one key fast but can't do WHERE id BETWEEN 100 AND 200 or ORDER BY without reading everything.
  • A B-tree keeps keys sorted (ranges are easy), inserts touch only a few pages, and lookups read height pages.

How short is "short"? Count the levels needed for a million rows.

blocks.code:
rows = 1_000_000
print("binary tree levels:", math.ceil(math.log2(rows)))
print("B-tree levels, 100 keys per page:", round(math.log(rows, 100)))
print("B-tree levels, 500 keys per page:", math.ceil(math.log(rows, 500)))

blocks.html: Twenty disk reads versus three. That's the difference between a slow and an instant query.

A node is {"keys": [...], "vals": [...], "kids": [...]}. Keys are sorted. In an internal node, kids[i] holds everything smaller than keys[i], and kids[-1] everything bigger than the last key. A leaf has no kids.

blocks.title: bt_search
blocks.prompt: Write bt_search(node, key) returning (value, pages): the value stored under key (or None if it isn't there) and the number of nodes visited. Use bisect.bisect_left(node["keys"], key) to find your place in each node.
blocks.tests:
root = bt_node()
for k in [20, 5, 33, 12, 41, 8, 27, 1, 15, 38, 3, 30, 22]:
    root = bt_insert(root, k, f"row {k}")
assert bt_search(root, 27)[0] == "row 27", "finds a key"
assert bt_search(root, 26)[0] is None, "a missing key returns None"
v, pages = bt_search(root, 1)
assert v == "row 1" and pages <= bt_height(root), f"never reads more pages than the height ({bt_height(root)}); read {pages}"
hints: Loop: count a page, bisect_left to find i, return if keys[i] == key, stop at a leaf, otherwise go down into kids[i].
blocks.starter:
def bt_search(node, key):
    return None, 0

blocks.html: When a node holds one key too many, it splits: the middle key goes up to the parent, the keys on its left become one node, the keys on its right another. Children split the same way: a node with 4 keys has 5 children, and the left half takes the first 3.

blocks.title: split
blocks.prompt: Write split(node) returning (left, middle_key, middle_val, right). With m = len(keys) // 2: the left node gets keys/vals before m and kids up to and including m; the right gets keys/vals after m and the kids after m. Build nodes with bt_node(keys, vals, kids).
blocks.tests:
leaf = bt_node([1, 2, 3, 4], ["a", "b", "c", "d"])
l, k, v, r = split(leaf)
assert (l["keys"], k, v, r["keys"]) == ([1, 2], 3, "c", [4]), "the middle key goes up"
kids = [bt_node([x]) for x in range(5)]
inner = bt_node([10, 20, 30, 40], list("abcd"), kids)
l, k, v, r = split(inner)
assert len(l["kids"]) == 3 and len(r["kids"]) == 2, "3 children go left, 2 go right"
assert len(l["kids"]) == len(l["keys"]) + 1 and len(r["kids"]) == len(r["keys"]) + 1, "every internal node has one more child than keys"
hints: Slices: keys[:m] and keys[m + 1:] for the halves, kids[:m + 1] and kids[m + 1:] for the children.
blocks.starter:
def split(node):
    return node, None, None, bt_node()
blocks.solution:
def split(node):
    m = len(node["keys"]) // 2
    left = bt_node(node["keys"][:m], node["vals"][:m], node["kids"][:m + 1])
    right = bt_node(node["keys"][m + 1:], node["vals"][m + 1:], node["kids"][m + 1:])
    return left, node["keys"][m], node["vals"][m], right

blocks.html: The full insert (provided in this chapter as bt_insert) walks down to a leaf, inserts in order, and splits on the way back up if needed. If the root splits, a new root holds just the middle key. Watch the height grow slowly:

blocks.title: How tall does it get?

blocks.html: SQL is a language, so a database needs a parser (chapters 2, 4, 5). We'll handle one shape: SELECT cols FROM table with an optional WHERE col op value, where op is =, < or >.

blocks.title: parse_select
blocks.prompt: Write parse_select(sql) returning a dict {"columns": [...], "table": name, "where": (col, op, value) or None}. Columns are comma-separated (strip spaces; gives [""]). The value is an int if it's all digits, otherwise a string with any surrounding single quotes removed. Keywords may be any case.
blocks.tests:
q = parse_select("SELECT name, age FROM users WHERE age > 30")
assert q == {"columns": ["name", "age"], "table": "users", "where": ("age", ">", 30)}, f"got {q}"
assert parse_select("select * from books")["where"] is None and parse_select("select * from books")["columns"] == ["*"], "no WHERE"
assert parse_select("SELECT title FROM books WHERE genre = 'scifi'")["where"] == ("genre", "=", "scifi"), "strings lose their quotes"
hints: One regular expression with groups is enough: select (cols) from (table) and an optional where (col) (op) (value) part. Use re.I for any case.
blocks.starter:
def parse_select(sql):
    return {"columns": [], "table": "", "where": None}

blocks.title: string_compare_bug
blocks.prompt: filter_rows(rows, where) scans every row (a full table scan) and keeps the ones that match. But WHERE age > 30 keeps a 9-year-old and drops a 100-year-old. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
people = [{"name": "Ana", "age": 9}, {"name": "Bo", "age": 100}, {"name": "Cy", "age": 31}]
assert [r["name"] for r in filter_rows(people, ("age", ">", 30))] == ["Bo", "Cy"], "numbers compare as numbers"
assert [r["name"] for r in filter_rows(people, ("name", "=", "Cy"))] == ["Cy"], "strings still work"
hints: As strings, "9" > "30" because "9" comes after "3". Compare the values themselves.

blocks.html: WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 20 on a B-tree: walk the tree in order (left child, key, next child, …) and skip subtrees that can't contain anything in range. A hash index can't do this; a B-tree does it naturally because the keys are sorted.

blocks.title: In-order walk
blocks.tests:
root = bt_node()
for k in [9, 2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 3, 6, 5]:
    root = bt_insert(root, k, None)
assert in_order(root, []) == list(range(1, 10)), "keys come out sorted"

blocks.title: A catalogue database for a community library
blocks.client: A volunteer-run library with 8,000 books and a spreadsheet that keeps breaking
blocks.brief: Store books as rows keyed by an integer id in your B-tree. Support get(id), between(lo, hi) for shelf ranges, and a mini SQL front end: SELECT title FROM books WHERE id > 7000 should use the index, while a filter on author falls back to a full scan. Print how many pages each query touched.
blocks.why: This is the core loop of every relational database: parse, plan (index or scan?), execute. Seeing the page counts side by side is how you learn when to add an index, why ORDER BY on an indexed column is free, and why indexes slow down writes a little.
milestones: Insert 8,000 book rows into the B-tree with bt_insert
Implement get(id) with your bt_search and count pages
Implement between(lo, hi) with a pruned in-order walk
Parse SELECT queries and route id conditions to the index, others to a scan
Print a little "query plan": index or scan, and pages read
stretch: A second index on year, mapping year → list of ids
Delete, with merging of nodes that get too empty
Save nodes to a file as fixed-size pages and read them back lazily

blocks.title: Catalogue
blocks.prompt: Write a class Catalogue with add(row) (insert into a B-tree keyed by row["id"], using bt_insert), get(id) returning the row or None, and between(lo, hi) returning the rows with lo <= id <= hi in id order. For between, walk the tree in order but skip child subtrees that can't overlap the range.
blocks.tests:
cat = Catalogue()
for i in [50, 3, 77, 12, 64, 29, 91, 8, 45, 33, 70, 18, 2, 99, 56]:
    cat.add({"id": i, "title": f"Book {i}"})
assert cat.get(64)["title"] == "Book 64" and cat.get(65) is None, "get by id"
assert [r["id"] for r in cat.between(10, 50)] == [12, 18, 29, 33, 45, 50], "range in order"
assert [r["id"] for r in cat.between(100, 200)] == [], "empty range"
assert [r["id"] for r in cat.between(0, 1000)] == sorted([50, 3, 77, 12, 64, 29, 91, 8, 45, 33, 70, 18, 2, 99, 56]), "everything"
hints: add is one line with bt_insert. get is your bt_search without the page count.
For between, adapt the in-order walk: only go into kids[i] when lo < keys[i] (something in there could be ≥ lo), stop once a key is past hi, and only visit the last child if the last key is below hi.

blocks.title: btree_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write find(node, key) for the B-tree nodes in this chapter, returning the value or None.
blocks.tests:
root = bt_node()
for k in range(0, 200, 7):
    root = bt_insert(root, k, k * 10)
assert find(root, 70) == 700 and find(root, 71) is None, "finds 70, not 71"
assert all(find(root, k) == k * 10 for k in range(0, 200, 7)), "finds every key"
hints: Find your place with bisect_left; return on a match; give up at a leaf; otherwise go down into the child at that position.
blocks.starter:
def find(node, key):
    pass

blocks.q: Explain why databases index tables with B-trees, how a B-tree stays balanced, and when an index doesn't help.
blocks.a: Storage reads whole pages, so the goal is to touch as few pages as possible. A B-tree packs hundreds of sorted keys into each page-sized node, so the tree is only a few levels deep even for billions of rows; a lookup reads one node per level. Because keys are sorted, range queries and ORDER BY are an in-order walk, which a hash index can't do. It stays balanced because inserts go into leaves, and an overfull node splits and pushes its middle key up; only a root split adds a level, so every leaf is always at the same depth. An index doesn't help for conditions on columns it doesn't cover (that's a full scan), for queries that return most of the table, and it costs extra work on every insert.

chapters.title: Git from scratch
chapters.tagline: Name every file by its fingerprint, and history becomes a graph of snapshots that share everything they can
goals: Explain why naming data by its SHA-1 hash gives free deduplication and tamper-evidence
Store blobs, trees and commits in a plain dictionary, exactly like git's object store
Treat branches and HEAD as movable pointers, and walk history by following parents
Diff two snapshots and find the merge base of two branches in the commit graph
Merge two branches file by file with a three-way merge, and spot real conflicts

blocks.html:
Most people picture git as "a list of changes". It isn't. Every commit is a full snapshot of your project. That sounds wasteful: 1,000 commits of a 1,000-file project would be a million files. Yet a .git folder is usually small.

The trick is one idea: name every piece of data by a fingerprint of its content. If a file didn't change, its fingerprint didn't change, so the new snapshot just points at the old copy. Nothing is stored twice.

There are only three kinds of object:

  1. Blob: the contents of one file.
  2. Tree: a folder, written as a list of name → blob id.
  3. Commit: a tree id, the id of the commit before it (its parent), and a message.

Play first. Each column is a commit (top), its tree (middle) and its file blobs (bottom).

blocks.name: bx-git
blocks.title: Snapshots that share what didn't change
blocks.goal: Make a branch, commit on both branches, then merge them into a commit with two parents.
blocks.intro: Edit one file and commit: only that file's blob, the tree and the commit get new ids. The other blobs are shared (lines back to the old blocks). Click any block to ask why.

blocks.q: You change one file out of three and commit. How many new objects does git store?

opts.t: 1: just the changed file
3: the new blob, a new tree (its list changed) and a new commit
5: three blobs, a tree and a commit
It stores the difference between the old and new file

blocks.why: The two untouched files keep their ids, so the new tree simply points at the old blobs. The tree itself is new because one of its lines changed, and the commit is new because it points at a new tree.

blocks.html:
A hash function turns any amount of data into a short fixed-size fingerprint. SHA-1 gives 40 hex characters. Two promises matter:

  • Same input → same hash, on every computer, forever.
  • Change one byte → a completely different hash. And nobody knows how to find two different files with the same SHA-1 by accident.

So the hash can be the file's name. That's called content addressing. Git hashes a small header (blob <length>, then a zero byte) followed by the content. This is exactly what git hash-object does.

blocks.code:
def oid(kind, body):
    data = f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}".encode()
    return hashlib.sha1(data).hexdigest()

print(oid("blob", "hello\n"))
print(oid("blob", "hello\n") == oid("blob", "hello\n"))
print(oid("blob", "Hello\n")[:12])
print(len(oid("blob", "a whole novel " * 1000)))

blocks.html: Two things fall out for free. Dedupe: storing the same content twice writes the same key twice, so the dictionary still holds one copy. Tamper-evidence: if someone edits a stored object, its contents no longer match its name, and you can check that.

blocks.title: hash_object
blocks.prompt: Write hash_object(store, kind, body). Build the bytes f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}", hash them with hashlib.sha1(...).hexdigest(), save store[oid] = (kind, body) and return oid. Storing the same body twice must leave one entry.
blocks.tests:
s = {}
a = hash_object(s, "blob", "hello\n")
assert a == "ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a", f"this is the id real git gives 'hello\\n'; got {a}"
assert s[a] == ("blob", "hello\n"), "the store should map the id to (kind, body)"
b = hash_object(s, "blob", "hello\n")
assert a == b and len(s) == 1, "same content must give the same id and be stored only once (dedupe)"
hash_object(s, "blob", "bye\n")
assert len(s) == 2, "different content gets a different id"
hints: Build the string with an f-string, then .encode() it before hashing: hashlib.sha1 wants bytes.
blocks.solution:
def hash_object(store, kind, body):
    data = f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}".encode()
    oid = hashlib.sha1(data).hexdigest()
    store[oid] = (kind, body)
    return oid

blocks.title: verify_store
blocks.prompt: find_tampered(store) should return the ids whose stored object no longer matches its name (someone edited the body after it was stored). It never finds anything. Fix it.
blocks.setup:
def oid_of(kind, body):
    return hashlib.sha1(f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}".encode()).hexdigest()
blocks.tests:
good = oid_of("blob", "rent: 900\n")
evil = oid_of("blob", "rent: 500\n")
store = {good: ("blob", "rent: 900\n"), evil: ("blob", "rent: 500\n")}
assert find_tampered(store) == [], "an untouched store has nothing tampered"
store[good] = ("blob", "rent: 9\n")
assert find_tampered(store) == [good], f"the edited object should be caught, got {find_tampered(store)}"
hints: What should the recomputed hash be compared with? The object's name is the hash it had when it was stored.

sections.title: Trees: a folder is a list of names

blocks.html: A blob has no filename. That's on purpose: two files with identical content (two copies of a licence, say) share one blob. The name lives one level up, in a tree: one line per file, name blob-id, sorted by name so the same folder always produces the same text, and so the same tree id.

blocks.title: write_tree turns {name: content} into a tree id
blocks.setup:
def hash_object(store, kind, body):
    oid = hashlib.sha1(f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}".encode()).hexdigest()
    store[oid] = (kind, body)
    return oid
blocks.tests:
s = {}
t1 = write_tree(s, {"b.txt": "two", "a.txt": "one"})
t2 = write_tree(s, {"a.txt": "one", "b.txt": "two"})
assert t1 == t2, "same folder in a different dict order must give the same tree id (sort the names)"
assert s[t1][0] == "tree" and s[t1][1].startswith("a.txt "), "the tree lists a.txt first"
assert len(s) == 3, "two blobs and one tree"

blocks.html: Now watch the sharing happen. Change one file and count which ids changed.
Two snapshots, three files each, but only 5 objects: the two unchanged blobs are shared. That's the "full snapshot that costs almost nothing" trick.

A commit is a tiny text object:

``` tree 3b18e5... parent 9f2c41...

add banana price ```

Because the commit's text includes its parent's id, its own id depends on the parent, which depends on its parent, all the way back. Change anything in old history and every later id changes. That's why you can't quietly rewrite a published commit.

A branch is not a copy of anything. It's a name pointing at one commit id: refs = {"main": "9f2c41..."}. Committing moves the pointer forward. HEAD says which branch you're on.

blocks.title: commit
blocks.prompt: Fill the blanks in commit. It writes the tree, builds the commit text with a parent line only when the branch already has a commit, saves it, and moves the branch pointer to the new commit.
blocks.tests:
s, refs = {}, {}
c1 = commit(s, refs, "main", {"a.txt": "one"}, "first")
assert refs["main"] == c1, "after committing, the branch must point at the new commit"
assert "parent" not in s[c1][1], "the very first commit has no parent"
c2 = commit(s, refs, "main", {"a.txt": "two"}, "second")
assert f"parent {c1}\n" in s[c2][1], "the second commit's text must contain 'parent <first id>' on its own line"
assert refs["main"] == c2, "main moved forward to the second commit"
hints: The parent line looks just like the tree line: f"parent {parent}\n". Moving the branch is one assignment into refs.
blocks.starter:
def commit(store, refs, head, files, message):
    tree = write_tree(store, files)
    body = f"tree {tree}\n"
    parent = refs.get(head)
    if parent:
        body += ____
    body += f"\n{message}"
    oid = hash_object(store, "commit", body)
    ____
    return oid
blocks.solution:
def commit(store, refs, head, files, message):
    tree = write_tree(store, files)
    body = f"tree {tree}\n"
    parent = refs.get(head)
    if parent:
        body += f"parent {parent}\n"
    body += f"\n{message}"
    oid = hash_object(store, "commit", body)
    refs[head] = oid
    return oid

blocks.html: Log is just "start at the branch, follow parent until there isn't one". Run this to see the chain:

blocks.title: a tiny repo and its log

blocks.html: Notice refs["idea"] = refs["main"]: creating a branch copies one id, not your files. That's why git branches are instant.

To show what changed between two commits, you don't compare file contents line by line first. Compare the trees: if a name has the same blob id on both sides, the file is identical and you skip it without reading it. Only names whose ids differ need a closer look.

blocks.title: diff_trees
blocks.prompt: Write diff_trees(old, new). Both are dicts {name: blob_id} (a tree already read back). Return a dict with three sorted lists: "added" (only in new), "removed" (only in old) and "changed" (in both, different id).
blocks.tests:
old = {"a.txt": "11", "b.txt": "22", "c.txt": "33"}
new = {"a.txt": "11", "b.txt": "99", "d.txt": "44"}
d = diff_trees(old, new)
assert d["added"] == ["d.txt"], f"d.txt is new, got {d['added']}"
assert d["removed"] == ["c.txt"], f"c.txt was removed, got {d['removed']}"
assert d["changed"] == ["b.txt"], f"only b.txt has a different blob id, got {d['changed']}"
assert diff_trees(old, old) == {"added": [], "removed": [], "changed": []}, "a tree compared with itself has no differences"
hints: Three comprehensions: names in new but not old, names in old but not new, and names in both whose ids differ.

blocks.html: In a real repo, trees contain other trees (sub-folders). If a sub-folder's tree id is the same on both sides, git skips the whole folder in one comparison. That's why git diff is fast even in huge projects.

Before you can merge main and idea, you need the commit where they split: the newest commit that both histories contain. It's called the merge base.

History is a graph where each commit points at its parents (a merge commit has two). The recipe:

  1. Collect every ancestor of a (including a) into a set.
  2. Walk back from b breadth-first (nearest commits first). The first commit you meet that is in the set is the merge base.

blocks.title: merge_base
blocks.prompt: Write merge_base(parents, a, b). parents maps each commit id to a list of parent ids (empty for the first commit). Return the closest common ancestor of a and b (a commit counts as its own ancestor). Return None if they share nothing.
blocks.tests:
#   A - B - C - D        (main)
#        \
#         E - F          (idea)
P = {"A": [], "B": ["A"], "C": ["B"], "D": ["C"], "E": ["B"], "F": ["E"]}
assert merge_base(P, "D", "F") == "B", f"main and idea split at B, got {merge_base(P, 'D', 'F')}"
assert merge_base(P, "F", "D") == "B", "the answer doesn't depend on the order"
assert merge_base(P, "D", "B") == "B", "if one is an ancestor of the other, it IS the merge base"
P2 = dict(P, G=["D", "F"], H=["F"])
assert merge_base(P2, "G", "H") == "F", "after merging idea into main (G), a newer idea commit H splits from G at F"
assert merge_base({"X": [], "Y": []}, "X", "Y") is None, "unrelated histories have no merge base"
hints: Part 1 is a plain graph walk with a stack and a seen set. Part 2 uses collections.deque so you look at the nearest commits first.
Remember a merge commit has two parents: always extend with the whole parents[c] list.

blocks.html:
Why do you need the base? Picture a.txt is different on your branch and on theirs. With only two versions you can't tell who changed it. With the base you can:

baseourstheirsresult
XXYY (only they changed it)
XYXY (only we changed it)
XYYY (we both made the same change)
XYZconflict: a human must decide

That's the whole idea of a three-way merge. A two-way comparison would call every difference a conflict.

blocks.code:
def pick(base, ours, theirs):
    if ours == theirs: return ours
    if ours == base: return theirs
    if theirs == base: return ours
    return "CONFLICT"

print(pick("x", "x", "y"))
print(pick("x", "y", "x"))
print(pick("x", "y", "y"))
print(pick("x", "y", "z"))
print(pick(None, None, "new file"))

blocks.title: merge_files
blocks.prompt: Write merge_files(base, ours, theirs). Each argument is a dict {name: content}; a missing name means the file doesn't exist on that side. Apply the table above to every name in any of the three. Return (merged, conflicts): merged is the result dict (leave out files whose result is "doesn't exist") and conflicts is a sorted list of names that conflict. For a conflicting name, put "<<<<<<< ours " + ours + " ======= " + theirs + " >>>>>>> theirs" in merged (use "" for a side that's missing).
hints: Loop over set(base) | set(ours) | set(theirs), and use .get(name) so a missing file is None. Then the four rows of the table are four ifs, in the same order as pick above.
blocks.starter:
def merge_files(base, ours, theirs):
    merged, conflicts = {}, []
    # your code here
    return merged, conflicts

blocks.html: A merge then makes a commit with two parents: your branch tip and theirs. That's the diamond you made in the simulation.

sections.title: Real-world project: version history for a notes app

blocks.html: Notion, Google Docs, Figma and Apple Notes all let you "see version history" and "restore this version". Under the hood, many store versions exactly like git: content-addressed snapshots in a key-value store, chained by parent ids.

blocks.title: Version history for a notes app
blocks.client: A small team whose shared meeting notes keep getting overwritten
blocks.brief: Every time someone presses Save, keep a version. People must be able to list versions newest first, restore any old one, and two people editing from the same version should be merged automatically when they touched different notes. Saving the same text twice must not use any extra storage.
blocks.why: Content-addressed storage is everywhere: git, Docker image layers, IPFS, backup tools like restic and borg, and the deduplicated blob storage behind Dropbox and Google Drive. Three-way merge is what lets two editors (or two phones syncing offline) combine their work without asking you every time.
milestones: Store each note's text as a blob with hash_object; check that saving identical text adds nothing
Make each save a commit object with a parent id and a message
List versions newest first by following parents
Restore a version by reading back its tree
Merge two people's versions with merge_base and merge_files
stretch: Show a diff between any two versions using diff_trees
Add a "verify" button that finds tampered objects
Pack old versions into one compressed file (git's "packfile") and measure the savings

blocks.title: NotesHistory
blocks.prompt: Write a class NotesHistory. save(notes, message) stores a snapshot of notes (a dict {title: text}) as a commit whose parent is the previous save, and returns its id. versions() returns the list of messages, newest first. restore(steps_back) returns the notes dict from that many saves ago (0 = latest). Use the given hash_object, write_tree and read_tree. Keep all objects in self.store.
blocks.tests:
h = NotesHistory()
h.save({"monday": "agenda: budget"}, "first draft")
n = len(h.store)
h.save({"monday": "agenda: budget", "tuesday": "hire?"}, "add tuesday")
assert len(h.store) == n + 3, f"one new blob (tuesday), one tree and one commit; the monday blob is shared. Store grew by {len(h.store) - n}"
h.save({"monday": "agenda: budget, rent", "tuesday": "hire?"}, "fix monday")
assert h.versions() == ["fix monday", "add tuesday", "first draft"], f"newest first, got {h.versions()}"
assert h.restore(0)["monday"] == "agenda: budget, rent", "restore(0) is the latest save"
assert h.restore(2) == {"monday": "agenda: budget"}, f"two saves back there was only monday, got {h.restore(2)}"
before = len(h.store)
h.save({"monday": "agenda: budget, rent", "tuesday": "hire?"}, "saved again")
assert len(h.store) == before + 1, "saving identical notes only adds a commit: blobs and tree are reused"
hints: Store the id of the latest commit in self.head. A small helper that splits a commit's text on "\n\n" into header lines and message makes versions and restore short.
restore(k) follows the parent link k times, then calls read_tree on that commit's tree id.

blocks.title: mini_git
blocks.prompt: From memory, write MiniGit with: commit(files, message) (snapshot files as blobs + tree + commit on the current branch, moving the branch), branch(name) (new branch at the current commit), checkout(name) (switch branch; return that commit's files as a dict), and log() (messages newest first along first parents). Objects live in self.store, keyed by SHA-1 like git (f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}").
blocks.tests:
g = MiniGit()
g.commit({"a.txt": "hello\n"}, "one")
assert "ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a" in g.store, "the blob for 'hello\\n' should have git's real id"
g.branch("idea")
g.checkout("idea")
g.commit({"a.txt": "hello\n", "b.txt": "x"}, "two")
assert g.log() == ["two", "one"], f"log on idea, got {g.log()}"
files = g.checkout("main")
assert files == {"a.txt": "hello\n"}, f"main still has only a.txt, got {files}"
assert g.log() == ["one"], "main never moved"
hints: You need four small pieces: put (hash and store), a commit reader (split on "\n\n"), commit, and walking parents for log.

blocks.q: Why can git keep a full snapshot of your project in every commit without the repository exploding in size, and why does changing an old commit change every commit after it?
blocks.a: Every object is named by the SHA-1 hash of its content. An unchanged file has the same hash, so a new tree just points at the existing blob: only changed files, their trees and the commit are new objects. A commit's text includes its parent's id, so its own id depends on the whole chain behind it; edit anything old and its id changes, which changes its child's text and id, and so on to the tip. That makes history deduplicated and tamper-evident.

chapters.title: A vim-style text editor
chapters.tagline: A gap buffer makes typing cheap, a state machine gives keys their meaning, and a stack of commands lets you take it all back
chapters.part: Part 3 · Tools you use every day
goals: Measure why "text as one string" gets slow, and fix it with a list of lines
Build a gap buffer and explain why inserting at the cursor is O(1)
Write cursor motions (h l w b 0 $) as small functions from position to position
Model NORMAL / INSERT / VISUAL as a state machine, and parse commands like 3j and dw
Undo and redo with a stack of commands, and say why it beats saving snapshots

sections.title: What happens when you press a key

blocks.html:
An editor looks simple: you press x, a letter appears. But three questions hide inside:

  1. Storage: where do the characters live, so that typing in the middle of a big file is still instant?
  2. Meaning: in vim, x in NORMAL mode deletes a character, while in INSERT mode it types an x. How does one key mean two things?
  3. Memory: how does u (undo) know what to put back?

The simulation answers all three. The row of cells is the text in memory; the empty cells are the gap (you'll see why soon). The three blocks behind it are the modes.

blocks.name: bx-editor
blocks.title: Gap buffer, cursor and modes
blocks.goal: Delete a word with an operator + motion (put the cursor on a word, press d then w), then press u to undo it.
blocks.intro: Click the key box and type like it's vim: i to insert, Esc to go back, h/l/w/b to move. Or use the buttons. Flip to plain string and type in the middle: count the characters that have to move.

blocks.q: You're in NORMAL mode and press i, then x, then Esc, then x. What happened to the text?

opts.t: Two x's were typed
Two characters were deleted
One x was typed, then one character was deleted
Nothing: i cancels the next key

blocks.why: i switches to INSERT mode, where x is just a letter. Esc goes back to NORMAL, where x means "delete the character under the cursor". Same key, different mode, different meaning.

blocks.html: The obvious design: keep the whole file in one string. But Python strings (and Java, JavaScript, Go…) can't be changed in place. To insert one character at position p, you build a new string: everything before p, the new character, everything after. Every character gets copied.

blocks.code:
text = "a" * 10
copied = 0
for _ in range(5):              # type 5 characters at the very start
    copied += len(text)         # the new string copies every old character
    text = "!" + text
print(text)
print(copied)

blocks.html:
Typing at the start of a 1 MB file would copy a million characters per keystroke. At 10 keys a second, that's 10 million copies a second just to keep up. That's why no serious editor stores text as one string.

A first fix: keep a list of lines. Typing only rebuilds the one line you're on, and lines are short.

blocks.title: lines_editing
blocks.prompt: Text is a list of strings, one per line. Fill the blanks: insert_char puts ch into line row at column col; press_enter splits line row at col into two lines (what Enter does).
blocks.tests:
doc = ["hello", "wrld"]
insert_char(doc, 1, 1, "o")
assert doc == ["hello", "world"], f"'o' goes at column 1 of line 1, got {doc}"
press_enter(doc, 0, 2)
assert doc == ["he", "llo", "world"], f"Enter at column 2 splits 'hello' into 'he' and 'llo', got {doc}"
press_enter(doc, 2, 5)
assert doc == ["he", "llo", "world", ""], "Enter at the end of a line makes an empty line after it"
hints: insert_char is the same slice-and-join as with one big string, but only on one line.
The new line goes right after row, and it holds the part of the old line from col on.
blocks.starter:
def insert_char(lines, row, col, ch):
    line = lines[row]
    lines[row] = ____

def press_enter(lines, row, col):
    line = lines[row]
    lines[row] = line[:col]
    lines.insert(____, ____)
blocks.solution:
def insert_char(lines, row, col, ch):
    line = lines[row]
    lines[row] = line[:col] + ch + line[col:]

def press_enter(lines, row, col):
    line = lines[row]
    lines[row] = line[:col]
    lines.insert(row + 1, line[col:])

blocks.html: Better, but a very long line (a minified JavaScript file is often one 500 KB line!) is back to the slow case. We want inserts at the cursor to cost the same no matter how long the line is.

Here's the trick Emacs has used since the 1980s. Keep the characters in an array with a block of empty slots right at the cursor: the gap.

`` h e l l o _ _ _ _ w o r l d ^gap_start ^gap_end ``

  • Typing writes into the first empty slot and moves gap_start right by one. Nothing else moves. O(1).
  • Backspace just moves gap_start left. The character is "deleted" by being inside the gap.
  • Moving the cursor moves the gap: each step copies one character from one side of the gap to the other.

People type in bursts at one spot, then move a bit, then type again. So nearly all the work is the cheap part.

blocks.title: insert into a gap buffer
blocks.tests:
g = GB("ab", 3)
insert(g, "c")
assert g.text() == "abc" and g.gap_start == 3, "c fills the last empty slot"
insert(g, "d")
assert g.text() == "abcd", "a full buffer must grow before writing"
assert len(g.buf) == 6, "grow doubles the size, without the list's own slow insert"

blocks.html: Moving the cursor is the one place characters move. Moving the gap left by one: the character just before the gap jumps to just before gap_end.

blocks.title: move_gap
blocks.prompt: Write move_gap(gb, pos) that moves the gap so that gap_start == pos (the cursor sits at text position pos). Move one character at a time across the gap, set emptied slots to None, and return how many characters you moved.
blocks.tests:
g = GB("helloworld", 14)
assert move_gap(g, 5) == 5, "moving from the end (10) to 5 moves 5 characters"
assert g.buf == list("hello") + [None] * 4 + list("world"), f"the gap should sit between hello and world, got {g.buf}"
assert g.text() == "helloworld", "moving the gap never changes the text"
assert move_gap(g, 7) == 2 and g.text() == "helloworld", "moving right by 2 moves 2 characters"
assert move_gap(g, 7) == 0, "already there: nothing moves"
hints: Two loops: one while the gap is too far right (gap_start > pos), one while it's too far left.
Moving left: shrink both ends by one, then copy buf[gap_start] to buf[gap_end]. Moving right is the mirror image.
blocks.starter:
def move_gap(gb, pos):
    moved = 0
    # your code here
    return moved
blocks.solution:
def move_gap(gb, pos):
    moved = 0
    while gb.gap_start > pos:
        gb.gap_start -= 1
        gb.gap_end -= 1
        gb.buf[gb.gap_end] = gb.buf[gb.gap_start]
        gb.buf[gb.gap_start] = None
        moved += 1
    while gb.gap_start < pos:
        gb.buf[gb.gap_start] = gb.buf[gb.gap_end]
        gb.buf[gb.gap_end] = None
        gb.gap_start += 1
        gb.gap_end += 1
        moved += 1
    return moved

blocks.html:
In NORMAL mode, keys move the cursor. Each motion is just a function: (text, position) → new position. That makes them easy to test and, as you'll see, easy to combine with operators.

keymoves to
h / lone left / right (stops at the ends)
0 / $start / last character of the line
wstart of the next word
bstart of this word, or the previous one
j / ksame column, line below / above (clamped if that line is shorter)

We'll call a word a run of non-space characters (vim also splits on punctuation, but the idea is the same).

blocks.title: word_forward
blocks.prompt: Write word_forward(text, pos): skip the rest of the current word (non-spaces), then skip the spaces after it, and return where you land. If there's no next word, return len(text).
blocks.tests:
t = "the quick  brown"
assert word_forward(t, 0) == 4, f"from 't' of 'the', w lands on 'q' (index 4), got {word_forward(t, 0)}"
assert word_forward(t, 6) == 11, "from inside 'quick', skip the rest and both spaces"
assert word_forward(t, 3) == 4, "from a space, just skip the spaces"
assert word_forward(t, 12) == len(t), "no next word: land at the end"
hints: Two while loops, one after the other, each with i < len(text) first so you never index past the end.
blocks.starter:
def word_forward(text, pos):
    i = pos
    # your code here
    return i

blocks.title: word_back
blocks.prompt: word_back(text, pos) should move to the first letter of the current word (or of the previous word if you're already at a word's start). It lands one character too early, on the space. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
t = "the quick brown"
assert word_back(t, 7) == 4, f"from inside 'quick', b goes to its 'q' (4), got {word_back(t, 7)}"
assert word_back(t, 4) == 0, "from the start of 'quick', b goes to the start of 'the'"
assert word_back(t, 10) == 4, "from the start of 'brown', b goes back to 'quick'"
assert word_back(t, 0) == 0, "at the very start, b stays put"
hints: The loop should stop when the character before i is a space, so that i itself is the first letter.

blocks.html: j and k remember which column you wanted. Go down from column 8 onto a 3-character line, and you'd land at column 2; go down again onto a long line, and a good editor jumps back to 8.

blocks.code:
lines = ["a long first line", "abc", "another long line"]
want = 8
for row in range(3):
    col = min(want, len(lines[row]) - 1)
    print(row, col, repr(lines[row][col]))

blocks.html:
Why does vim have modes at all? Because then every letter on the keyboard can be a command without holding Ctrl. dw, ciw, >>: one-handed, no chords.

The cost is that the same key means different things, so the editor must always know which mode it's in. That's a state machine: a current state, and a table of (state, key) → next state. Anything not in the table stays put.

Look at the second v: in INSERT mode it's just a letter, so the mode stays INSERT. The table is the whole design: to add a mode (vim has REPLACE, COMMAND-LINE and more), you add rows, not if statements scattered everywhere.

NORMAL-mode commands have a little grammar:

`` [count] operator [count] motion 3dw d2w dd [count] motion 3j w $ ``

An operator (d delete, c change, y copy) says what to do; a motion says over which text. Learn 5 operators and 10 motions and you know 50 commands. This is why vim users get fast: they compose, they don't memorise.

The text between the cursor and where the motion lands is what the operator acts on. So dw = "delete from here to wherever w would go".

blocks.title: parse_command
blocks.prompt: Write parse_command(keys) returning (count, operator, motion). count is the number in front (default 1; a count before and after the operator multiply, so 2d3w is 6). operator is "d", "c", "y" or None. motion is the last key. Doubling an operator (dd, yy) means "whole line": return motion "line".
blocks.tests:
assert parse_command("w") == (1, None, "w"), "a bare motion: count 1, no operator"
assert parse_command("3j") == (3, None, "j"), f"3j moves down 3 lines, got {parse_command('3j')}"
assert parse_command("dw") == (1, "d", "w"), "dw: delete to the next word"
assert parse_command("12dw") == (12, "d", "w"), "counts can have several digits"
assert parse_command("2d3w") == (6, "d", "w"), "counts before and after the operator multiply"
assert parse_command("dd") == (1, "d", "line"), "dd deletes the whole line"
assert parse_command("3yy") == (3, "y", "line"), "3yy copies 3 lines"
hints: Read digits (if any) into a number, then check for an operator letter, then read digits again.
After the operator, if the next key is the same operator, it's the line form.
blocks.solution:
def parse_command(keys):
    i, count = 0, 1
    def number():
        nonlocal i
        j = i
        while i < len(keys) and keys[i].isdigit():
            i += 1
        return int(keys[j:i]) if i > j else 1
    count *= number()
    op = None
    if keys[i] in "dcy":
        op = keys[i]
        i += 1
        count *= number()
        if i < len(keys) and keys[i] == op:
            return count, op, "line"
    return count, op, keys[i]

blocks.html:
The simple way to undo: save a snapshot (a full copy of the text) before every change. Undo = go back one snapshot. It works, and it's terrible for memory: 1,000 edits to a 1 MB file = 1 GB of snapshots.

The better way: save the command and enough to reverse it. "Inserted abc at 10" is undone by "delete 3 characters at 10". "Deleted fox at 16" is undone by "insert fox at 16". Each entry is as small as the edit itself.

blocks.code:
text_size = 100_000
edits = [5, 1, 1, 12, 3]           # characters changed by each edit
print("snapshots:", len(edits) * text_size)
print("commands: ", sum(edits))

blocks.html: Undo pops the last command, applies its inverse and pushes it onto a redo stack. Making a fresh edit clears the redo stack: once you've gone a different way, the old future is gone.

blocks.title: undo_redo
blocks.prompt: Write class Editor with self.text, insert(pos, s), delete(pos, n), undo() and redo(). Store commands as tuples ("insert", pos, s) or ("delete", pos, removed_text) on self.undo_stack; never store a copy of the whole text. A new insert/delete clears the redo stack. Undo/redo with an empty stack does nothing.
blocks.tests:
e = Editor("the fox")
e.insert(4, "quick ")
assert e.text == "the quick fox", "insert works"
e.delete(0, 4)
assert e.text == "quick fox", "delete works"
assert e.undo_stack[-1] == ("delete", 0, "the "), f"the delete command must remember the removed text, got {e.undo_stack[-1:]}"
e.undo()
assert e.text == "the quick fox", "undo puts 'the ' back"
e.undo()
assert e.text == "the fox", "a second undo removes 'quick '"
e.redo()
assert e.text == "the quick fox", "redo re-applies the insert"
e.insert(0, "see ")
e.redo()
assert e.text == "see the quick fox", "a new edit clears the redo stack, so redo does nothing"
e.undo(); e.undo(); e.undo(); e.undo()
assert e.text == "the fox", "extra undos on an empty stack are harmless"
assert all(len(c[2]) < 10 for c in e.redo_stack), "commands store only the changed text, not snapshots"
hints: Write one private _apply(cmd) that performs either kind of command. The inverse of ("insert", p, s) is ("delete", p, s) and vice versa.
A delete must read the text it's about to remove before removing it, and store that in the command.

blocks.html: Vim groups a whole INSERT session (from i to Esc) into one undo step, so u takes back the whole word you typed, not one letter at a time.
/fox jumps to the next fox after the cursor. If there isn't one, vim wraps around to the top. That's two searches: from the cursor to the end, then from the start.
Notice pos + 1: without it, searching again from a match would find the same match forever.

sections.title: Real-world project: a modal note-taking app

blocks.html: Terminal apps like vim, less, htop, tig and lazygit, and "vim mode" in VS Code, Obsidian and Jupyter, all have this core: a buffer, a mode, and a loop that turns each keystroke into a command.

blocks.title: A modal note editor for the terminal
blocks.client: A writer who wants distraction-free notes and keeps reaching for vim keys
blocks.brief: Build the engine of a tiny vim-style notes editor. It reads keystrokes one at a time (exactly what a terminal sends: \x1b for Esc) and updates the text and cursor. It needs INSERT mode for typing, NORMAL mode for moving and deleting, counts like 2dw, and u to undo.
blocks.why: Every interactive program is a loop over input events plus a state machine: terminal UIs, game controllers, form wizards, network protocol parsers. Command-based undo is what Google Docs, Figma and Photoshop's history panel use, because snapshots of big documents don't fit in memory.
milestones: A loop over keys with a mode variable: i/a enter INSERT, \x1b returns to NORMAL
Motions h l 0 $ w move a cursor in NORMAL mode; x deletes under the cursor
d + motion deletes the range the motion covers; counts multiply (2dw)
Every edit pushes an undo command; u pops and reverses it, one INSERT session at a time
Wrap it in a real terminal loop with curses (stretch)
stretch: Add VISUAL mode: v, move, then d deletes the selection
Store the text in your gap buffer instead of a string
Add / search with wrap-around and n for "next match"

blocks.title: run_keys
blocks.prompt: Write run_keys(text, keys) that returns the text after feeding every key in keys to a one-line vim engine, starting in NORMAL mode with the cursor at 0. Support: i (insert before cursor), a (insert after cursor), ESC (back to NORMAL; the cursor steps back one, like vim), h l 0 $ w motions, x (delete under cursor), d + w (delete to next word), counts in front (2dw, 3x) and u (undo the last change; a whole INSERT session is one change). word_forward(text, pos) is given.
blocks.tests:
assert run_keys("hello world", "x") == "ello world", "x deletes under the cursor"
assert run_keys("hello world", "wx") == "hello orld", "w jumps to 'world', x deletes its w"
assert run_keys("hello world", "dw") == "world", f"dw deletes 'hello ', got {run_keys('hello world', 'dw')!r}"
assert run_keys("one two three", "2dw") == "three", "2dw deletes two words"
assert run_keys("hello world", "dwu") == "hello world", "u undoes the dw"
assert run_keys("cat", "$aS" + ESC) == "catS", "$ then a appends after the last character"
assert run_keys("ab", "ixy" + ESC + "u") == "ab", "a whole INSERT session is undone in one u"
assert run_keys("ab", "ixy" + ESC + "x") == "xab", "after ESC the cursor steps back onto the y, so x deletes the y"
assert run_keys("abcdef", "l3x") == "aef", "3x deletes three characters"
assert run_keys("x y", "ixd" + ESC) == "xdx y", "in INSERT mode, d and x are just letters"
hints: Handle INSERT mode first and continue: there, every key except ESC is just typed. Remember where the INSERT session started so ESC can push one undo entry for all of it.
For counts, collect digits into a string (but a 0 with no digits before it is the 0 motion). When you see d, remember the count and wait for the next key, the motion.

blocks.title: GapBuffer
blocks.prompt: From memory, write class GapBuffer(text, size) with buf, gap_start, gap_end, and methods text(), move_to(pos), insert(ch) (grow by doubling when the gap is empty) and backspace().
blocks.tests:
g = GapBuffer("helo", 6)
g.move_to(3)
g.insert("l")
assert g.text() == "hello", f"insert in the middle, got {g.text()!r}"
for c in " world":
    g.move_to(len(g.text()))
    g.insert(c)
assert g.text() == "hello world", "the buffer grows when it runs out of gap"
g.move_to(5)
g.backspace()
assert g.text() == "hell world", "backspace removes the character before the cursor"
assert g.gap_start == 4, "the cursor moved back by one"
hints: Text = everything before the gap + everything after it. Every method only touches gap_start, gap_end and the slots right next to the gap.

blocks.q: Why does a gap buffer make typing fast, why does vim need modes, and why does undo store commands instead of copies?
blocks.a: A gap buffer keeps empty slots at the cursor, so typing just fills the next slot (O(1)); only moving the cursor shifts characters, one per step, and people type in bursts in one place. Modes let plain letters be commands in NORMAL mode and text in INSERT mode; a state machine (mode + key → action/next mode) keeps that straight. Undo stores each edit and how to reverse it (inserted X at p ↔ delete X at p), which costs as much memory as the edit itself, while a snapshot costs the whole document every time.

chapters.title: A web framework
chapters.tagline: HTTP is just text; a framework is a parser, a router and a chain of wrappers around your functions
chapters.part: Part 3 · Tools you use every day
goals: Read and write raw HTTP requests and responses
Build a router that matches patterns like /users/<id> and extracts parameters
Compose middleware so logging and auth live in one place
Explain the order middleware runs in, on the way in and on the way out
Assemble a small JSON API from your own parts

sections.title: What Flask, Express and Django actually do

blocks.html:
When you write @app.get("/users/<id>") in a framework, it feels like magic. Underneath there are only three ideas:

  1. HTTP is text. A request is a few lines: GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1, some Name: value headers, a blank line, maybe a body.
  2. A router maps (method, path pattern) to one of your functions, pulling parameters like 42 out of the path.
  3. Middleware wraps the whole thing in layers. Each layer can look at the request on the way in, stop it, or change the response on the way out.

Send some requests through a tiny framework and watch where each answer comes from.

blocks.name: bx-web
blocks.title: A request's journey
blocks.goal: Get a 200, a 401 and a 404, and notice which stage produced each.
blocks.intro: Each block is a stage of the framework. Click any of them to ask why it exists.

blocks.q: The POST without a token got a 401. Which code produced it?

opts.t: The POST /users handler checked the token
The router
The auth middleware, before the router even ran
The browser

blocks.why: Putting the check in middleware means no handler can forget it. That's the main reason middleware exists: one place for jobs that every request needs (logging, auth, error handling, compression).

blocks.html:
A request, exactly as it arrives (lines end with \r\n on the wire; we'll accept plain \n too):

POST /users HTTP/1.1 Host: shop.test Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "Ida"}

The first line is the request line. Then headers until a blank line. Everything after the blank line is the body.

blocks.code:
raw = "GET /search?q=cats HTTP/1.1
Host: pets.test
Accept: text/html

"
head, _, body = raw.partition("

")
lines = head.split("
")
print(lines[0].split(" "))
print(len(lines) - 1, "headers,", repr(body))

blocks.title: parse_request
blocks.prompt: Write parse_request(raw) returning a dict with "method", "path" (without any ?query), "query" (a dict from a=1&b=2, empty if none), "headers" (a dict with lower-case names) and "body" (a string). Accept \r\n or \n line endings.
blocks.tests:
r = parse_request("POST /users?ref=home HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.test
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "Ida"}")
assert r["method"] == "POST" and r["path"] == "/users", "request line"
assert r["query"] == {"ref": "home"}, "query string"
assert r["headers"]["content-type"] == "application/json", "headers, lower-case names"
assert json.loads(r["body"]) == {"name": "Ida"}, "body"
r = parse_request("GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: x

")
assert r["query"] == {} and r["body"] == "", "no query, no body"
hints: Normalise line endings, then raw.partition("\n\n") separates head from body. The first head line splits on spaces into three parts.
target.partition("?") splits the path from the query string; split the query on &, then each pair on the first =.
blocks.starter:
def parse_request(raw):
    return {"method": "", "path": "", "query": {}, "headers": {}, "body": ""}

blocks.html: Responses are text too: a status line, headers, a blank line, the body. Content-Length tells the client where the body ends.

blocks.title: make_response
blocks.prompt: Write make_response(status, body, content_type="text/plain") returning the response text with \r\n line endings: HTTP/1.1 <status> <reason>, then Content-Type and Content-Length headers, a blank line, and the body. Reasons: 200 OK, 201 Created, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error. Content-Length is the body's length in bytes (UTF-8).
blocks.tests:
r = make_response(404, "nope")
assert r == "HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Length: 4

nope", repr(r)
assert "Content-Length: 6
" in make_response(200, "café!"), "é is two bytes in UTF-8: count bytes, not characters"
hints: len(body.encode("utf-8")) counts bytes. Build the string with f-strings and \r\n.
blocks.starter:
def make_response(status, body, content_type="text/plain"):
    return ""

blocks.html: A route is a method plus a pattern like /users/<id>/orders/<n>. The router compares the path segment by segment: a literal segment must match exactly; a <name> segment matches anything and is captured as a parameter.

blocks.title: Router
blocks.prompt: Write a class Router with add(method, pattern, handler) and match(method, path), which returns (handler, params) for the first route whose method matches and whose pattern has the same number of segments with every literal equal; params maps each <name> to its segment. Return None if nothing matches.
blocks.tests:
r = Router()
home, user, order = (lambda req: "home"), (lambda req: "user"), (lambda req: "order")
r.add("GET", "/", home)
r.add("GET", "/users/<id>", user)
r.add("GET", "/users/<id>/orders/<n>", order)
assert r.match("GET", "/") == (home, {}), "the root"
assert r.match("GET", "/users/42") == (user, {"id": "42"}), "captures id"
assert r.match("GET", "/users/42/orders/7") == (order, {"id": "42", "n": "7"}), "two parameters"
assert r.match("POST", "/users/42") is None, "wrong method"
assert r.match("GET", "/users") is None and r.match("GET", "/cart") is None, "no match"
hints: Store each pattern pre-split into segments. To match, split the path the same way, skip routes with the wrong method or segment count, then compare segment by segment.
Python's for … else: the else runs only if the loop didn't break, which is exactly "every segment matched".

blocks.html:
A handler is a function request → response. A middleware takes a handler and returns a new handler that does something before and/or after calling the original. Stack them and you get layers, like an onion:

app = logging(auth(router_handler))

A request enters logging first, then auth, then the router. The response leaves in the reverse order. That's why a logger on the outside sees the final status of everything, including requests that auth turned away.

blocks.title: Compose middleware
blocks.tests:
trace = []
def tag(name):
    def mw(nxt):
        def h(req):
            trace.append("in " + name)
            res = nxt(req)
            trace.append("out " + name)
            return res
        return h
    return mw
app = compose([tag("log"), tag("auth")], lambda req: "ok")
assert app({}) == "ok" and trace == ["in log", "in auth", "out auth", "out log"], "the first middleware listed is the outermost"

blocks.title: auth_order_bug
blocks.prompt: require_token should answer 401 without calling the handler when the request has no authorization header. Right now the handler runs first (and creates a user!) and only then is the response replaced. Fix it so the handler never runs for unauthenticated requests.
blocks.tests:
created = []
def create_user(req):
    created.append("Ida")
    return (201, "created")
app = require_token(create_user)
assert app({"headers": {}}) == (401, "login required"), "no token: 401"
assert created == [], "the handler must not run without a token"
assert app({"headers": {"authorization": "Bearer abc"}}) == (201, "created"), "with a token it runs"
hints: Check first, and return early. Only call handler(req) once the check has passed.

sections.title: Real-world project: a JSON API for a to-do app

blocks.title: A to-do list API on your own framework
blocks.client: A friend building a phone to-do app who needs a small backend
blocks.brief: Build an App that takes raw HTTP text and returns raw HTTP text. Routes: GET /todos (list), POST /todos (create from a JSON body), GET /todos/<id> (one, or 404). Add middleware for logging every request with its status, and for turning any exception in a handler into a 500 instead of crashing the server. Finally, put it behind a real socket with Python's socketserver and call it with curl.
blocks.why: Every web framework, from Flask to Rails, is this design with more features. Once you've built the parse → middleware → route → handler pipeline yourself, framework docs stop being magic: you know where a decorator plugs in, why middleware order matters, and what "the request object" really is.
milestones: Parse raw requests with parse_request and build responses with make_response
Register the three routes on your Router
Return JSON with the right status codes (200, 201, 404)
Add logging and error-catching middleware with compose
Serve it on a socket and test it with curl
stretch: A decorator API: @app.route("GET", "/todos")
Query parameters: GET /todos?done=true
Static files from a folder, with the right Content-Type

blocks.title: TodoApp
blocks.prompt: Write TodoApp with a method handle(raw) that takes raw request text and returns (status, body_dict_or_list). Support GET /todos (the list, in creation order), POST /todos with a JSON body {"title": ...} (store {"id": n, "title": ..., "done": False} with ids 1, 2, 3, … and return status 201 with it), and GET /todos/<id> (200 with the item, or 404 with {"error": "not found"}). Anything else: 404 with the same error. The helpers parse_request and Router are provided.
blocks.tests:
app = TodoApp()
post = lambda title: app.handle("POST /todos HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

" + json.dumps({"title": title}))
assert post("buy milk") == (201, {"id": 1, "title": "buy milk", "done": False}), "create returns 201 and the item"
post("call mum")
status, items = app.handle("GET /todos HTTP/1.1
Host: x

")
assert status == 200 and [t["title"] for t in items] == ["buy milk", "call mum"], "list in order"
assert app.handle("GET /todos/2 HTTP/1.1

") == (200, {"id": 2, "title": "call mum", "done": False}), "get one"
assert app.handle("GET /todos/9 HTTP/1.1

") == (404, {"error": "not found"}), "missing id: 404"
assert app.handle("DELETE /todos/1 HTTP/1.1

")[0] == 404, "unknown route: 404"
hints: In __init__, register bound methods (self.list, …) on a Router. In handle, parse, match, and call handler(req, **params).
Path parameters are strings: compare str(t["id"]) == id.

blocks.title: match_route
blocks.prompt: From memory: write match_route(pattern, path) returning a dict of parameters if the path matches a pattern like /a/<x>/b/<y>, or None if it doesn't.
blocks.tests:
assert match_route("/users/<id>", "/users/7") == {"id": "7"}, "one param"
assert match_route("/a/<x>/b/<y>", "/a/1/b/2") == {"x": "1", "y": "2"}, "two params"
assert match_route("/a/<x>/b/<y>", "/a/1/c/2") is None, "a literal mismatch"
assert match_route("/", "/") == {}, "the root matches with no params"
assert match_route("/users/<id>", "/users") is None, "segment counts differ"
hints: Split both on / after stripping slashes; different lengths can't match; then compare segment by segment.
blocks.starter:
def match_route(pattern, path):
    pass

blocks.q: Explain what happens inside a web framework between receiving a request and sending a response, and why middleware runs in the order it does.
blocks.a: The server receives text over a socket. A parser turns it into a request: method, path, query, headers and body. The request passes through a stack of middleware: each is a function wrapping the next one, so it can act before (log, check auth, parse JSON) and after (record status, add headers, catch errors). The innermost layer is the router, which matches method and path against patterns, extracts parameters like an id, and calls one handler; no match gives a 404. The handler returns a response, which travels back out through the middleware in reverse, and is turned back into text with a status line, headers and body. The first middleware listed is the outermost, so it sees requests first and responses last, which is why logging goes on the outside and auth goes before the router.

chapters.title: A 3D graphics engine
chapters.tagline: Vectors, a divide by depth, triangles into pixels, and the z-buffer that settles every argument
goals: Use the dot and cross products to get angles and surface normals
Rotate points with a matrix and project them to the screen by dividing by depth
Fill a triangle with pixels using edge functions
Explain why sorting triangles (the painter's algorithm) fails, and fix it with a z-buffer
Shade a surface with Lambert's law and render a cube into a numpy image
chapters.prelude:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

blocks.html: Every 3D game, CAD program and phone map does the same thing millions of times a second: take triangles in 3D, figure out where they land on a flat screen, colour the pixels they cover, and make sure near things hide far things. That last part is harder than it sounds.

blocks.name: bx-raster
blocks.title: From triangles to pixels
blocks.goal: Switch to Crossing cards and find a view where the Painter's algorithm draws the wrong card in front (the z-buffer gets it right).
blocks.intro: Press Step to rasterize one triangle at a time onto the pixel wall. Try Colour: depth to see the z-buffer itself. Click any pixel or vertex to ask why.

blocks.q: The painter's algorithm sorts triangles from far to near and draws them in that order, like a painter covering the background first. When does it fail?

opts.t: When there are more than 100 triangles
When the light is behind the camera
When two triangles cross through each other, so neither is entirely in front
Never; it's what modern GPUs use

blocks.why: Sorting needs one "depth" per triangle, but two crossing triangles are each in front over part of their area. No order can be right. The z-buffer decides per pixel instead, so crossing is no problem.

blocks.html:
Two operations do almost all the geometry in graphics:

  • The dot product a·b = ax·bx + ay·by + az·bz measures how much two directions agree: positive when they point the same way, zero at right angles, negative when opposite. For unit vectors it's the cosine of the angle between them.
  • The cross product a×b gives a vector perpendicular to both. Take two edges of a triangle, cross them, and you get the direction the triangle faces: its normal.

blocks.code:
a = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
b = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0])
print(np.dot(a, b), np.dot(a, a), np.dot(a, -a))
print(np.cross(a, b))

blocks.title: normal
blocks.prompt: Write normal(p0, p1, p2): the unit normal of the triangle with corners p0, p1, p2 (numpy arrays), using the cross product of the edges p1 - p0 and p2 - p0. With counter-clockwise corners (seen from the front), the normal points toward the viewer.
blocks.tests:
a = np.array
assert np.allclose(normal(a([0, 0, 0.0]), a([1, 0, 0.0]), a([0, 1, 0.0])), [0, 0, 1]), "a triangle in the xy plane, counter-clockwise, faces +z"
assert np.allclose(normal(a([0, 0, 0.0]), a([0, 1, 0.0]), a([1, 0, 0.0])), [0, 0, -1]), "swap two corners and it faces the other way"
n = normal(a([0, 0, 0.0]), a([5, 0, 0.0]), a([0, 0, -3.0]))
assert np.isclose(np.linalg.norm(n), 1), "unit length, however big the triangle"
hints: np.cross(p1 - p0, p2 - p0), then divide by its length np.linalg.norm(...).
blocks.starter:
def normal(p0, p1, p2):
    return np.zeros(3)

blocks.html:
To spin a model, multiply every point by a rotation matrix. Turning by angle θ around the vertical (y) axis:

[ cos θ 0 sin θ ] [ 0 1 0 ] [ -sin θ 0 cos θ ]

Why a matrix and not a formula per point? Because matrices compose: "rotate, then tilt, then move" becomes one matrix you multiply every vertex by, and that's exactly what a GPU is built to do fast. With numpy, points @ R.T rotates thousands of points in one line.

blocks.title: rotate_y
blocks.prompt: Fill in the rotation matrix around the y axis, then apply it to an (n, 3) array of points.
blocks.tests:
p = np.array([[1.0, 2.0, 0.0]])
q = rotate_y(p, np.pi / 2)
assert np.allclose(q, [[0, 2, -1]]), f"a quarter turn takes +x to -z and leaves y alone; got {q.round(3)}"
assert np.allclose(rotate_y(p, 2 * np.pi), p), "a full turn changes nothing"
pts = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(50, 3))
assert np.allclose(np.linalg.norm(rotate_y(pts, 0.7), axis=1), np.linalg.norm(pts, axis=1)), "rotation never changes a point's distance from the origin"
hints: Copy the matrix above row by row: [[c, 0, s], [0, 1, 0], [-s, 0, c]].
blocks.starter:
def rotate_y(points, theta):
    c, s = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)
    R = np.array(____)
    return points @ R.T
blocks.solution:
def rotate_y(points, theta):
    c, s = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)
    R = np.array([[c, 0, s], [0, 1, 0], [-s, 0, c]])
    return points @ R.T

blocks.html:
Why do far things look small? Picture rays from your eye through a window to the world. A point twice as far away needs to be twice as far sideways to hit the same spot on the window. So the screen position is the sideways position divided by the depth:

x_screen = f · x / z, y_screen = f · y / z

f is the focal length (zoom). That one division is perspective. Then we map screen coordinates (−1 … 1) to pixel columns and rows; rows count down from the top.

blocks.title: project
blocks.prompt: Write project(p, f, w, h): the camera sits at the origin looking down +z. Return the pixel coordinates (px, py) of 3D point p as floats: first sx = f*x/z, sy = f*y/z, then px = (sx + 1) w / 2 and py = (1 - sy) h / 2 (so +y is up on screen).
blocks.tests:
assert project((0, 0, 5), 1, 100, 100) == (50.0, 50.0), "straight ahead lands in the middle of the screen"
assert project((1, 1, 2), 1, 100, 100) == (75.0, 25.0), "up and to the right lands up and to the right (rows count down)"
a, b = project((1, 0, 2), 1, 100, 100), project((1, 0, 4), 1, 100, 100)
assert a[0] > b[0] > 50, "the same sideways offset looks smaller when it's further away"
hints: Divide by z first; then map −1…1 onto 0…w for columns and flip the rows with 1 - sy.
blocks.solution:
def project(p, f, w, h):
    x, y, z = p
    sx, sy = f * x / z, f * y / z
    return (sx + 1) * w / 2, (1 - sy) * h / 2

blocks.html:
Given a triangle's three corners in pixels, which pixels does it cover? For each edge a → b, the edge function

E(a, b, p) = (b.x − a.x)(p.y − a.y) − (b.y − a.y)(p.x − a.x)

is positive on one side of the line and negative on the other. A pixel is inside when all three edges give the same sign. GPUs do this test for millions of pixels in parallel, because each pixel's test is independent.

blocks.title: Inside or outside?
blocks.tests:
assert inside((0, 0), (10, 0), (0, 10), (2, 2)), "(2,2) is inside"
assert not inside((0, 0), (10, 0), (0, 10), (8, 8)), "(8,8) is beyond the long edge"
assert inside((0, 0), (0, 10), (10, 0), (2, 2)), "works for either winding"
lines: return (e0 >= 0 and e1 >= 0 and e2 >= 0) or (e0 <= 0 and e1 <= 0 and e2 <= 0)

blocks.title: rasterize
blocks.prompt: Write rasterize(a, b, c, w, h): return a (h, w) boolean numpy array that is True for every pixel whose centre (col + 0.5, row + 0.5) is inside the triangle (either winding). edge is defined. Use numpy so it's fast: build arrays of all pixel centres with np.meshgrid.
blocks.tests:
m = rasterize((0, 0), (20, 0), (0, 20), 20, 20)
assert m.shape == (20, 20), "one entry per pixel, rows first"
assert 190 <= m.sum() <= 210, f"half of a 20x20 square is about 200 pixels; got {m.sum()}"
assert m[1, 1] and not m[18, 18], "the corner near (0,0) is in, the far corner is out"
assert rasterize((0, 0), (0, 20), (20, 0), 20, 20).sum() == m.sum(), "winding doesn't matter"
hints: edge works on arrays too: pass p = (xs, ys) where xs, ys = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w) + 0.5, np.arange(h) + 0.5).
blocks.starter:
def rasterize(a, b, c, w, h):
    return np.zeros((h, w), dtype=bool)

blocks.html: Keep a second image the same size as the screen, the depth buffer, filled with infinity. When a triangle wants to colour a pixel, compare its depth there with what's stored. Nearer wins: write the colour and the new depth. Otherwise, skip it. Triangles can now be drawn in any order and crossing surfaces come out right, at the cost of one number per pixel.

blocks.title: zbuffer_bug
blocks.prompt: This plot(img, zbuf, row, col, z, color) should draw a pixel only if it's nearer than what's there. But far triangles keep painting over near ones. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
img, zb = np.zeros((1, 1)), np.full((1, 1), np.inf)
plot(img, zb, 0, 0, 5.0, 1)
plot(img, zb, 0, 0, 9.0, 2)
assert img[0, 0] == 1, "a far pixel (z=9) must not cover a near one (z=5)"
plot(img, zb, 0, 0, 2.0, 3)
assert img[0, 0] == 3 and zb[0, 0] == 2.0, "a nearer pixel (z=2) wins and updates the depth"
hints: The camera looks down +z, so a smaller z is closer to the eye. And the buffer starts at infinity: with >, nothing would ever be drawn.

blocks.html:
A surface facing the light head-on is bright; tilted away, the same light spreads over more area, so it's dimmer; facing away, it's dark. The brightness is the dot product of the unit normal and the unit direction toward the light, clipped at zero:

brightness = max(0, n · l)

blocks.title: A 3D product viewer for an online furniture shop
blocks.client: A furniture start-up that wants customers to spin a table before they buy it
blocks.brief: Build a renderer that turns a list of 3D triangles into an image: rotate the model, project every corner, rasterize each triangle, keep the nearest one per pixel with a z-buffer, and shade it by how much it faces the light. Then render 36 frames turning 10° each and play them as a turntable animation.
blocks.why: This is the pipeline in every GPU, from phones to film render farms, and the same steps run inside three.js, which draws the 3D labs on this site. Product viewers (IKEA, Shopify's 3D models), CAD tools and map apps all depend on it. Writing it once by hand is how graphics programmers learn why the GPU is built the way it is.
milestones: Describe a cube as 12 triangles (2 per face) with corner order facing outward
Rotate it, push it away from the camera, and project every vertex
Rasterize each triangle with interpolated depth and a z-buffer
Shade each triangle with Lambert's law and skip back-facing ones (culling)
Render a 36-frame turntable with flipbook
stretch: Smooth (Gouraud) shading: compute brightness per corner and blend across the triangle
Load a real model from an .obj file (it's just lines of v x y z and f a b c)
Add a second, coloured light

blocks.title: render
blocks.prompt: Write render(tris, w, h). Each item in tris is (pts, value): pts is three (x, y, z) tuples already in pixel coordinates (x = column, y = row, z = depth), and value is the colour number to paint. Return an (h, w) float image (background 0) with a z-buffer so the nearest triangle wins at every pixel. Interpolate z inside a triangle with barycentric weights: wa = edge(b, c, p) / area etc., where area = edge(a, b, c). edge is defined and works on arrays.
blocks.tests:
near = ((0, 0, 1.0), (30, 0, 1.0), (0, 30, 1.0)), 1.0
far = ((0, 0, 5.0), (30, 0, 5.0), (0, 30, 5.0)), 2.0
assert render([far, near], 30, 30)[5, 5] == 1.0, "the near triangle wins even when it's drawn second"
assert render([near, far], 30, 30)[5, 5] == 1.0, "...and when it's drawn first: order doesn't matter any more"
tilted = ((0, 0, 0.0), (30, 0, 10.0), (0, 30, 0.0)), 3.0
flat = ((0, 0, 5.0), (30, 0, 5.0), (0, 30, 5.0)), 4.0
img = render([tilted, flat], 30, 30)
assert img[5, 2] == 3.0 and img[2, 26] == 4.0, "crossing triangles: each wins on its own side of the crossing line, per pixel"
assert render([], 10, 10).sum() == 0, "no triangles, empty picture"
blocks.show:
cube_v = np.array([[x, y, z] for x in (-1, 1) for y in (-1, 1) for z in (-1, 1)], dtype=float)
faces = [(0, 1, 3, 2), (4, 6, 7, 5), (0, 4, 5, 1), (2, 3, 7, 6), (0, 2, 6, 4), (1, 5, 7, 3)]
light = np.array([0.4, 0.6, -0.7]); light /= np.linalg.norm(light)
frames = []
for k in range(36):
    t = k * np.pi / 18
    c, s = np.cos(t), np.sin(t)
    R = np.array([[c, 0, s], [0, 1, 0], [-s, 0, c]]) @ np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, np.cos(0.5), -np.sin(0.5)], [0, np.sin(0.5), np.cos(0.5)]])
    v = cube_v @ R.T + [0, 0, 5]
    tris = []
    for f in faces:
        q = v[list(f)]
        n = np.cross(q[1] - q[0], q[2] - q[0]); n /= np.linalg.norm(n)
        shade = 0.15 + 0.85 * max(0.0, float(-np.dot(n, light)))
        pix = [((x / z + 1) * 40, (1 - y / z) * 40, z) for x, y, z in q]
        tris += [((pix[0], pix[1], pix[2]), shade), ((pix[0], pix[2], pix[3]), shade)]
    frames.append(render(tris, 80, 80))
print("A shaded cube, rendered by YOUR z-buffer:")
flipbook(frames, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1, fps=12)
hints: Barycentric weights wa, wb, wc are all ≥ 0 exactly inside the triangle (for either winding, once you divide by the signed area), and they blend the three corner depths.
blocks.solution:
def render(tris, w, h):
    img = np.zeros((h, w))
    zbuf = np.full((h, w), np.inf)
    xs, ys = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w) + 0.5, np.arange(h) + 0.5)
    p = (xs, ys)
    for (a, b, c), value in tris:
        area = edge(a, b, c)
        if area == 0:
            continue
        wa, wb, wc = edge(b, c, p) / area, edge(c, a, p) / area, edge(a, b, p) / area
        inside = (wa >= 0) & (wb >= 0) & (wc >= 0)
        z = wa * a[2] + wb * b[2] + wc * c[2]
        win = inside & (z < zbuf)
        zbuf[win] = z[win]
        img[win] = value
    return img

blocks.prompt: From memory: write draw_triangle(img, zbuf, a, b, c, value) that paints one triangle (corners in pixel coordinates with depth, either winding) into img with z-buffering, interpolating depth with barycentric weights. Modify img and zbuf in place.
blocks.tests:
img, zb = np.zeros((20, 20)), np.full((20, 20), np.inf)
draw_triangle(img, zb, (0, 0, 3.0), (20, 0, 3.0), (0, 20, 3.0), 1.0)
draw_triangle(img, zb, (0, 0, 9.0), (0, 20, 9.0), (20, 0, 9.0), 2.0)
assert img[3, 3] == 1.0, "the farther triangle (z=9) doesn't cover the nearer one"
assert 150 < (img == 1).sum() < 250, "about half the square is painted"
assert zb[3, 3] == 3.0, "the depth buffer remembers the nearest depth"
hints: Edge functions → barycentric weights → interpolated z → one boolean mask inside & nearer.
