blocks.q: Explain how a search engine finds and ranks documents quickly, and why rare words count for more.
blocks.a: Ahead of time, every document is tokenized (lower-cased, split into words, often stemmed) and an inverted index is built: for each word, a sorted posting list of the documents containing it. A query is tokenized the same way, and only the posting lists for its words are read, so the cost depends on those lists, not on the size of the collection; AND queries intersect sorted lists with two pointers. To rank, each document is scored by TF-IDF: for each query word, how often it appears in the document times log(N / df), where df is how many documents contain it. A word in every document has idf 0 and can't tell documents apart, while a rare word is strong evidence of relevance, so documents win by containing the distinctive query words rather than filler. Real engines add more signals, like links (PageRank), titles and freshness, on top of the same skeleton.

chapters.title: Reliable delivery (how TCP works)
chapters.tagline: The network loses, duplicates and reorders packets; numbers, acks and timers turn that into a perfect stream
goals: Explain why the internet itself is unreliable, and what "end to end" fixes
Detect corruption with a checksum and reorder packets by sequence number
Compare send-and-hope, stop-and-wait and a sliding window
Build a receiver that buffers out-of-order packets and delivers a gap-free stream
Estimate round-trip time and grow a congestion window like TCP does

blocks.html:
When you send data across the internet, it's chopped into packets of about 1500 bytes. Each one is passed from router to router, and any of them may:

  • drop it (its queue was full),
  • corrupt it (a flipped bit on a noisy link),
  • reorder it (two packets took different paths),
  • or duplicate it.

The internet's designers decided not to fix this inside the network: routers stay simple and fast. Instead the two ends fix it, in software. That software is TCP, and this chapter builds its core ideas.

blocks.name: bx-tcp
blocks.title: Getting a message across a lossy link
blocks.goal: Deliver RELIABLE intact over a link losing 20% or more, using the sliding window, faster than stop-and-wait at that loss.
blocks.intro: Pick a protocol, set the loss, and press Send. Click a packet to ask what it carries.

blocks.q: With stop-and-wait, why was the link mostly idle?

opts.t: Because packets were lost
After each packet the sender waits a whole round trip for its ack before sending the next
Because the receiver was slow
Because the checksum takes time to compute

blocks.why: Throughput is at most one packet per round trip. A window of W packets allows W per round trip, which is why TCP's windows can be hundreds of packets on fast, long links.

blocks.html: Every packet carries a checksum: a number computed from its bytes. The receiver recomputes it; if it differs, the packet was damaged, and it's thrown away (and later resent, just like a lost one).

blocks.title: packets
blocks.prompt: Write make_packet(seq, payload) returning bytes: 2 bytes of sequence number (big-endian), 2 bytes of checksum, then the payload. The checksum is the sum of all payload bytes plus seq, modulo 65536. Write parse_packet(packet) returning (seq, payload), or None if the checksum doesn't match.
blocks.tests:
p = make_packet(7, b"hi")
assert p == bytes([0, 7, 0, 7 + 104 + 105]) + b"hi", p
assert parse_packet(p) == (7, b"hi"), "round trip"
damaged = p[:4] + b"ho"
assert parse_packet(damaged) is None, "a changed byte is detected"
assert parse_packet(make_packet(300, b"")) == (300, b""), "empty payload, seq above 255"
hints: n.to_bytes(2, "big") and int.from_bytes(b, "big") convert between numbers and 2-byte fields. sum(payload) adds a bytes object's byte values.

blocks.q: This checksum adds up bytes. Which damage can it miss?

opts.t: One byte changing value
Two bytes swapping places
A byte being removed
The sequence number changing

blocks.why: Addition doesn't care about order, so swapped bytes give the same sum. Real protocols use checksums that mix in position (TCP's own is weak too; Ethernet adds a much stronger CRC underneath).

sections.title: Putting the pieces back in order

blocks.html: Packets arrive in any order, maybe twice. Sequence numbers let the receiver rebuild the original stream.

blocks.title: reassemble
blocks.prompt: Write reassemble(packets, n) where packets is a list of (seq, text) in arrival order (possibly out of order, possibly with duplicates), and n is how many packets the message has (numbered 0 to n−1). Return the joined text, or None if any packet is missing.
blocks.tests:
assert reassemble([(2, "c"), (0, "a"), (1, "b")], 3) == "abc", "out of order"
assert reassemble([(0, "a"), (0, "a"), (1, "b")], 2) == "ab", "a duplicate is harmless"
assert reassemble([(0, "a"), (2, "c")], 3) is None, "packet 1 never arrived"
assert reassemble([], 0) == "", "an empty message"

blocks.html: The simplest reliable protocol: send one packet, wait for its acknowledgement, and if nothing comes back before a timeout, send it again. Repeat for each packet.

Keep resending each packet until it succeeds. Return the list of every sequence number you sent, in order.
hints: An outer loop over the packets, and an inner while True that sends (records) and stops once the channel returns True.

blocks.html: How fast can it go? At most one packet per round-trip time (RTT), however fast the link is.

blocks.code:
packet_bytes = 1500
rtt = 0.1                       # 100 ms, roughly Europe to the US and back
for window in (1, 10, 100):
    print(window, "packets in flight:", round(window * packet_bytes / rtt / 1e6, 2), "MB/s")

blocks.html: With a window, many packets are in flight, so some arrive out of order. The simulation used go-back-N: the receiver throws away anything out of order, and the sender resends from the gap. Real TCP is smarter: the receiver buffers out-of-order packets and hands the application a gap-free stream as soon as the gap fills. It always acknowledges with the next sequence number it still needs (a cumulative ack).

assert r.receive(0, "R") == 3, "0 fills the gap, so 0, 1 and 2 are all delivered"
assert r.delivered == ["R", "E", "L"], r.delivered
assert r.receive(1, "E") == 3 and r.delivered == ["R", "E", "L"], "an old duplicate changes nothing"

sections.title: How long to wait? And how fast to send?

blocks.html:
Two more problems make TCP what it is.

The timeout. Too short and you resend packets that weren't lost; too long and a loss stalls everything. TCP measures the round-trip time continuously and keeps a smoothed average plus a measure of how much it varies, then waits a bit longer than "usual".

Congestion. If every sender blasts at full speed, router queues overflow and everyone's packets get dropped. TCP's congestion control uses AIMD: each round trip without loss, grow the window by 1 packet (additive increase); on a loss, halve it (multiplicative decrease). The result is the sawtooth that has kept the internet from collapsing since 1988.

assert aimd([False] * 5 + [True] + [False] * 2) == [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 3, 4, 5], "the sawtooth"
assert aimd([True, True], start=1) == [1, 1], "never below 1"
hints: Keep one variable for the window. Each step is either w + 1 or max(1, w // 2).

sections.title: Real-world project: reliable file transfer over UDP

blocks.title: A file-transfer tool for a lab's flaky Wi-Fi
blocks.client: A research lab copying sensor logs between machines over a network that drops a lot of packets
blocks.brief: Build send.py and recv.py that copy a file over UDP, which gives you none of TCP's guarantees, and add them yourself: packets with sequence numbers and checksums, cumulative acks, a sliding window, and timeouts. Add a --loss 0.2 option that drops packets on purpose so you can test on a perfect network. Print the throughput and the number of retransmissions at the end.
blocks.why: Writing this makes every line of a TCP diagram concrete. It's also exactly how QUIC (the protocol under HTTP/3) works: reliability rebuilt on top of UDP, in ordinary user-space code, so it can evolve faster than the kernel.
milestones: Packet format with seq, checksum and payload; the receiver drops damaged packets
Stop-and-wait first: correct but slow, with a timing table
A sliding window with cumulative acks and go-back-N on timeout

A buffering receiver; compare throughput at 0%, 10% and 30% loss

Fast retransmit: resend after 3 duplicate acks without waiting for the timer
Selective acknowledgements: tell the sender exactly which packets you have

blocks.title: rtt_estimator
blocks.prompt: Write rto(samples, alpha=0.125, beta=0.25) implementing TCP's timeout rule (RFC 6298) and returning the timeout after processing every round-trip sample. On the first sample r: srtt = r, rttvar = r / 2. On each later sample: first rttvar = (1 − beta) × rttvar + beta × |srtt − r|, then srtt = (1 − alpha) × srtt + alpha × r. The timeout is srtt + 4 × rttvar.
blocks.tests:

assert abs(rto([100, 100, 100, 100]) - (100 + 4 * 50 * 0.75 ** 3)) < 1e-9, "steady RTTs: the timeout shrinks toward the RTT"
jumpy, steady = rto([100, 40, 160, 50, 150]), rto([100, 100, 100, 100, 100])
assert jumpy > steady, "a jumpy network gets a longer, safer timeout"
hints: Keep two variables, set from the first sample, then updated in the order given: rttvar uses the old srtt.

blocks.title: in_order_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write deliver(arrivals) that takes a list of (seq, data) in arrival order and returns (delivered, acks): the data handed to the application in order (buffering anything that arrives early, ignoring duplicates), and the cumulative ack sent after each arrival (the next sequence number still needed).

blocks.q: Explain how TCP delivers a reliable, in-order stream over a network that drops, corrupts and reorders packets.
blocks.a: Every packet carries a sequence number and a checksum. The receiver discards damaged packets, buffers ones that arrive early, delivers data to the application only in order with no gaps, and sends cumulative acknowledgements naming the next sequence number it needs. The sender keeps copies of unacknowledged packets and resends any whose ack doesn't arrive before a timeout; the timeout adapts to a smoothed round-trip time plus four times its variation. Stop-and-wait is reliable but sends one packet per round trip, so TCP keeps a sliding window of many packets in flight. The window's size is set by congestion control: grow by one packet per round trip without loss, halve it on a loss (AIMD), so senders share the network instead of overwhelming it. The network itself stays simple; reliability is built end to end.

chapters.title: Distributed consensus (how Raft works)
chapters.tagline: Five servers, any two can crash, and they still agree on every write, in the same order
chapters.part: Part 7 · Many machines, and machines that learn
goals: Explain why replicated systems need consensus, and why "majority" is the magic word
Run leader election with terms, votes and randomised timeouts
Replicate a log with AppendEntries and its consistency check
Decide when an entry is committed, and apply committed entries to a key-value store
Explain why Raft stops (rather than diverging) when a majority is down

sections.title: One copy is one crash away from gone

blocks.html:
A database on one server loses everything when that disk dies, and is down whenever that server is. So real systems keep copies on several servers. But copies create a new problem: two clients write at the same moment to different servers, a network cable is cut, a server reboots halfway through. Now the copies disagree. Which one is right?

The servers need to agree on one sequence of writes, even while some of them are crashed or unreachable. That's consensus, and the algorithm most systems use for it today (etcd, which runs Kubernetes; Consul; CockroachDB; TiDB) is Raft. It was designed in 2014 to be understandable, and you'll build its core in this chapter.

The whole design rests on one fact: any two majorities of the same group share at least one member. If 3 of 5 servers agreed on something, any later group of 3 includes at least one that remembers it.

blocks.name: bx-raft
blocks.title: Five servers agreeing on a log
blocks.goal: Crash the leader, let the others elect a new one, then make a Client write and get it committed (solid).
blocks.intro: A leader is elected within a second or two. Click any server to crash or restart it; click a message or a log entry to ask what it is.

blocks.q: The network splits five servers into a group of 2 and a group of 3. What happens?

opts.t: Both groups elect a leader and keep accepting writes
Only the group of 3 can elect a leader and commit writes; the group of 2 stalls until the split heals
Neither group can do anything
The group with the old leader keeps working, whatever its size

blocks.why: Winning an election, and committing a write, both need 3 of 5. Only one side can have 3. If the old leader is in the group of 2, it can keep trying, but its writes never commit, and when the network heals it sees the higher term and steps down.

blocks.html:
Raft splits time into numbered terms. Each term starts with an election and has at most one leader. Every message carries its sender's term, and a server that sees a higher term than its own updates its term and becomes a follower at once: that's how a stale leader finds out it's been replaced.

Each server votes at most once per term, first come, first served, with one more condition: it only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. Compare the term of the last entry first (the later term wins); if those are equal, the longer log wins.

blocks.title: up_to_date_bug
blocks.prompt: up_to_date(my_log, last_idx, last_term) should say whether a candidate's log (its length last_idx and the term of its last entry last_term) is at least as up to date as my_log (a list of terms, one per entry). It gives the wrong answer whenever the last terms differ. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
assert up_to_date([1, 1, 1], 2, 2), "shorter, but its last entry is from a later term"
assert not up_to_date([1, 2], 5, 1), "longer, but stuck in an older term"
assert up_to_date([1, 2], 2, 2), "identical"
assert not up_to_date([1, 2], 1, 2), "same last term, but shorter"
assert up_to_date([], 0, 0), "two empty logs"
hints: When the last terms differ, the candidate is up to date only if its last term is the later one.

blocks.title: grant_vote
blocks.prompt:
Write grant_vote(state, term, candidate, last_idx, last_term). state is a dict {"term", "voted_for", "log"} (the log is a list of terms). Follow Raft's rules, updating state in place:

  1. A request from an older term (term < state["term"]) is refused.
  2. A request from a newer term moves this server to that term, with no vote cast yet (voted_for = None).
  3. Grant the vote (and record it) if this server hasn't voted this term, or already voted for this same candidate, and the candidate's log is up to date (use the rule from the last exercise).

Return True if the vote is granted.
blocks.tests:
s = {"term": 1, "voted_for": None, "log": [1, 1]}
assert grant_vote(s, 2, "A", 2, 1) and s["term"] == 2 and s["voted_for"] == "A", "a new term, a fine log: yes"
assert not grant_vote(s, 2, "B", 5, 1), "already voted for A this term"
assert grant_vote(s, 2, "A", 2, 1), "A asking again (a retried request) is fine"
s2 = {"term": 3, "voted_for": None, "log": [1, 3]}
assert not grant_vote(s2, 4, "C", 5, 2) and s2["term"] == 4, "older last term: refused, but the term still moves up"
assert grant_vote(s2, 4, "D", 2, 3), "D's log is as good as ours"
assert not grant_vote(s2, 3, "E", 9, 9), "a stale term is always refused"
hints: Check the term first, then the vote, then the log. state["voted_for"] in (None, candidate) covers both "not voted" and "voted for you already".
blocks.starter:
def grant_vote(state, term, candidate, last_idx, last_term):
    return False

blocks.html: Why do elections usually end in one round? Each follower waits a random timeout (say 150–300 ms) without hearing a leader before it stands. One server nearly always wakes up first and collects its votes before anyone else even starts.

blocks.q: What goes wrong if every server uses exactly the same election timeout?

opts.t: Nothing: the timeout only matters for heartbeats
They all become candidates together, each votes for itself, nobody gets a majority, and this can repeat forever
Two leaders get elected in the same term
The log entries get out of order

blocks.why: A split vote just means a new term and another try, so safety is fine, but the cluster could stay leaderless indefinitely. Randomness breaks the symmetry.

blocks.code:
for n in (3, 4, 5, 6, 7):
    print(n, "servers: majority is", n // 2 + 1, "so it survives", (n - 1) // 2, "crashes")

blocks.html: Four servers survive no more crashes than three, and cost more. That's why clusters almost always have an odd size: 3 or 5, sometimes 7.

Once elected, the leader handles every write: it appends the write to its own log, then sends it to every follower in an AppendEntries message. Each message also says where the new entries go: the index and term of the entry just before them. The follower accepts only if its log has a matching entry there. If not, it says no, and the leader retries one entry earlier, until they find the point where their logs agree.

That one check gives Raft its log matching property: if two logs have an entry with the same index and term, everything up to that point is identical.

blocks.title: The follower's consistency check
blocks.tests:
log = [(1, "x=1"), (1, "x=2"), (2, "x=3")]
assert log_matches(log, 0, 0), "the start always matches"
assert log_matches(log, 3, 2), "entry 3 is from term 2"
assert not log_matches(log, 3, 1), "entry 3 is from term 2, not 1"
assert not log_matches(log, 5, 2), "we don't have entry 5 at all"

blocks.title: append_entries
blocks.prompt:
Write append_entries(log, prev_idx, prev_term, entries) for a follower. log and entries are lists of (term, command); indexes count from 1, and prev_idx = 0 means "from the start". Return (ok, new_log):

  • If the consistency check fails, return (False, log) unchanged.
  • Otherwise place each new entry at index prev_idx + 1, prev_idx + 2, …: if an entry already there has a different term, delete it and everything after it; if it's the same, keep it; append entries the log doesn't have yet.

Don't simply cut the log at prev_idx: a delayed, duplicated message would then delete entries the leader already counted as stored here.
blocks.tests:
log = [(1, "a"), (1, "b")]
assert append_entries(log, 2, 1, [(2, "c")]) == (True, [(1, "a"), (1, "b"), (2, "c")]), "a plain append"
assert append_entries(log, 3, 2, [(2, "d")]) == (False, log), "we don't have entry 3 yet: the leader must step back"
assert append_entries([(1, "a"), (1, "b"), (1, "x"), (1, "y")], 2, 1, [(2, "c")]) == (True, [(1, "a"), (1, "b"), (2, "c")]), "a conflict at entry 3 deletes it and everything after"
full = [(1, "a"), (1, "b"), (1, "c")]
assert append_entries(full, 1, 1, [(1, "b")]) == (True, full), "an old duplicate message deletes nothing"
assert append_entries(log, 0, 0, []) == (True, log), "a heartbeat"
hints: First the check from the parsons puzzle. Then walk the new entries with their position k = prev_idx + i (0-based in the Python list): truncate on a term conflict, append when k is past the end.
blocks.starter:
def append_entries(log, prev_idx, prev_term, entries):
    return False, log

blocks.html:
An entry is committed once the leader has stored it on a majority. From then on it's permanent: any future leader needs votes from a majority, that majority includes a server with the entry, and the up-to-date rule means a server missing it can't win. Only committed entries are applied to the database and reported to clients as done.

There's one subtle extra rule: a leader only commits entries from its own term by counting copies. Older entries become committed along with them. (The Raft paper's Figure 8 shows how counting old-term copies can commit an entry that a later leader then overwrites.)

blocks.title: commit_index
blocks.prompt: Write commit_index(match, log_terms, term). match has one number per server, including the leader: how many entries of the leader's log that server is known to store. log_terms is the term of each entry in the leader's log, and term is the leader's current term. Return the largest k such that more than half the servers have at least k entries and entry k is from the current term, or 0 if there is none.
blocks.tests:
assert commit_index([5, 5, 3, 2, 1], [1, 1, 2, 2, 2], 2) == 3, "3 of 5 servers have entries 1 to 3"
assert commit_index([5, 5, 3, 2, 1], [1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 3) == 0, "entry 3 is on a majority, but it's from an older term"
assert commit_index([5, 5, 5, 1, 1], [1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 3) == 5, "entry 5 is from this term, which commits 1 to 4 too"
assert commit_index([2, 2, 2], [1, 1], 1) == 2
assert commit_index([1], [], 1) == 0, "an empty log"
hints: Try each k from the end of the log down to 1, count how many servers have m >= k, and stop at the first k that passes both checks.
blocks.starter:
def commit_index(match, log_terms, term):
    return 0

blocks.title: apply_committed
blocks.prompt: The log only stores commands; the state machine is what they build. Write apply(log, commit) that runs the first commit entries of log (a list of (term, command)) against an empty dict and returns it. Commands are "set KEY VALUE" and "del KEY" (deleting a missing key does nothing). Uncommitted entries must not be applied.
hints: cmd.split() gives ["set", "x", "1"]. dict.pop(key, None) removes a key if it's there.
blocks.starter:
def apply(log, commit):
    return {}

blocks.html: Because every server applies the same committed entries in the same order, every server ends up with the same database. That's the trick behind every replicated database: agree on the log, and the data follows.

sections.title: Real-world project: a replicated key-value store

blocks.title: A tiny etcd
blocks.client: A team running a small fleet of services that need one reliable place to store configuration and pick a "primary" worker
blocks.brief: Build a 3- or 5-node key-value store in Python where each node is a process with an HTTP or socket API. Nodes run Raft: elections with randomised timeouts, AppendEntries heartbeats, the vote and log rules from this chapter, and a commit index. PUT /key goes to the leader (followers redirect), and returns only once the write is committed. Persist term, voted_for and the log to disk so a restarted node rejoins correctly.
blocks.why: etcd, the store behind every Kubernetes cluster, is exactly this, with a lot of engineering on top. Building it once is the best way to understand what "strongly consistent" costs and why distributed systems fail the way they do.
milestones: Nodes as processes that send JSON messages to each other, with random delays
Leader election with terms and votes; kill the leader and time the recovery
Log replication with the consistency check and nextIndex back-off
Commit index and a state machine; PUT returns after commit
Persistence: kill -9 a node mid-run, restart it, and check it catches up
stretch: A chaos test: randomly kill, restart and partition nodes while a client writes, then check every node's database is identical
Linearizable reads (the leader confirms it's still leader before answering)
Snapshots so the log doesn't grow forever

blocks.title: commit_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write majority_index(match) that returns the largest k stored on more than half the servers, where match[i] is how many log entries server i has (ignore the current-term rule this time). Do it by sorting.
blocks.tests:
assert majority_index([5, 5, 3, 2, 1]) == 3
assert majority_index([1, 1, 1]) == 1
assert majority_index([7, 0, 0]) == 0, "only the leader has anything"
assert majority_index([4, 4, 2, 1]) == 2, "with 4 servers, 3 of them must have it"
hints: Sort from most to fewest. The value at position len // 2 is held by that server and every server before it: len // 2 + 1 servers, a majority.
blocks.starter:
def majority_index(match):
    pass

blocks.q: Explain how Raft keeps five servers agreeing on one log while servers crash and come back.
blocks.a: Time is split into terms, each with at most one leader. Followers that hear nothing from a leader for a random timeout become candidates, start a new term and ask for votes; a server votes once per term, and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date (later last term, or same last term and at least as long). A majority of votes makes a leader, and any higher term seen in a message makes a server step down. The leader appends client writes to its log and sends them in AppendEntries, which also carry the index and term of the preceding entry; a follower rejects a mismatch, and the leader backs up until the logs agree, then the follower's log is overwritten to match. An entry from the leader's current term stored on a majority is committed, and everything before it with it; committed entries are applied to the state machine in order on every server. Because any two majorities overlap and the vote rule refuses out-of-date candidates, every future leader already has every committed entry. With a majority down, nothing can be elected or committed: Raft stays unavailable rather than letting servers diverge.

chapters.title: A tiny GPT (how attention works)
chapters.tagline: Predict the next word, over and over; attention is how each word decides which earlier words matter
chapters.part: Part 7 · Many machines, and machines that learn
goals: Explain a language model as "predict the next token", and generate text by sampling
Build a bigram model and see exactly what it can't do
Split text into tokens with byte-pair encoding
Implement softmax, temperature and scaled dot-product attention in numpy
Add a causal mask and project words into queries, keys and values: one attention head
chapters.prelude:
import math
import random
import numpy as np

sections.title: A language model predicts the next word

blocks.html:
Strip away the hype and a GPT does one thing: given some text, it outputs a probability for every possible next token. To write a paragraph, it picks a token from those probabilities, appends it, and asks again. Everything it "knows" is whatever helps it make that one prediction well.

The simplest model that does this looks only at the last word: count, in a pile of text, which words followed which.

blocks.title: bigrams
blocks.prompt: Write train_bigrams(words) that returns a dict mapping each word to a dict of {next_word: count}. Then write most_likely(counts, word): the most frequent next word (ties: the alphabetically first), or None if the word never had a next word.
blocks.tests:
words = "the cat sat on the mat the cat ran".split()
c = train_bigrams(words)
assert c["the"] == {"cat": 2, "mat": 1}, c["the"]
assert most_likely(c, "the") == "cat"
assert most_likely(c, "cat") == "ran", "a tie between ran and sat: alphabetical"
assert most_likely(c, "ran") is None, "nothing ever followed ran"
hints: zip(words, words[1:]) gives every pair of neighbours. max(sorted(d), key=d.get) returns the first of the tied maximums in sorted order.

blocks.html: A bigram model writes locally plausible nonsense: every pair of words is fine, and the sentence goes nowhere. To finish "the cat chased the mouse because it was …" you need to know that it is the cat, six words back. The model needs a way to look at the whole context and pick out the parts that matter. That's attention.

blocks.name: bx-attention
blocks.title: Where does each word look?
blocks.goal: Pick the word it, switch to attention, and raise the sharpness until more than 60% of its attention goes to one word.
blocks.intro: Each word has a key (what it offers) and a query (what it looks for). Click a word or a block to ask why.

blocks.html: A model's raw outputs are scores (logits) of any size and sign. Softmax turns them into probabilities: exponentiate each, then divide by the total. Bigger scores get exponentially bigger shares.

blocks.title: softmax
blocks.prompt: Write softmax(scores, temperature=1.0) for a 1-D numpy array: divide the scores by the temperature, subtract their maximum (so exp can't overflow), exponentiate, and normalise to sum to 1.
blocks.tests:
p = softmax(np.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.1]))
assert np.allclose(p, np.exp([2, 1, 0.1]) / np.exp([2, 1, 0.1]).sum()) and abs(p.sum() - 1) < 1e-12
assert np.allclose(softmax(np.array([1000.0, 1000.0])), [0.5, 0.5]), "huge scores must not overflow"
assert softmax(np.array([2.0, 1.0]), 0.1)[0] > 0.99, "low temperature: nearly certain"
assert np.allclose(softmax(np.array([5.0, 0.0, -5.0]), 1e6), [1 / 3] * 3, atol=1e-4), "high temperature: nearly uniform"
hints: Subtracting the max doesn't change the result (it cancels when you divide) but keeps every exponent at most 0.
blocks.starter:
def softmax(scores, temperature=1.0):
    return scores

blocks.code:
logits = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]
for t in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
    e = [math.exp(x / t) for x in logits]
    print("temperature", t, [round(v / sum(e), 2) for v in e])

blocks.html: That's the "temperature" setting in every chatbot API. Low: it nearly always picks the top word (safe, repetitive). High: it takes chances (creative, sometimes wrong).

blocks.title: Generating text, one token at a time
blocks.tests:
table = {"a": {"b": 1.0}, "b": {"c": 1.0}, "c": {"a": 1.0}}
nxt = lambda ctx: table[ctx[-1]]
assert generate(nxt, "a", 4, random.Random(0)) == ["a", "b", "c", "a", "b"]
assert generate(nxt, "c", 0, random.Random(0)) == ["c"]
lines: out.append(rng.choices(words, weights=[probs[w] for w in words])[0])

blocks.html: GPTs don't see letters or words but tokens: common chunks like the, ing or hungry. They're found by byte-pair encoding: start from single characters, then repeatedly find the most common adjacent pair and merge it into a new token. After a few thousand merges, frequent words are one token and rare words are a few pieces, so no word is ever "unknown".

blocks.title: byte_pair
blocks.prompt: Write most_common_pair(tokens): the most frequent pair of adjacent tokens (ties: the pair that appears first), or None if there are fewer than 2 tokens. Then write merge(tokens, pair, new): scan left to right and replace each occurrence of the pair with the single token new.
blocks.tests:
t = list("aaabdaaabac")
assert most_common_pair(t) == ("a", "a")
t = merge(t, ("a", "a"), "Z")
assert t == list("ZabdZabac"), t
assert most_common_pair(t) == ("Z", "a"), "a tie with (a, b): (Z, a) comes first"
assert merge(list("aaaa"), ("a", "a"), "Z") == ["Z", "Z"], "no overlapping matches"
assert most_common_pair(["x"]) is None
hints: Counter.most_common keeps first-seen order among ties. In merge, a while loop lets you skip two positions after a match.

blocks.html:
Each word gets three vectors, made by multiplying its embedding by three learned matrices:

  • a query: what am I looking for?
  • a key: what do I contain?
  • a value: what do I pass on if someone looks at me?

A word's score for another word is query · key. Softmax turns its scores into weights, and its output is the weighted sum of the values. With all the words stacked as rows of matrices Q, K and V, that's three lines:

attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d) V

where d is the length of a key, and the softmax runs along each row.

blocks.title: attention
blocks.prompt: Write attention(Q, K, V): Q is (T, d), K is (S, d), V is (S, dv). Compute the scores Q @ K.T / sqrt(d), softmax each row (subtract each row's max first), and return the weights times V, shape (T, dv).
blocks.tests:
Q = np.array([[1.0, 0.0]])
K = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
V = np.array([[10.0, 0.0], [0.0, 10.0]])
e = np.exp(1 / np.sqrt(2))
assert np.allclose(attention(Q, K, V), [[10 * e / (e + 1), 10 / (e + 1)]]), attention(Q, K, V)
assert np.allclose(attention(np.ones((2, 3)), np.zeros((4, 3)), np.arange(8.0).reshape(4, 2)), [[3, 4], [3, 4]]), "equal scores: the plain average of V"
assert attention(np.ones((5, 4)), np.ones((7, 4)), np.ones((7, 3))).shape == (5, 3)
hints: axis=1, keepdims=True keeps a column of row maxima (and row sums) that broadcasts back over each row.
blocks.starter:
def attention(Q, K, V):
    return V
blocks.solution:
def attention(Q, K, V):
    d = Q.shape[1]
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    w = np.exp(scores - scores.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    w = w / w.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return w @ V

blocks.q: Why divide the scores by √d?

opts.t: To make the computation faster
Because keys and queries have different lengths
Dot products of long vectors are large, which would push the softmax to put ~100% on one word and make learning stall
To turn the scores into probabilities

blocks.why: A dot product of d random numbers grows like √d. Dividing by √d keeps scores around the same size whatever d is, so the softmax stays soft enough for gradients to flow during training.

blocks.html: A GPT is trained to predict every next word of a text at once, in parallel. If word 3 could attend to word 4, it could just copy the answer. So each word may only attend to itself and earlier words: a causal mask sets every "future" score to −∞ before the softmax, which makes its weight exactly 0.

blocks.title: causal_bug
blocks.prompt: This masked attention multiplies the future scores by 0 instead of removing them. A score of 0 isn't "no attention": exp(0) = 1, so future words still get weight. Fix it so future positions get a weight of exactly 0.
blocks.tests:
Z = np.zeros((3, 2))
V = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
assert np.allclose(causal_attention(Z, Z, V), [[1], [1.5], [2]]), "word 1 sees only itself; word 2 averages 1 and 2; word 3 all three"
Q = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0], [5.0, 0.0]])
K = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0], [5.0, 0.0]])
assert np.allclose(causal_attention(Q, K, V)[:2], [[1], [1.5]]), "the third word's big key is invisible to earlier words"
hints: np.where(mask == 1, scores, -np.inf) keeps the allowed scores and puts −∞ elsewhere; exp(-inf) is exactly 0. The diagonal is always allowed, so no row is all −∞.
blocks.starter:
def causal_attention(Q, K, V):
    T, d = Q.shape
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    mask = np.tril(np.ones((T, T)))
    scores = scores * mask
    w = np.exp(scores - scores.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    w = w / w.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return w @ V
blocks.solution:
def causal_attention(Q, K, V):
    T, d = Q.shape
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    mask = np.tril(np.ones((T, T)))
    scores = np.where(mask == 1, scores, -np.inf)
    w = np.exp(scores - scores.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    w = w / w.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return w @ V

blocks.html: Where do Q, K and V come from? Each word starts as an embedding vector (a learned row per token), and three learned weight matrices project it: Q = X Wq, K = X Wk, V = X Wv. That's one head. A GPT runs several heads side by side (each learns to look for something different: the subject, the previous word, a matching bracket), then a small feed-forward network, and stacks that block dozens of times. Training adjusts every number by gradient descent to make the next-token predictions better.

blocks.title: attention_head
blocks.prompt: Write self_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv): X is (T, d_model), one row per word; the weight matrices are (d_model, d). Project to queries, keys and values, then return causal scaled dot-product attention, shape (T, d).
blocks.tests:
X = np.eye(3)
out = self_attention(X, np.zeros((3, 2)), np.zeros((3, 2)), np.eye(3))
assert np.allclose(out, [[1, 0, 0], [0.5, 0.5, 0], [1 / 3, 1 / 3, 1 / 3]]), "no preferences: each word averages its past"
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X, Wq, Wk, Wv = rng.normal(size=(5, 4)), rng.normal(size=(4, 3)), rng.normal(size=(4, 3)), rng.normal(size=(4, 3))
out = self_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv)
assert out.shape == (5, 3)
assert np.allclose(out[0], (X @ Wv)[0]), "the first word can only attend to itself"
hints: Three matrix products, then exactly the causal attention from the bug exercise.
blocks.starter:
def self_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    return X
blocks.solution:
def self_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    T, d = Q.shape
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    scores = np.where(np.tril(np.ones((T, T))) == 1, scores, -np.inf)
    w = np.exp(scores - scores.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    w = w / w.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return w @ V

sections.title: Real-world project: train your own tiny GPT

blocks.title: A character-level GPT that writes like your favourite author
blocks.client: Yourself, and anyone who wants to see what's inside a language model instead of taking it on faith
blocks.brief: Take a text of about 1 MB (a public-domain novel, a pile of song lyrics you wrote, your own notes). Build a GPT with character tokens: an embedding table, position embeddings, 4 layers of (multi-head causal attention + feed-forward + residual connections + layer norm), and an output layer to logits. Train it to predict the next character with cross-entropy loss, then sample from it with a temperature.
blocks.why: This is the same architecture as the models behind chatbots, a few million times smaller. After you've watched your own model go from random characters to words to sentences, "AI" stops being magic and becomes a thing you can reason about: what it learns, why it makes things up, and what more data and bigger models change.
milestones: Encode the text as integers and train the bigram model first, as a baseline loss
One attention head over a context of 32 characters; the loss beats the bigram baseline
Multi-head attention, feed-forward layers and residual connections
Training loop with batches and a validation loss; plot both
Sample 500 characters at temperatures 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 and compare
stretch: Replace characters with your own byte-pair tokenizer from this chapter
Visualise one head's attention weights on a sentence
Implement it with only numpy, writing the backward pass by hand

blocks.title: attention_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write causal_attention(Q, K, V) in numpy: scaled dot-product scores, a causal mask with −∞, a numerically stable row-wise softmax, and the weighted sum of values.
blocks.tests:
Z = np.zeros((3, 2))
V = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
assert np.allclose(causal_attention(Z, Z, V), [[1], [1.5], [2]])
Q = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [10.0, 0.0]])
K = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
V2 = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
out = causal_attention(Q, K, V2)
assert np.allclose(out[0], [1, 0]) and out[1][0] > 0.99, "word 2's query matches word 1's key strongly"
hints: Scores, mask, subtract the row max, exp, divide by the row sum, multiply by V.
blocks.starter:
def causal_attention(Q, K, V):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def causal_attention(Q, K, V):
    T, d = Q.shape
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    scores = np.where(np.tril(np.ones((T, T))) == 1, scores, -np.inf)
    w = np.exp(scores - scores.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    w = w / w.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return w @ V

blocks.q: Explain how a GPT predicts the next word, and what attention does inside it.
blocks.a: Text is split into tokens by byte-pair encoding, and each token becomes an embedding vector. The model's job is to output, for every position, a probability for every possible next token; generating text means sampling a token from those probabilities (sharpened or flattened by the temperature), appending it, and repeating. A bigram model only sees the last word; attention lets each word use the whole context. Each word is projected into a query (what it looks for), a key (what it offers) and a value (what it passes on). Its scores against every word are query · key divided by √d, a causal mask removes future words with −∞, a softmax turns the scores into weights, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. Several heads run in parallel, followed by a feed-forward layer, and these blocks are stacked; every weight is learned by gradient descent on next-token prediction.

chapters.title: A blockchain (hashes and proof of work)
chapters.tagline: A ledger anyone can check and nobody can quietly rewrite, built from one hash function
chapters.part: Part 8 · Engines behind the apps you use
goals: Use a cryptographic hash as a fingerprint, and explain the avalanche effect
Link blocks by storing the previous block's hash, and detect tampering
Mine a block by searching for a nonce, and estimate how long it takes
Summarise many transactions in one Merkle root
Pick the valid chain with the most work, and replay it into balances

sections.title: A ledger with no one in charge

blocks.html:
A bank keeps one ledger, and you trust the bank not to edit it. What if a group of strangers has to share one ledger, nobody is in charge, and some of them would happily cheat? Everyone can keep a copy, but then two questions remain: how do you notice if someone changes an old entry, and when copies disagree, which one wins?

A blockchain answers both with one tool, the cryptographic hash: a function that turns any input into a short fingerprint (SHA-256 gives 64 hex digits). Three properties make it useful:

  • the same input always gives the same fingerprint;
  • changing one character changes the whole fingerprint unpredictably (the avalanche effect);
  • nobody knows how to find an input that gives a chosen fingerprint, except by trying inputs one at a time.

The same idea, without the mining, protects Git commits (chapter 8), certificate-transparency logs and many audit logs.

blocks.name: bx-chain
blocks.title: Five blocks, each locked to the one before
blocks.goal: Tamper with an old block, then mine your way back to a fully valid chain.
blocks.intro: Each block shows its data and nonce; the blue bar under it is its hash. Click anything to ask what it is.

blocks.q: In the linked chain, you change the data in block 1 of 5. How many blocks must you re-mine to make the chain valid again?

opts.t: Only block 1
Only blocks 1 and 2
Blocks 1, 2, 3 and 4: the changed block and every block after it
All five, including the genesis block

blocks.why: Block 1's hash changes, so block 2's stored "previous hash" is wrong; fixing it changes block 2's hash, which breaks block 3, and so on to the end. Blocks before the change are untouched.

blocks.code:
from hashlib import sha256
a = sha256(b"Ana pays Ben 5").hexdigest()
b = sha256(b"Ana pays Ben 6").hexdigest()
print(len(a), len(b))
print(a == b, a[:8] == sha256(b"Ana pays Ben 5").hexdigest()[:8])
print(16 ** 4)

blocks.html: The last line is how many hashes you'd expect to try before one starts with four zeros: each hex digit is 0 with chance 1 in 16.

blocks.title: block_hash
blocks.prompt: Write block_hash(index, prev, data, nonce) that returns the SHA-256 hex digest of the text "{index}|{prev}|{data}|{nonce}", encoded as UTF-8. Every field is part of the input, so changing any one of them changes the hash.
blocks.tests:
h = block_hash(1, "00ab", "Ana pays Ben 5", 7)
assert h == hashlib.sha256(b"1|00ab|Ana pays Ben 5|7").hexdigest()
assert len(h) == 64, "64 hex digits"
assert block_hash(1, "00ab", "Ana pays Ben 5", 8) != h, "a different nonce, a different hash"
assert block_hash(1, "00ac", "Ana pays Ben 5", 7) != h, "a different previous hash, a different hash"
hints: hashlib.sha256(some_bytes).hexdigest(); turn a string into bytes with .encode("utf-8").
blocks.starter:
def block_hash(index, prev, data, nonce):
    pass

blocks.html:
Anyone can compute a hash in a microsecond, so a chain of hashes alone stops nobody: a cheater would just recompute every hash after their change. Proof of work makes each block expensive. A block counts only if its hash starts with difficulty zeros, and the only way to get one is to change a number in the block, the nonce, and try again, and again.

Checking the work takes one hash. Doing it takes about 16<sup>difficulty</sup>. That asymmetry is the whole trick.

blocks.title: Search for a nonce
blocks.setup:
def block_hash(index, prev, data, nonce):
    return hashlib.sha256(f"{index}|{prev}|{data}|{nonce}".encode()).hexdigest()
blocks.tests:
n, h = mine(1, "0" * 64, "hi", 3)
assert h.startswith("000") and h == block_hash(1, "0" * 64, "hi", n)
assert all(not block_hash(1, "0" * 64, "hi", k).startswith("000") for k in range(n)), "the first nonce that works"

blocks.title: make_chain
blocks.prompt: Blocks are dicts {"index", "prev", "data", "nonce", "hash"}. Write make_chain(datas, difficulty) that mines one block per item of datas and returns the list. Block 0's prev is 64 zeros; every other block's prev is the hash of the block before it. mine and block_hash are ready for you.
blocks.tests:
c = make_chain(["genesis", "Ana->Ben:5", "Ben->Cy:2"], 2)
assert len(c) == 3 and c[0]["prev"] == "0" * 64
assert c[1]["prev"] == c[0]["hash"] and c[2]["prev"] == c[1]["hash"], "each block points at the one before"
assert all(b["hash"].startswith("00") for b in c), "every block has its proof of work"
assert c[2]["hash"] == block_hash(2, c[2]["prev"], "Ben->Cy:2", c[2]["nonce"])
hints: Keep a variable prev, start it at "0" * 64, and set it to each new block's hash after you append the block.
blocks.solution:
def make_chain(datas, difficulty):
    chain = []
    prev = "0" * 64
    for i, data in enumerate(datas):
        nonce, h = mine(i, prev, data, difficulty)
        chain.append({"index": i, "prev": prev, "data": data, "nonce": nonce, "hash": h})
        prev = h
    return chain

blocks.title: valid_chain_bug
blocks.prompt: valid_chain(chain, difficulty) should return True only if every block's stored hash is correct, starts with enough zeros, and links to the block before it. It accepts a forged chain where block 1's data was changed and re-mined but the blocks after it were left alone. Find the missing check and add it.
blocks.tests:
good = build(["g", "a", "b", "c"], 2)
assert valid_chain(good, 2), "an honest chain"
forged = [dict(b) for b in good]
forged[1]["data"] = "a, plus 500 for me"
forged[1]["nonce"], forged[1]["hash"] = mine(1, forged[1]["prev"], forged[1]["data"], 2)
assert not valid_chain(forged, 2), "block 2 still points at block 1's old hash"
lazy = [dict(b) for b in good]
lazy[2]["data"] = "x"
assert not valid_chain(lazy, 2), "changed but not re-mined: the stored hash is wrong"
hints: Each block also stores prev. Compare it with the hash of the block before it (skip block 0).

blocks.title: first_broken
blocks.prompt: An auditor wants to know where a chain went wrong, not just whether it did. Write first_broken(chain, difficulty) that returns the index of the first block that fails any of the three checks (correct stored hash, enough zeros, links to the previous block), or None if the whole chain is valid.
blocks.tests:
c = build(["g", "a", "b", "c", "d"], 2)
assert first_broken(c, 2) is None
c2 = [dict(b) for b in c]; c2[3]["data"] = "evil"
assert first_broken(c2, 2) == 3, "block 3's stored hash no longer matches its data"
assert first_broken(c, 3) in (0, 1, 2, 3, 4), "mined for difficulty 2, so most blocks fail difficulty 3"
assert first_broken([], 2) is None, "an empty chain has nothing wrong with it"

blocks.html: A real block holds thousands of transactions. Instead of hashing them all as one long string, Bitcoin builds a Merkle tree: hash each transaction, then hash pairs of hashes, then pairs of those, until one hash is left, the Merkle root, which goes in the block. A phone wallet can then check that one transaction is in a block with just a handful of hashes (one per level) instead of downloading the whole block.

blocks.title: merkle_root
blocks.prompt:
Write merkle_root(txs) for a non-empty list of strings. Use h(s) = sha256(s.encode()).hexdigest():

  1. The first level is [h(tx) for tx in txs].
  2. While more than one hash remains: if the level has an odd length, repeat its last hash; then replace each pair a, b with h(a + b).
  3. Return the one hash left.
blocks.tests:
h = lambda s: hashlib.sha256(s.encode()).hexdigest()
assert merkle_root(["a"]) == h("a"), "one transaction is its own root"
assert merkle_root(["a", "b"]) == h(h("a") + h("b"))
ab, cc = h(h("a") + h("b")), h(h("c") + h("c"))
assert merkle_root(["a", "b", "c"]) == h(ab + cc), "an odd level repeats its last hash"
assert merkle_root(["a", "b", "c"]) != merkle_root(["a", "c", "b"]), "order matters"
hints: Each loop pass halves the level. range(0, len(level), 2) walks the pairs.

blocks.html:
Two miners can find a block at almost the same moment, so the network briefly has two different chains. Every node follows the same rule: among valid chains, keep the one with the most work (with a fixed difficulty, the longest). The tie soon breaks, because the next block lands on one side, and everyone switches to that side.

This is why rewriting history is so hard. To replace a block 6 deep, a cheater must re-mine those 6 blocks and overtake the honest miners, who keep extending their chain all the while. With less than half the network's computing power, the chance of ever catching up shrinks exponentially with depth.

blocks.title: choose_chain
blocks.prompt: Write choose_chain(chains, is_valid) that returns the longest chain for which is_valid(chain) is True. If two valid chains have the same length, keep the one that came first in chains (a node doesn't switch on a tie). Return None if no chain is valid.
blocks.tests:
ok = lambda c: "X" not in c
assert choose_chain([["a"], ["a", "b", "c"], ["a", "b"]], ok) == ["a", "b", "c"]
assert choose_chain([["a", "b", "X", "d"], ["a", "b"]], ok) == ["a", "b"], "a longer chain doesn't help if it's invalid"
assert choose_chain([["a", "p"], ["a", "q"]], ok) == ["a", "p"], "on a tie, keep the first"
assert choose_chain([["X"]], ok) is None
hints: Strictly greater (>) is what keeps the first chain on a tie.

blocks.title: balances
blocks.prompt: The chain only stores transactions; the balances are what you get by replaying them in order, like the state machine in the Raft chapter. Write balances(txs, start) where each transaction is "Ana->Ben:5" and start is a dict of opening balances. Apply them in order to a copy of start; skip (don't apply) any transaction whose sender can't afford it. Return (balances, skipped), where skipped lists the skipped transaction strings.
blocks.tests:
b, s = balances(["Ana->Ben:5", "Ben->Cy:2"], {"Ana": 10})
assert b == {"Ana": 5, "Ben": 3, "Cy": 2} and s == []
b, s = balances(["Ben->Cy:1", "Ana->Ben:4", "Ben->Cy:1"], {"Ana": 4})
assert s == ["Ben->Cy:1"] and b == {"Ana": 0, "Ben": 3, "Cy": 1}, "Ben can't pay until Ana has paid him"
start = {"Ana": 1}
balances(["Ana->Ben:1"], start)
assert start == {"Ana": 1}, "don't change the caller's dict"
hints: "Ana->Ben:5".split(":") gives ["Ana->Ben", "5"], and "Ana->Ben".split("->") gives the two names.
blocks.starter:
def balances(txs, start):
    return dict(start), []
blocks.solution:
def balances(txs, start):
    bal, skipped = dict(start), []
    for tx in txs:
        who, amount = tx.split(":")
        src, dst = who.split("->")
        amount = int(amount)
        if bal.get(src, 0) < amount:
            skipped.append(tx)
            continue
        bal[src] -= amount
        bal[dst] = bal.get(dst, 0) + amount
    return bal, skipped

blocks.html: Real coins add one more ingredient: digital signatures. Each transaction is signed with the sender's private key, and everyone checks it with their public key, so nobody can spend someone else's coins even though the ledger is public. The hashing and the work you built here are what stop anyone from rewriting the history afterwards.

blocks.q: Why does a blockchain need proof of work at all, if the hash links already reveal tampering?

opts.t: To make the hashes longer
To encrypt the transactions so nobody can read them
Because a cheater could otherwise recompute every hash after their change in a moment; the work makes each rewritten block expensive
Because SHA-256 is slow

blocks.why: The links make a change visible unless the cheater rebuilds everything after it. Without proof of work that rebuild is instant. With it, every block costs as much work as the honest network spent on it, and the honest network keeps going.

sections.title: Real-world project: a tamper-evident audit log

blocks.title: A tamper-evident audit log for a clinic's records
blocks.client: A small clinic that must prove to an inspector that nobody edited or deleted old access records
blocks.brief: Build an append-only audit log in Python: each line is a JSON record (who, what, when) plus the hash of the previous line, and the hash of itself. Write a log.py append command, a log.py verify command that reports the first broken line, and a daily "anchor": the latest hash, printed or emailed somewhere the clinic can't edit, so even rewriting the whole file is caught. No mining needed: here the anchor plays the role of proof of work.
blocks.why: This is how certificate-transparency logs, Git and many compliance systems work: a hash chain makes edits evident, and publishing the latest hash somewhere independent makes a silent rewrite impossible.
milestones: Append a record with its previous hash and its own hash
Verify the whole file and print the first line that fails
Anchor: save the head hash daily and check the log against every saved anchor
A test that edits, deletes and reorders lines and checks each is caught
stretch: A Merkle tree over each day's records, so one record can be proved without revealing the others
Sign each anchor with an Ed25519 key (cryptography package)

blocks.title: append_record
blocks.prompt: Write append_record(log, record) for the audit log. log is a list of dicts {"record", "prev", "hash"}. Add a new entry whose prev is the last entry's hash (or "start" for the first), and whose hash is the SHA-256 hex digest of prev + "|" + record. Return the new entry (and append it to log).
blocks.tests:
log = []
e = append_record(log, "dr_li viewed file 12")
assert e["prev"] == "start" and log == [e]
assert e["hash"] == hashlib.sha256(b"start|dr_li viewed file 12").hexdigest()
e2 = append_record(log, "nurse_o edited file 12")
assert e2["prev"] == e["hash"] and len(log) == 2
hints: log[-1]["hash"] if log else "start" picks the previous hash.

blocks.title: audit
blocks.prompt: Write audit(log, anchor=None) that returns the index of the first entry whose prev or hash is wrong, or None if the log checks out. If anchor is given (a hash published earlier), also check that some entry has exactly that hash; if none does, history was rewritten, so return len(log).
blocks.tests:
def add(log, r):
    p = log[-1]["hash"] if log else "start"
    log.append({"record": r, "prev": p, "hash": hashlib.sha256((p + "|" + r).encode()).hexdigest()})
log = []
for r in ["a", "b", "c", "d"]: add(log, r)
assert audit(log) is None
anchor = log[1]["hash"]
assert audit(log, anchor) is None, "the anchor is still in the log"
edited = [dict(e) for e in log]; edited[2]["record"] = "z"
assert audit(edited) == 2
gone = log[:1] + log[2:]
assert audit(gone) == 1, "a deleted entry breaks the next link"
fresh = []
for r in ["a", "x", "c", "d"]: add(fresh, r)
assert audit(fresh) is None and audit(fresh, anchor) == 4, "rebuilt from scratch: only the anchor catches it"
hints: Walk the log keeping the hash you expect as prev. The anchor check is one all(...) after the loop.

blocks.q: Explain how a blockchain lets strangers share a ledger that nobody can quietly rewrite.
blocks.a: Each block holds its data, the hash of the previous block and a nonce, and its own hash covers all three. Because a hash changes completely when any input changes, editing an old block changes its hash, which breaks the link stored in the next block, and so on to the end: tampering is visible. Proof of work makes repairing it expensive: a block only counts if its hash starts with a number of zeros, which takes about 16^d tries to find but one hash to check. So a cheater must redo the work for the changed block and every block after it. Nodes keep the valid chain with the most work, and honest miners keep extending theirs, so a cheater with less than half the computing power falls further behind; the chance of rewriting a block k deep shrinks exponentially in k. Merkle roots summarise a block's transactions in one hash, balances come from replaying the transactions in order, and signatures (not built here) prove who authorised each payment.

chapters.title: A spreadsheet engine
chapters.tagline: Type a number, and every formula that depends on it updates, in the right order, instantly
chapters.part: Part 8 · Engines behind the apps you use
goals: Parse which cells a formula reads, and evaluate it
Model a sheet as a dependency graph
Recalculate in topological order, touching only the cells that changed
Detect circular references instead of looping forever
Expand ranges like A1:B3 for functions such as SUM

blocks.html:
More people program in spreadsheets than in every other language combined: every =B2*C2 is a little program. Behind the grid sits an engine with one job. When you change a cell, work out which other cells depend on it, and recompute them in an order where every cell comes after the cells it reads. Get the order wrong and the sheet shows wrong numbers; recompute everything and a big sheet gets slow.

That problem, "update what depends on a change, in the right order", is everywhere: build tools (make, Bazel) rebuild only the files affected by an edit, React re-renders only components whose inputs changed, and package managers install dependencies before the packages that need them. You'll build it here with a 3 × 3 sheet.

blocks.name: bx-sheet
blocks.title: Recalculating a sheet when A1 changes
blocks.goal: Change A1 in naive mode and spot the wrong numbers, then switch to dependency order and get every cell right.
blocks.intro: The lines show which cells each formula reads. Click a cell to see its formula and its correct value.

sections.title: Which cells does a formula read?

blocks.title: refs
blocks.prompt: Write refs(formula) that returns the cell names a formula reads, in the order they first appear, without repeats, in upper case. A cell name is one or more letters followed by one or more digits. Formulas start with =; anything else is a plain value that reads nothing.
blocks.tests:
assert refs("=A1+B2*2") == ["A1", "B2"]
assert refs("=a1*A1+c10") == ["A1", "C10"], "case-insensitive, no repeats"
assert refs("=AB12/2") == ["AB12"], "column AB"
assert refs("42") == [], "a plain number"
assert refs("=3*4") == []
hints: re.findall(r"[A-Za-z]+[0-9]+", formula) finds every name; then upper-case and skip ones already in the list.
blocks.starter:
def refs(formula):
    return []

blocks.title: evaluate
blocks.prompt: Write evaluate(formula, values). If formula doesn't start with =, return it as a float. Otherwise replace every cell name (as in refs, any case) with that cell's value from values (a dict like {"A1": 10.0}), and compute the arithmetic with Python's eval. Pass {"__builtins__": {}} as globals so a formula can't call anything dangerous.
blocks.tests:
assert evaluate("7", {}) == 7.0
assert evaluate("=A1*2+b1", {"A1": 10.0, "B1": 1.0}) == 21.0
assert evaluate("=(A1+A2)/2", {"A1": 3.0, "A2": 4.0}) == 3.5
try:
    evaluate("=__import__('os')", {})
    assert False, "builtins must be unavailable"
except (NameError, TypeError, KeyError):
    pass
hints: re.sub(pattern, lambda m: repr(values[m.group().upper()]), text) swaps each name for its number.

blocks.html: Reading order (left to right, top to bottom) is the obvious order, and it's wrong whenever a formula reads a cell that comes later. The fix is to treat the sheet as a graph: an arrow from each cell to every formula that reads it. You need an order where every arrow points forwards: a topological order.

blocks.title: A topological order by depth-first search
blocks.tests:
deps = {"C1": ["B3", "B1"], "B1": ["A1"], "B3": ["A2"], "A2": ["B2"], "B2": ["A1"], "A1": []}
o = topo_order(deps)
assert all(o.index(d) < o.index(c) for c in deps for d in deps[c]), "every cell after the cells it reads"
assert sorted(o) == sorted(deps)

blocks.html: deps maps each cell to the cells it reads. Visiting what a cell reads before appending the cell itself puts every cell after its inputs.

blocks.title: recalc_order_bug
blocks.prompt: recalc_all(formulas) recomputes every formula cell, but it visits them in the dict's order (reading order), so cells that read a later cell come out wrong. topo_order(deps) from the puzzle is ready for you. Make recalc_all compute the cells in dependency order instead.
blocks.tests:
sheet = {"A1": "10", "B1": "=A1*2", "C1": "=B3+B1", "A2": "=B2+1", "B2": "=A1+5", "A3": "3", "B3": "=A2*A3"}
v = recalc_all(sheet)
assert v["B2"] == 15 and v["A2"] == 16, "A2 reads B2, which comes after it"
assert v["B3"] == 48 and v["C1"] == 68, "C1 reads B3, from the bottom row"
hints: Build deps = {cell: refs(f) for cell, f in formulas.items()} and loop over topo_order(deps) instead of formulas.

blocks.html: Recomputing every cell is correct but slow on a sheet with a million cells, when you changed one. The engine keeps the reverse graph too: for each cell, the formulas that read it. After an edit it collects every cell downstream of the change, and recomputes only those, in topological order.

blocks.prompt: Write dependents(deps, cell) that returns the set of every cell that reads cell directly or indirectly (not including cell itself, unless it's on a cycle). deps maps each cell to the list of cells it reads.

blocks.html: If B3 reads C3 and C3 (through a chain) reads B3, there is no topological order: some cell would have to be computed before itself. A spreadsheet must spot this and show an error (#CYCLE, or Excel's circular reference warning) instead of recursing forever.

blocks.title: find_cycle
blocks.prompt: Write has_cycle(deps) that returns True if the dependency graph contains a cycle. Use depth-first search with three states per cell: not visited, on the current path, and finished. Reaching a cell that's on the current path means you've gone round a loop. Cells that appear only in someone's list have no dependencies of their own.
blocks.tests:
assert not has_cycle({"B1": ["A1"], "C1": ["A1", "B1"]}), "a diamond is not a cycle"
assert has_cycle({"A1": ["A1"]}), "a cell reading itself"
assert has_cycle({"B3": ["C3"], "C3": ["C2"], "C2": ["C1"], "C1": ["B3"]})
assert not has_cycle({}), "an empty sheet"
hints: A cell you finished earlier ("done") is safe to meet again: that's a diamond, not a loop. Only "path" means a cycle.

blocks.q: Why does the engine need the three states ("on the path" vs "finished") rather than just "visited"?

opts.t: To make it faster
Because meeting a finished cell again is normal (two formulas can read the same cell), while meeting a cell on the current path means a loop
Because cells can have three values
It doesn't: "visited" is enough

blocks.why: With only "visited", the diamond B1 → A1, C1 → A1 and B1 would look like a cycle when C1's search reaches A1 a second time. A cycle is only a cell that's still waiting for its own inputs.

blocks.q: Explain how a spreadsheet engine updates the sheet after you edit one cell.
blocks.a: Each formula's cell references are parsed out, giving a dependency graph: an edge from each cell to every formula that reads it. After an edit, the engine collects every cell downstream of the changed one (walking the reverse edges), then recomputes those cells in a topological order, so every cell is computed after all the cells it reads; cells not downstream keep their values. Computing in plain reading order would use stale values whenever a formula reads a later cell, and recomputing everything is correct but wastes time on big sheets. If the graph has a cycle there is no topological order, so a depth-first search with "on the current path" and "finished" states detects it and the cells involved show an error instead of looping. Ranges like A1:B3 expand to lists of cells, which become ordinary dependencies of functions like SUM.

chapters.title: A ray tracer
chapters.tagline: For every pixel, ask "what does this see?", and shadows and mirrors come almost for free
chapters.part: Part 8 · Engines behind the apps you use
goals: Turn a pixel into a ray from the camera
Intersect a ray with a sphere by solving a quadratic
Shade a point with Lambert's cosine law
Cast shadow rays and reflection rays, and count what they cost
Render a whole image (as text) from these pieces

sections.title: Two ways to draw a picture

blocks.html:
In chapter 11 you built a rasterizer: take each triangle, project it onto the screen, fill its pixels. That's how games draw 60 frames a second. But a triangle drawn on its own knows nothing about the rest of the scene, so shadows, mirrors and glass all have to be faked with tricks.

A ray tracer turns the question around. For every pixel it asks: if I look through this pixel, what do I see? It shoots a ray from the camera through the pixel, finds the first object it hits, and works out that point's colour. Need to know if the point is in shadow? Shoot another ray toward the light. Is the object a mirror? Shoot another ray in the mirrored direction. Every film studio renders this way, and modern GPUs have hardware for it.

The vectors in this chapter are plain tuples (x, y, z), with add, sub, mul, dot, length and norm (scale to length 1) ready in the prelude.

blocks.name: bx-ray
blocks.title: One ray per pixel
blocks.goal: Turn on shadows, then click a pixel that's in shadow to see which object blocks the light.
blocks.intro: The picture renders one row at a time. Click any pixel to follow its ray.

blocks.html: The dot product of two length-1 vectors is the cosine of the angle between them: 1 when they point the same way, 0 at right angles, −1 when opposite. Ray tracing uses it everywhere.

blocks.code:
up = (0, 1, 0)
print(dot(up, up), dot(up, (1, 0, 0)), dot(up, (0, -1, 0)))
d = norm((1, 1, 0))
print(round(length(d), 3), round(dot(d, up), 3))

blocks.html:
A ray is a start point o and a direction d (length 1); its points are o + t·d for t ≥ 0. A sphere is every point at distance r from its centre c. Put the ray into the sphere's equation and you get a quadratic in t:

t² + 2 (oc · d) t + (oc · oc − r²) = 0, where oc = o − c.

With b = oc · d and k = oc · oc − r², the roots are t = −b ± √(b² − k). A negative b² − k means the ray misses. The smaller positive root is where it enters the sphere.

blocks.title: ray_sphere
blocks.prompt: Write ray_sphere(o, d, c, r) that returns the distance t to the nearest point where the ray hits the sphere, or None if it misses. d has length 1. Only count hits in front of the ray (t > 1e-6): if the smaller root is behind the start but the larger isn't (the ray starts inside the sphere), return the larger.
blocks.tests:
assert abs(ray_sphere((0, 0, -5), (0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 0), 1) - 4) < 1e-9, "straight at it: enters at distance 4"
assert ray_sphere((0, 0, -5), (0, 0, -1), (0, 0, 0), 1) is None, "pointing away"
assert ray_sphere((0, 2, -5), (0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 0), 1) is None, "passes above it"
assert abs(ray_sphere((0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 0), 2) - 2) < 1e-9, "from inside, it exits at the far side"
hints: Compute b, k and disc = b*b - k. Try -b - sqrt(disc) first, then -b + sqrt(disc).
blocks.starter:
def ray_sphere(o, d, c, r):
    return None

blocks.title: closest_hit
blocks.prompt: A scene is a list of spheres (centre, radius). Write closest_hit(o, d, spheres) that returns (t, i): the distance to the nearest hit and the index of the sphere hit, or None if the ray hits nothing. Nearer objects hide farther ones: that's the whole visibility problem, solved by one min. ray_sphere is ready for you.
blocks.tests:
scene = [((0, 0, 10), 1), ((0, 0, 5), 1), ((5, 0, 5), 1)]
t, i = closest_hit((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), scene)
assert i == 1 and abs(t - 4) < 1e-9, "the sphere at z=5 is in front of the one at z=10"
assert closest_hit((0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), scene) is None
assert closest_hit((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), []) is None
hints: Keep best = None, and replace it whenever a hit is nearer.

blocks.html:
A surface facing a light head-on is brightest; tilted away, the same light spreads over more area, so it's dimmer. The brightness is the cosine of the angle between the surface normal n (the direction the surface faces, length 1) and the direction to the light: max(0, n · l). Facing away gives a negative cosine, which means no light at all.

For a sphere, the normal at point p is norm(p − c).

blocks.title: lambert

blocks.tests:

assert lambert((0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, -5, 0)) == 0, "the light below a floor that faces up"
assert abs(lambert((0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (3, 3, 0)) - math.cos(math.pi / 4)) < 1e-9, "45 degrees"
hints: Direction to the light: norm(sub(light, p)).

    return 0

blocks.html:
To know whether a point is lit, ask the scene: does anything sit between this point and the light? Shoot a shadow ray from the point toward the light. If it hits something closer than the light, the point is in shadow. Two details make or break this:

  • Start the shadow ray a tiny step off the surface (along the normal). Starting exactly on it, rounding errors make the ray hit its own surface and you get speckled "shadow acne".
  • Only blockers between the point and the light count. Something behind the light casts no shadow here.

blocks.title: in_shadow_bug
blocks.prompt: in_shadow(p, n, light, spheres) should return True when an object blocks the light. It already steps off the surface, but it reports shadows from objects that are behind the light, which makes a whole lit wall go dark. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
floor_pt, up, lamp = (0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 4, 0)
assert in_shadow(floor_pt, up, lamp, [((0, 2, 0), 0.5)]), "a ball between the floor and the lamp"
assert not in_shadow(floor_pt, up, lamp, [((0, 8, 0), 1)]), "a ball above the lamp casts no shadow here"
assert not in_shadow(floor_pt, up, lamp, [((3, 2, 0), 0.5)]), "a ball off to the side"
hints: The light is length(to_light) away. A hit only blocks it if it's nearer than that.

blocks.q: A scene has 4 lights and is rendered at 1920 × 1080 with one ray per pixel. Each ray hits something. How many shadow rays does one frame need?

opts.t: 4 × 1920 × 1080, about 8.3 million
None, if the lights are bright

blocks.why: One shadow ray per light for every point you shade. That's why real renderers use clever data structures (bounding-volume hierarchies) so each ray tests only a few objects instead of all of them.

sections.title: Mirrors are one more ray, too

blocks.html: A mirror shows whatever a ray bouncing off it would see. The bounced direction is the incoming direction with its component along the normal flipped: r = d − 2 (d · n) n. Trace r the same way as a camera ray (it might hit another mirror, so limit the depth), then blend: colour = (1 − k) × own colour + k × reflected colour, where k is how mirror-like the surface is.

blocks.title: reflect
blocks.prompt: Write reflect(d, n) that returns d − 2 (d · n) n for a direction d and a length-1 normal n.
blocks.tests:
assert reflect((1, -1, 0), (0, 1, 0)) == (1, 1, 0), "a ball bouncing off the floor"
assert reflect((0, 0, 1), (0, 0, -1)) == (0, 0, -1), "straight into a mirror comes straight back"
assert reflect((1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)) == (1, 0, 0), "grazing along the surface: unchanged"
hints: sub(d, mul(n, 2 * dot(d, n))).
blocks.starter:
def reflect(d, n):
    return d
blocks.solution:
def reflect(d, n):
    return sub(d, mul(n, 2 * dot(d, n)))

blocks.html: Put it together: for each pixel, build a ray from the camera through that pixel, find the closest hit, shade it. Here the "image" is text, one character per pixel, from dark to bright: .:-=+*#%@.

blocks.title: The render loop
blocks.tests:
img = render(40, 20, [((0, 0, 3), 1)], (-5, 5, 0))
rows = img.split("\n")
assert len(rows) == 20 and all(len(r) == 40 for r in rows)
assert rows[0].strip() == "" and rows[10][20] != " ", "sky at the top, the ball in the middle"
assert rows[6][14] in "%@#*" and rows[13][25] in " .:", "lit from the upper left"

blocks.html: Run it yourself with print(render(60, 30, [((0, 0, 3), 1), ((1.2, -0.6, 2.5), 0.4)], (-5, 5, 0))). That's a real ray tracer: everything else (colour, shadows, reflections, glass, soft light) is more rays and more maths on top of the same loop.

sections.title: Real-world project: sun hours for a rooftop

blocks.title: A sun-hours estimator for a rooftop solar installer
blocks.client: A small solar company that needs to know which parts of a roof are shaded by trees and chimneys through the day
blocks.brief: Model a flat roof as a grid of points, and the trees, chimneys and nearby buildings as spheres and boxes. For every hour of a chosen day, compute the sun's direction, and for every roof point cast a shadow ray toward the sun: if nothing blocks it, that point gets sun for that hour. Output a heat map (a PNG or a text grid) of sunny hours per point, and the best place for N panels.
