blocks.title: ray_sphere_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write hits(o, d, c, r) that returns True if the ray from o in direction d (length 1) hits the sphere with centre c and radius r anywhere in front of o.
hints: The quadratic with b = oc·d; a negative discriminant is a miss, and the larger root must be in front.
blocks.starter:
def hits(o, d, c, r):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def hits(o, d, c, r):
    oc = sub(o, c)
    b = dot(oc, d)
    disc = b * b - (dot(oc, oc) - r * r)
    if disc < 0:
        return False
    return -b + math.sqrt(disc) > 1e-6

blocks.q: Explain how a ray tracer turns a scene into an image, including shadows and reflections.
blocks.a: For every pixel it builds a ray from the camera through that pixel and finds the first object the ray hits (for a sphere, by solving the quadratic from putting o + t·d into the sphere's equation and taking the smallest positive root; the nearest hit over all objects wins, which solves visibility). It shades the hit point with Lambert's law: brightness is max(0, n·l), the cosine between the surface normal and the direction to the light. For shadows it casts a second ray from the point (nudged off the surface to avoid self-hits) toward each light; a hit nearer than the light means shadow. For mirrors it casts a reflected ray r = d − 2(d·n)n, traces it recursively up to a depth limit, and blends its colour in. Rasterizers draw objects one at a time and must fake these effects; a ray tracer gets them by asking what each pixel sees, at the cost of many more rays.

chapters.title: A distributed cache (LRU and consistent hashing)
chapters.tagline: Keep the hot data in memory, across many machines, and survive adding one more
chapters.part: Part 8 · Engines behind the apps you use
goals: Build an LRU cache with O(1) get and put
Measure a cache's hit rate, and see why it depends on capacity and access pattern
Explain why hash mod N reshuffles almost everything when N changes
Build a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes
Add expiry (TTL), so cached data can't get too stale
chapters.prelude:
import hashlib
from bisect import bisect_left
from collections import OrderedDict

sections.title: Memory is fast, databases are not

blocks.html:
Reading from memory takes about 100 nanoseconds. Asking a database across the network takes about a millisecond, 10,000 times longer, and the database can only answer so many questions per second. So almost every big website puts a cache in front of it: a key → value store in memory (Redis, Memcached) that remembers recent answers. A hit is answered from memory; a miss goes to the database and the answer is saved for next time.

Two questions decide whether a cache works:

  1. Memory is limited. When it's full, what do you throw away? The classic answer is the least recently used item (LRU): if nobody has asked for it lately, they probably won't soon.
  2. One machine isn't enough. Which machine holds which key? And what happens when you add a machine?

blocks.name: bx-ring
blocks.title: Forty keys, a few cache servers
blocks.goal: Add a server with hash mod N, then switch to consistent hashing and add one again: see how many fewer keys move.
blocks.intro: Each key's colour is the server that stores it. Raised, glowing keys are the ones that just moved.

blocks.html: An LRU cache needs two things to be fast: find a key in O(1) (a dict), and find the least recently used key in O(1) (a list ordered by use, where touching a key moves it to the end). Python's OrderedDict is both at once: move_to_end(key) marks a key as just used, and popitem(last=False) removes the oldest.

blocks.title: LRUCache
blocks.prompt:
Write a class LRUCache(capacity) with:

  • get(key): return the value, or None on a miss. A hit makes the key the most recently used.
  • put(key, value): store it as the most recently used. If that makes the cache hold more than capacity items, evict the least recently used one.

Use an OrderedDict (imported in the prelude).
blocks.tests:
c = LRUCache(2)
c.put("a", 1); c.put("b", 2)
assert c.get("a") == 1, "a hit"
c.put("c", 3)
assert c.get("b") is None, "b was least recently used (a was just read)"
assert c.get("a") == 1 and c.get("c") == 3
c.put("a", 10)
c.put("d", 4)
assert c.get("a") == 10 and c.get("c") is None, "updating a counts as using it"
hints: get: move_to_end(key) on a hit. put: assign, move_to_end, then popitem(last=False) if it's too big.

blocks.title: lru_get_bug
blocks.prompt: This cache evicts keys that were just read. Under a workload where a few keys are read over and over, it keeps throwing them out. Find the bug.
blocks.tests:
c = LRU(2)
c.put("home", "<html>"); c.put("x", 1)
c.get("home")
c.put("y", 2)
assert c.get("home") == "<html>", "home was read most recently, so x should have gone"
assert c.get("x") is None
hints: Reading a key is using it. Where does get record that?

blocks.html: The hit rate (hits ÷ requests) is the number that matters: at 90%, the database sees a tenth of the traffic; at 99%, a hundredth. Real traffic is skewed (a few popular items get most of the requests), which is why a small cache can have a high hit rate.

blocks.title: hit_rate
blocks.prompt: Write hit_rate(requests, capacity) that replays a list of requested keys through an LRU cache of that capacity (a miss loads the key into the cache) and returns hits ÷ requests. Return 0.0 for no requests.
blocks.tests:
assert hit_rate(["a", "a", "a", "a"], 1) == 0.75, "one miss, then hits"
assert hit_rate(["a", "b", "c"] * 3, 2) == 0.0, "a loop one bigger than the cache: LRU always evicts what's needed next"
assert hit_rate(["a", "b", "c"] * 3, 3) == 6 / 9
assert hit_rate([], 5) == 0.0
hints: The same replay as the predict block, with a counter for hits.
blocks.starter:
def hit_rate(requests, capacity):
    return 0.0

blocks.html: The second test is LRU's famous weak spot: scanning a loop just bigger than the cache gives zero hits. Databases guard against it (for example, by keeping pages read once by a big scan out of the main cache).

One machine has maybe 100 GB of memory; big sites cache terabytes. So the keys are split across N servers. The obvious rule is server = hash(key) % N. (Use a real hash like MD5 here, not Python's hash(), which gives different answers in different processes.)

It works, until N changes. Add a fifth server to four, and a key stays put only if hash % 4 == hash % 5, which is true for about 1 key in 5. The other 80% are now looked up on a server that doesn't have them: the cache is effectively empty, and every request lands on the database at once.

blocks.title: moved_fraction
blocks.prompt: Write moved_fraction(keys, n_old, n_new) that returns the fraction of keys whose server changes when the number of servers goes from n_old to n_new, using server = h(key) % n with h(key) = int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16).
blocks.tests:
keys = [f"user:{i}" for i in range(2000)]
f = moved_fraction(keys, 4, 5)
assert 0.75 < f < 0.85, f"about 80% move, got {f:.2f}"
assert moved_fraction(keys, 4, 4) == 0
assert moved_fraction(keys, 4, 8) < 0.55, "doubling keeps about half"
hints: A key moves if h(k) % n_old != h(k) % n_new; sum of booleans counts the Trues.
blocks.starter:
def moved_fraction(keys, n_old, n_new):
    return 0.0

blocks.html:
Consistent hashing (1997, the idea behind Akamai, Amazon's Dynamo, Cassandra and many Memcached clients) puts the servers on the same ring as the keys: hash each server's name to a point on the ring, and give each key to the first server clockwise from it. Add a server, and it takes over only the arc just before it, from one neighbour: about 1/N of the keys move, and everything else stays cached.

With a few servers, the arcs come out uneven by luck, so one server might get twice its share. The fix is virtual nodes: put each server on the ring many times (cache-1#0, cache-1#1, …). Its share becomes the sum of many small arcs, which averages out.

blocks.title: Find a key's server on the ring
blocks.setup:
def ring_hash(s):

blocks.q: With consistent hashing and 10 servers, one server crashes. Roughly what happens to the cache?

opts.t: Every key moves, like hash mod N
About a tenth of the keys (the crashed server's) move to the servers just after its points; the rest stay cached
Nothing, because the keys are replicated
The ring has to be rebuilt from scratch before anything works

blocks.why: Only that server's arcs change owner. With virtual nodes those arcs are spread around the ring, so its keys are shared among many servers instead of all landing on one neighbour.

blocks.html: A cache holds a copy. When the database changes, the copy is wrong until it's replaced. The simplest defence is a time to live (TTL): each entry expires a fixed time after it was stored, so nothing stays stale for longer than that. ("There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.")

blocks.q: Explain how a distributed cache decides what to keep and where each key lives, and why consistent hashing matters.
blocks.a: Each cache server keeps a bounded key-value store in memory and evicts the least recently used entry when full; with a dict plus a use-ordered list (an OrderedDict), get and put are O(1). Its value is the hit rate, which skewed real traffic makes high even for small caches, though a loop just larger than the cache defeats LRU. Entries also carry a TTL so stale copies expire. To spread keys over N servers, hash mod N is simple but changing N moves almost every key (only about 1/N stay), emptying the cache and flooding the database. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on one hash ring and gives each key to the next server clockwise, so adding or removing a server moves only about 1/N of the keys, to or from its neighbours; many virtual nodes per server even out the arcs and spread a failed server's keys across many others. Clients use cache-aside: read the cache, on a miss fetch from the database and store the result.

chapters.title: A diff tool (how git diff finds changes)
chapters.tagline: Add one line at the top of a file, and a good diff says "one line added", not "everything changed"
goals: See why comparing files line by line, by position, fails
Compute the longest common subsequence with a table
Walk the table back to produce a diff of added, removed and kept lines
Group changes into hunks with context, like git diff shows them
Apply a patch, and refuse when it doesn't fit

blocks.html:
Every code review, every git diff, every "track changes" in a document answers one question: given an old version and a new version, what is the smallest set of lines that were added and removed? The obvious way is to compare line 1 with line 1, line 2 with line 2, and so on. It breaks the moment someone adds a line near the top: everything below shifts by one, and every line looks different.

The real answer is to find the longest common subsequence (LCS): the most lines both files share, in the same order. Those lines were kept. Everything else in the old file was removed, and everything else in the new file was added.

blocks.name: bx-diff
blocks.title: Comparing two versions of a file
blocks.goal: Make an edit, and see the LCS diff report fewer changes than comparing line by line.
blocks.intro: Each cell compares one old line (row) with one new line (column). Click a cell to see what its height means.

blocks.code:
old = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
new = ["x", "a", "b", "c", "d"]
changed = 0
for i in range(max(len(old), len(new))):
    if i >= len(old) or i >= len(new) or old[i] != new[i]:
        changed += 1
print(changed)
print(len(set(old) & set(new)))

blocks.html: Comparing by position says 5 lines differ, although only one line (x) is new. The four shared lines are all still there, in the same order, just shifted down.

A subsequence keeps some items in their original order, with gaps allowed: a c d is a subsequence of a b c d. The LCS of two files is the longest list of lines that's a subsequence of both.

Build a table where t[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i old lines and the first j new lines. Row 0 and column 0 are all 0 (an empty file shares nothing). Then, for each cell:

  • if old line i equals new line j, the LCS can use it: t[i][j] = t[i-1][j-1] + 1
  • otherwise drop the last line of one file or the other, whichever keeps more: t[i][j] = max(t[i-1][j], t[i][j-1])

That's the height of each cell in the simulation, and the answer sits in the bottom-right corner.

blocks.title: lcs_length
blocks.prompt: Write lcs_table(a, b) that builds the table above as a list of len(a) + 1 lists, each of length len(b) + 1, and lcs_length(a, b) that returns the bottom-right value. a and b are lists (or strings: the code is the same).
blocks.tests:
assert lcs_length(["a", "b", "c", "d"], ["x", "a", "b", "c", "d"]) == 4
assert lcs_length("ABCBDAB", "BDCABA") == 4, "the textbook example: BCBA"
assert lcs_length([], ["a"]) == 0
t = lcs_table("ab", "b")
assert len(t) == 3 and len(t[0]) == 2, "one extra row and column of zeros"
assert t[2][1] == 1
hints: [[0] * (len(b) + 1) for _ in range(len(a) + 1)] makes the table. Remember the lists are 0-based: row i talks about a[i - 1].

sections.title: From the table to a diff

blocks.html:
The length alone isn't a diff. To find which lines were kept, start at the bottom-right corner and walk back to the top-left:

  • if the two current lines are equal, they're kept: step diagonally
  • otherwise step toward the neighbour with the bigger value: stepping left means the new line was added, stepping up means the old line was removed

You collect the steps backwards, so reverse them at the end. In the simulation that's the yellow and green path.

elif j > 0 and (i == 0 or t[i][j - 1] >= t[i - 1][j]):

blocks.prompt: diff(a, b) from the puzzle is ready. Write summary(a, b) that returns the string git prints after a commit, like "1 insertion(+), 2 deletions(-)". Count the "+" and "-" operations.
blocks.tests:
assert summary(["a", "b"], ["x", "a", "b"]) == "1 insertion(+), 0 deletions(-)"
assert summary(["a", "b", "c"], ["a"]) == "0 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)"
assert summary(["a", "b"], ["a", "c"]) == "1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)", "a changed line is one of each"
hints: "insertion" gets an s unless the count is exactly 1; same for "deletion".
blocks.starter:
def summary(a, b):
    return ""
blocks.solution:
def summary(a, b):
    ops = diff(a, b)
    plus = sum(1 for tag, _ in ops if tag == "+")
    minus = sum(1 for tag, _ in ops if tag == "-")
    s = lambda n: "" if n == 1 else "s"
    return f"{plus} insertion{s(plus)}(+), {minus} deletion{s(minus)}(-)"

blocks.q: Filling the table takes one step per cell. For two files of 10,000 lines each, roughly how many steps is that, and what does git do about it?

opts.t: 20,000: it's fast enough
100 million: git uses Myers' algorithm, which is quick when the files are mostly the same
10,000: one per line
It's impossible, so git compares by position

blocks.why: The table has len(a) × len(b) cells. Myers' algorithm finds the same kind of shortest edit, but its work grows with the number of differences, which is small for a typical commit.

blocks.q: Explain how a diff tool finds what changed between two versions of a file, and why it doesn't compare line by line.
blocks.a: Comparing line i of the old file with line i of the new one fails as soon as a line is added or removed: everything after it shifts, so unchanged lines look changed. Instead the tool finds the longest common subsequence: the most lines both files share in the same order. A table t[i][j] holds the LCS length of the first i old lines and first j new lines; when the lines are equal it's the diagonal value plus one, otherwise the bigger of the cell above and the cell to the left. Walking back from the bottom-right corner gives the diff: a diagonal step on equal lines keeps a line, a step left adds a new line, a step up removes an old one. The changes are grouped into hunks with a few lines of context. The table costs one step per pair of lines, so git uses Myers' algorithm, whose work grows with the number of differences instead.

chapters.title: A build system (like make)
chapters.tagline: Change one file in a thousand, and rebuild only what depends on it
goals: Describe a build as a graph of targets, inputs and commands
Decide whether a target is stale from modified times
Build inputs before targets, and only rebuild what's stale
Parse a tiny Makefile
Use content hashes instead of times, and find work that can run in parallel

blocks.html:
A big program is thousands of files. Turning them into an app means running thousands of commands: compile each source file, then link the results. Rerunning all of them after every edit could take an hour. A build system remembers what each output is made from, and after an edit it reruns only the commands whose inputs changed.

make (1976) does it with one rule: a target is stale if any of its inputs is newer than it. Modern tools (Bazel, Gradle, Cargo, Vite, Turborepo) refine the idea with content hashes, caches and parallel builds, but the graph is the same.

blocks.q: You run git checkout to an older branch and back. Every file you touched now has a brand new modified time, though its content is the same as before. What does make do?

opts.t: Nothing: make compares content
Rebuilds everything those files feed into, because they look newer
Refuses to build
Rebuilds only files whose content changed

blocks.why: make only sees times. Times also break with clocks that differ between machines, or a file restored from a backup with an old time (then make wrongly skips it). That's why Bazel, Cargo and ccache key their work on a hash of the content instead.

blocks.title: hash_stale
blocks.prompt: Write needs_rebuild(target, inputs, contents, record) for a hash-based build. contents maps each input to its current text. record maps each target to the fingerprint it was last built from (missing = never built). The fingerprint is the SHA-256 hex digest of the inputs' contents joined in order with "\0". Return True if the target must be rebuilt, and in that case store the new fingerprint in record.
blocks.tests:
rec = {}
c = {"main.c": "int main(){}", "util.h": "#define N 3"}
assert needs_rebuild("main.o", ["main.c", "util.h"], c, rec), "never built"
assert not needs_rebuild("main.o", ["main.c", "util.h"], c, rec), "same content: skip, whatever the times say"
c["util.h"] = "#define N 4"
assert needs_rebuild("main.o", ["main.c", "util.h"], c, rec)
c["util.h"] = "#define N 3"
assert needs_rebuild("main.o", ["main.c", "util.h"], c, rec), "content changed back: differs from the last build"
hints: hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest(). Compare it with record.get(target) before storing it.
blocks.solution:
import hashlib

def needs_rebuild(target, inputs, contents, record):
    fp = hashlib.sha256("\0".join(contents[i] for i in inputs).encode()).hexdigest()
    if record.get(target) == fp:
        return False
    record[target] = fp
    return True

blocks.title: make_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write build(target, rules, mtime, ran). rules maps a target to (inputs, command); files without a rule are sources. Build the inputs first, then, if the target is missing from mtime or older than any input, append its command to the list ran and set its time to one more than the largest time in mtime.
blocks.tests:
rules = {"app": (["a.o", "b.o"], "link"), "a.o": (["a.c"], "cc a"), "b.o": (["b.c", "h.h"], "cc b")}
m = {"a.c": 1, "b.c": 1, "h.h": 9, "a.o": 5, "b.o": 5, "app": 6}
ran = []
build("app", rules, m, ran)
assert ran == ["cc b", "link"]
ran = []
build("app", rules, m, ran)
assert ran == []
hints: Sources have no rule: return. Recurse into the inputs before comparing times.
blocks.starter:
def build(target, rules, mtime, ran):
    pass

blocks.q: Explain how make decides what to rebuild after you edit a file, and one weakness of its approach.
blocks.a: The build is a graph: each target has inputs and a command that makes it from them, and files with no rule are sources. To build a target, make first builds each of its inputs recursively, so their times are current, and only then compares: if the target is missing or any input has a newer modified time, it runs the command, which gives the target a new time; otherwise it skips it. So editing a header rebuilds every object file that includes it and then relinks the app, while untouched parts are skipped. Checking staleness before building the inputs would miss changes that arrive through an intermediate file. The weakness is that it trusts modified times: a checkout, a copied file or a skewed clock can make unchanged files look new or changed files look old, so tools like Bazel and Cargo compare hashes of the content instead. Targets whose inputs don't depend on each other can be built in parallel, level by level.

chapters.title: A package manager (resolving versions)
chapters.tagline: Two of your libraries need different versions of a third. Find the versions that make everyone happy
goals: Parse and compare version numbers correctly
Check versions against constraints like ^1.4, ~2.1 and >=3.0
See why "newest of everything" can break an install
Resolve versions by backtracking search
Write a lock file, and an install order

blocks.html:
You ask for two packages. Each of them needs other packages, at certain versions, and those need more. The package manager has to choose one version of every package so that every requirement, from you and from every package, is satisfied at once. That's called dependency resolution, and it's a genuinely hard search problem (in general, as hard as Sudoku).

When it fails you see errors like pip's ResolutionImpossible or npm's ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree. After this chapter you'll know exactly what they mean.

blocks.name: bx-resolve
blocks.title: Choosing versions for web, db and the log package they share
blocks.goal: Install the newest of everything and watch it break, then let the backtracking resolver find versions that fit.
blocks.intro: Each column lists one package's published versions, newest on top. Click a version to see what it needs.

blocks.html: Most packages use semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A patch fixes bugs, a minor version adds features without breaking anything, and a major version may break your code.
Comparing as strings goes character by character, and "1" < "9", so 1.10 looks older than 1.9. Split on the dots and compare tuples of numbers instead.

blocks.title: parse_version
blocks.prompt: Write parse(v) that turns a version string into a tuple of three ints, padding missing parts with 0 ("2.1" → (2, 1, 0), "3" → (3, 0, 0)). Then write newest(versions) that returns the newest version string from a list.
hints: max(versions, key=parse) compares the tuples, not the strings.

blocks.title: sort_bug
blocks.prompt: This function should list versions newest first, but it puts 0.9.0 above 0.10.0. Fix it.
hints: Sort by a key that turns each version into a tuple of ints.
blocks.starter:
def newest_first(versions):
    return sorted(versions, reverse=True)
blocks.solution:
def newest_first(versions):
    return sorted(versions, key=lambda v: tuple(int(x) for x in v.split(".")), reverse=True)

blocks.html:
A package doesn't ask for one exact version; it asks for a range, so that bug fixes can flow in. The common shorthands (npm and Cargo write them like this; pip writes >=1.4,<2):

constraintmeanswhy
^1.4.0>=1.4.0, <2.0.0any compatible version: same major
^0.3.0>=0.3.0, <0.4.0before 1.0, every minor may break things
~1.4.0>=1.4.0, <1.5.0bug fixes only
>=1.2at least 1.2
==1.3.0exactly 1.3.0

blocks.title: satisfies
blocks.prompt: Write satisfies(version, constraint) for the five kinds in the table, plus "*" (anything). parse is ready. Versions in constraints may be short ("^1.4" means ^1.4.0).
blocks.tests:
assert satisfies("1.9.3", "^1.4") and not satisfies("2.0.0", "^1.4") and not satisfies("1.3.9", "^1.4")
assert satisfies("0.3.7", "^0.3.0") and not satisfies("0.4.0", "^0.3.0"), "below 1.0, ^ locks the minor"
assert satisfies("1.4.9", "~1.4.0") and not satisfies("1.5.0", "~1.4.0")
assert satisfies("3.0.0", ">=1.2") and not satisfies("1.1.9", ">=1.2")
assert satisfies("1.3.0", "==1.3.0") and not satisfies("1.3.1", "==1.3")
assert satisfies("0.0.1", "*")
hints: Work out a lower bound lo and an upper bound hi (exclusive) for ^ and ~, then check lo <= v < hi with tuples.
blocks.starter:
def satisfies(version, constraint):
    return True

sections.title: Search, and go back when stuck

blocks.html:
The simulation showed the problem: taking the newest web forces log 2.x, and the newest db forces log 1.x. The fix is a backtracking search:

  1. take the next package that still needs a version
  2. try its versions, newest first, skipping any that break a requirement already collected
  3. for a version that fits, add its requirements and solve the rest recursively
  4. if the rest can't be solved, undo this choice and try the next older version

blocks.title: A backtracking resolver
lines: for v in sorted(registry[pkg], key=parse, reverse=True):
if not all(satisfies(v, c) for c in reqs.get(pkg, [])):
new_reqs = {p: list(cs) for p, cs in reqs.items()}
result = resolve(rest, registry, new_reqs, {**chosen, pkg: v})

blocks.html: new_reqs is a fresh copy, so when a choice is undone its requirements disappear with it. The order of todo assumes every package that needs log comes before log; real resolvers discover packages as they go.

blocks.q: npm doesn't always need to backtrack. When two packages need incompatible versions of log, it can install both: one copy of log in web's folder and another in db's. Why can't pip do that?

opts.t: pip is older
Python imports a module once by name, so only one log can exist in a program; JavaScript resolves each require from the requiring file's own folder
pip doesn't support version ranges
It would use too much disk

blocks.why: Node looks for node_modules next to the file that calls require, so different files can get different copies. Python has one sys.modules["log"]. Cargo can also keep two major versions side by side, but within a major it must pick one.

blocks.html: Resolving is slow and depends on what's been published today. So once it succeeds, the manager writes a lock file (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, Cargo.lock) with the exact versions, and everyone on the team installs exactly those.

blocks.title: lockfile
blocks.prompt: Write lockfile(chosen) that turns a dict {package: version} into the text of a pip-style lock file: one name==version line per package, sorted by name, ending with a newline. An empty dict gives "".
hints: sorted(chosen) gives the names in order.
blocks.starter:
def lockfile(chosen):
    return ""
blocks.solution:
def lockfile(chosen):
    return "".join(f"{name}=={chosen[name]}\n" for name in sorted(chosen))

blocks.title: install_order
blocks.prompt: Packages must be installed after the packages they need (their setup may import them). Write install_order(needs) where needs maps each chosen package to the list of packages it needs. Return a list where each package comes after everything it needs. When several could go next, take them in alphabetical order, so the result is predictable.
blocks.tests:
assert install_order({"web": ["log"], "db": ["log"], "log": [], "app": ["web", "db"]}) == ["log", "db", "web", "app"]
assert install_order({}) == []
try:
    install_order({"a": ["b"], "b": ["a"]})
    assert False
except ValueError:
    pass
hints: Repeatedly pick, from the packages whose needs are all installed, the alphabetically first one. If none is ready, there's a cycle.
blocks.starter:
def install_order(needs):
    return []

sections.title: Real-world project: a mini pip for internal tools

blocks.title: An installer for a team's internal Python tools
blocks.client: A data team of 12 that shares 30 in-house packages on a file server, and keeps breaking each other's environments
blocks.brief: Build minipip: read a registry (a JSON file listing every package, its versions and their requirements in pip syntax like pandas>=1.5,<3), resolve a project's requirements.txt with backtracking, and write a lock file. minipip install installs from the lock file in dependency order, minipip outdated lists packages with newer versions that would still fit, and when resolution fails it explains which requirements clash.
blocks.why: Broken environments waste days. Knowing how resolution works tells you how to fix "ResolutionImpossible", why lock files exist, and why loose or overly strict pins both cause pain.
milestones: Parse requirements like name>=1.5,<3 and name==2.0
Resolve with backtracking, newest versions first
Write and read a lock file
Install in dependency order
On failure, print the clashing requirements and who asked for each
stretch: outdated: newer versions that still satisfy everything
Prefer versions already in the lock file, so upgrades are minimal
Cache the registry and resolve offline

blocks.title: parse_requirement
blocks.prompt: Write parse_requirement(line) for pip-style lines such as "pandas>=1.5,<3", "requests==2.31.0" or "numpy". Return (name, [(op, version), ...]) with the name in lower case, and the operators >=, <=, ==, !=, <, > kept as strings. Ignore spaces and anything after a #.
blocks.tests:
assert parse_requirement("pandas>=1.5,<3") == ("pandas", [(">=", "1.5"), ("<", "3")])
assert parse_requirement("Requests == 2.31.0  # pinned") == ("requests", [("==", "2.31.0")])
assert parse_requirement("numpy") == ("numpy", [])
assert parse_requirement("my-lib!=1.2") == ("my-lib", [("!=", "1.2")])
hints: Match the name with a regex first. For each comma-separated part, the two-character operators must be tried before < and >.
blocks.starter:
def parse_requirement(line):
    return ("", [])
blocks.solution:
import re

def parse_requirement(line):
    line = line.split("#")[0].replace(" ", "")
    m = re.match(r"[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+", line)
    name, rest = m.group().lower(), line[m.end():]
    specs = [re.match(r"(>=|<=|==|!=|<|>)(.+)", part).groups() for part in rest.split(",") if part]
    return name, specs

blocks.title: outdated
blocks.prompt: Write outdated(locked, available, allowed). locked maps each package to its locked version, available maps each package to a list of published versions, and allowed(pkg, version) says whether a version would still satisfy every requirement. Return a sorted list of (pkg, locked_version, newest_allowed_version) for packages where a newer allowed version exists. Versions are dotted numbers.
hints: Compare versions as tuples of ints; keep only versions that are allowed and newer than the locked one.
blocks.starter:
def outdated(locked, available, allowed):
    return []

blocks.title: caret_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write caret(version, constraint) that returns whether version satisfies a caret constraint like "^1.4.0" or "^0.3": at least the given version, and below the next major (or, if the major is 0, below the next minor). Versions may have fewer than three parts.
blocks.tests:
assert caret("1.9.9", "^1.4") and not caret("2.0.0", "^1.4.0") and not caret("1.3", "^1.4")
assert caret("0.3.5", "^0.3") and not caret("0.4.0", "^0.3")
hints: Parse both into 3-tuples of ints, compute the exclusive upper bound, and compare tuples.
blocks.starter:
def caret(version, constraint):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def caret(version, constraint):
    p = lambda s: tuple((list(map(int, s.split("."))) + [0, 0])[:3])
    v, lo = p(version), p(constraint[1:])
    hi = (lo[0] + 1, 0, 0) if lo[0] > 0 else (0, lo[1] + 1, 0)
    return lo <= v < hi

blocks.q: Explain how a package manager picks versions, and why taking the newest version of everything can fail.
blocks.a: Every package states its dependencies as version ranges, like ^1.4 (any 1.x from 1.4) or >=2.0,<3. The manager must pick exactly one version of each package so that every range from the project and from every chosen package is satisfied. Taking the newest of everything ignores the packages' own requirements: two libraries can need incompatible ranges of a shared dependency, and only one copy can be installed (in Python, imports are by name). So it searches: pick a package, try its versions newest first, skip ones that break collected requirements, add the chosen version's own requirements, and recurse; if the rest can't be satisfied, undo the choice and try an older version (backtracking). Versions must be compared as tuples of numbers, not strings, or 1.10 sorts below 1.9. The result is written to a lock file so everyone installs the same versions, and packages are installed after the packages they need.

chapters.title: A test framework (like pytest)
chapters.tagline: Find every test, run each one in isolation, and report exactly what broke
goals: Discover test functions by name and run them all
Keep going after a failure, and tell failures from errors
Check that code raises the right exception
Give each test a fresh fixture, so order doesn't matter
Run one test over many inputs (parametrize)

blocks.html:
You write def test_total(): assert cart.total() == 3 and run pytest. Behind that one word, a framework finds every function whose name starts with test_, runs each one, catches whatever goes wrong so the next test still runs, and reports what passed and failed. It also hands each test the objects it needs (fixtures), fresh every time.

That last part matters more than it looks. Tests that share state can pass or fail depending on the order they run in, which is the worst kind of test: a red result that isn't the code's fault.

blocks.name: bx-tests
blocks.title: Five tests sharing one shopping cart
blocks.goal: Run shuffled with one shared cart and watch a test fail, then switch to fresh fixture per test and shuffle again with everything passing.
blocks.intro: Click a test to see what it does and why it passed or failed.

blocks.html: A Python module is a namespace: a dict from names to objects (globals(), or vars(module)). Discovery is just a loop over it.

blocks.title: run_tests
blocks.prompt: Write run_tests(namespace). For every name in the dict namespace that starts with test_ and whose value is callable, call it with no arguments, in sorted name order. Return a dict from test name to "pass", "fail" (it raised AssertionError) or "error" (any other exception). One failing test must not stop the others.
hints: Two except clauses: AssertionError first, then Exception. Skip names that don't start with test_ and values that aren't callable.
blocks.starter:
def run_tests(namespace):
    return {}

blocks.html: A failure means the code gave a wrong answer: an assert didn't hold. An error means the test itself crashed before it could check anything. pytest reports them separately because they need different fixes.

blocks.title: stop_bug
blocks.prompt: This runner stops at the first failing test, so one broken test hides how many others are broken. Make it run every test and return the list of names that didn't pass, in the order they ran.
blocks.tests:
def test_a(): assert True
def test_b(): assert False
def test_c(): raise ValueError
def test_d(): assert 3 > 2
assert failures([test_a, test_b, test_c, test_d]) == ["test_b", "test_c"]
hints: Wrap each call in try / except Exception and record fn.__name__ when it raises. (AssertionError is an Exception too.)

blocks.html: Good tests also check that bad input is rejected. pytest writes it as with pytest.raises(ValueError):. Under the hood that's a context manager whose __exit__ looks at the exception that happened inside the block.

blocks.title: A raises() context manager
blocks.tests:
with raises(ValueError):
    int("abc")
try:
    with raises(ValueError):
        int("42")
    assert False, "should complain that nothing was raised"
except AssertionError as e:
    assert "did not raise ValueError" in str(e)
try:
    with raises(ValueError):
        {}["k"]
    assert False
except KeyError:
    pass

blocks.html: __exit__ returning True swallows the exception (the test goes on, it passed). Returning False lets an unexpected exception escape, so the test errors. issubclass means raises(Exception) also accepts a ValueError.

sections.title: Fixtures: a fresh start for every test

blocks.q: The simulation's tests passed in the written order and failed when shuffled. Where was the bug?

opts.t: In the cart's code
In the tests: they shared one cart, so each depended on what earlier tests left in it
In the shuffle
In Python's random number generator

blocks.why: The cart worked. The tests silently relied on running in one particular order. pytest-randomly shuffles on purpose to catch this; fixtures prevent it.

blocks.html: pytest looks at a test's parameter names and, for each one, calls the fixture function with that name to make a fresh object: def test_total(cart): gets a new cart every time.

blocks.title: fixtures
blocks.prompt: Write run_with_fixtures(tests, fixtures). tests is a list of functions; fixtures maps a name to a zero-argument function that builds a fresh object. For each test, read its parameter names with inspect.signature(fn).parameters, build a new object for each one by calling the fixture with that name, and call the test with them as keyword arguments. Return a dict from test name to "pass" or "fail" (any exception).
blocks.tests:
fixtures = {"cart": list, "prices": lambda: {"pear": 3, "apple": 2}}
def test_add(cart): cart.append("apple"); assert cart == ["apple"]
def test_empty(cart): assert cart == []
def test_total(cart, prices): cart.append("pear"); assert sum(prices[x] for x in cart) == 3
def test_plain(): assert True
r = run_with_fixtures([test_add, test_empty, test_total, test_plain], fixtures)
assert r == {"test_add": "pass", "test_empty": "pass", "test_total": "pass", "test_plain": "pass"}, r
hints: {name: fixtures[name]() for name in inspect.signature(fn).parameters}: the () makes a new object for every test.

blocks.title: parametrize
blocks.prompt: Write parametrize(fn, cases) that runs fn(*case) for each tuple in cases and returns a dict from an id like "test_square[0]", "test_square[1]", … (the function's name and the case's index) to "pass" or "fail" (any exception). That's how pytest reports @pytest.mark.parametrize.
hints: enumerate(cases) gives the index; fn(*case) unpacks the tuple into arguments.
blocks.starter:
def parametrize(fn, cases):
    return {}

blocks.title: A tiny pytest that grades student homework
blocks.client: A secondary-school computing teacher grading 90 Python homework files by hand every week
blocks.brief: Build grade.py HOMEWORK_DIR TESTS.py: import each student's file, discover the test functions in TESTS.py, run every test against every submission with fresh fixtures, and stop any single test after 2 seconds (an infinite loop shouldn't freeze the grader). Report per student: passed, failed (with the assertion message) and errored (with the exception type), plus a score, and write a CSV for the gradebook. Compare floats with a tolerance so 0.1 + 0.2 counts as 0.3.
blocks.why: Every CI system, autograder and coding interview platform is a test runner underneath. Building one shows exactly what assert, fixtures and "flaky test" mean.
milestones: Discover and run test functions, separating failures from errors
Fresh fixtures for every test
approx for floats, and raises for expected exceptions
A per-test time limit
A summary line and a CSV of scores
stretch: Shuffle test order with a printed seed, so a flaky failure can be replayed
Show the line of the failed assert (look at the traceback)
Run students in parallel with a process pool

blocks.title: approx
blocks.prompt: Floats can't be compared with == (0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False). Write approx(actual, expected, rel=1e-6, abs_=1e-12) that returns True when |actual - expected| is at most the larger of rel * |expected| and abs_. Like pytest's approx.
blocks.tests:
assert approx(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)
assert not approx(0.31, 0.3)
assert approx(1_000_000.4, 1_000_000.0), "relative: 0.4 in a million is fine"
assert approx(1e-14, 0.0), "near zero, the absolute tolerance applies"
assert not approx(1e-3, 0.0)
hints: One line: compare the difference with max(rel * abs(expected), abs_).
blocks.starter:
def approx(actual, expected, rel=1e-6, abs_=1e-12):
    return actual == expected
blocks.solution:
def approx(actual, expected, rel=1e-6, abs_=1e-12):
    return abs(actual - expected) <= max(rel * abs(expected), abs_)

blocks.title: summary_line
blocks.prompt: Write summary(results, seconds) that builds pytest's last line from a dict of test name → "pass", "fail" or "error": for example "3 passed, 1 failed, 1 error in 0.42s". List only the kinds that occurred, in the order passed, failed, error (the word is "errors" when there's more than one). Seconds get 2 decimals. With no tests at all, return "no tests ran in 0.00s".
blocks.tests:
r = {"a": "pass", "b": "pass", "c": "fail", "d": "pass", "e": "error"}
assert summary(r, 0.4213) == "3 passed, 1 failed, 1 error in 0.42s"
assert summary({"a": "error", "b": "error"}, 1) == "2 errors in 1.00s"
assert summary({"a": "pass"}, 0.05) == "1 passed in 0.05s"
assert summary({}, 0) == "no tests ran in 0.00s"
hints: Count each kind with list.count, skip zeros, and join the parts with ", ".
blocks.starter:
def summary(results, seconds):
    return ""

blocks.title: runner_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write run_tests(namespace) that runs every callable whose name starts with test_ (sorted by name) and returns {name: "pass" | "fail" | "error"}, where "fail" is an AssertionError and "error" any other exception.
blocks.tests:
def test_1(): assert True
def test_2(): assert False
def test_3(): 1 / 0
assert run_tests({"test_1": test_1, "test_2": test_2, "test_3": test_3, "x": 1}) == {"test_1": "pass", "test_2": "fail", "test_3": "error"}
hints: Loop, filter by name and callable, then try with two except clauses.
blocks.starter:
def run_tests(namespace):
    pass

blocks.q: Explain what a test framework like pytest does when you run it, and why fixtures matter.
blocks.a: It discovers tests by looking through each module's namespace for callables named test_..., then runs each one inside try/except so one failure doesn't stop the rest. An AssertionError is reported as a failure (the code gave a wrong answer); any other exception is an error (the test crashed). It reports every result and a summary line. Helpers like raises() are context managers whose __exit__ checks that the expected exception happened, and approx() compares floats with a tolerance. Fixtures are functions that build fresh objects; the runner reads each test's parameter names and passes a new object for each, so tests don't share state. Without them, tests can pass only because of what earlier tests left behind, and fail when the order changes: a flaky test that isn't the code's fault. Parametrize runs one test over many inputs, each reported separately.

chapters.title: A command-line tool kit (like argparse)
chapters.tagline: Turn a typed line into tokens, flags, options and subcommands, with help and exit codes
goals: Split a command line into tokens the way a shell does, with quotes and escapes
Parse long options, short flag bundles, values with "=", and the "--" separator
Dispatch subcommands and print useful help
Use exit codes so scripts can tell success from failure

sections.title: What happens when you press Enter

blocks.html:
You type git commit -am "fix typo" --no-verify. Two programs share the work:

  1. The shell splits the line into tokens (argv): spaces separate, quotes group, backslashes escape. The quotes never reach git; it gets ["git", "commit", "-am", "fix typo", "--no-verify"].
  2. The program's parser reads those tokens left to right, using a spec: which names are on/off flags, which options take a value, which subcommands exist.

The conventions are old and nearly universal:

  • --name=value or --name value for a long option.
  • -v for a short flag, and -vq for two at once.
  • -- means "options end here": everything after is plain text, even --draft. That's how you delete a file called -rf.
  • -h / --help prints usage. Exit code 0 means success, 1 a runtime error, 2 a usage error (that's what argparse uses).

blocks.name: bx-cli
blocks.title: One line, two readers
blocks.goal: Run split on spaces to the end, then run shell split + parser and compare.
blocks.intro: The same typed line, read two ways.

blocks.title: split_args
blocks.prompt: Write split_args(line), a small version of the shell's splitting (Python's shlex.split). Spaces separate tokens. Text in double or single quotes is one token piece, spaces included, and the quotes are dropped. A backslash outside quotes makes the next character literal. "" on its own is an empty token.
blocks.tests:
assert split_args('todo add "buy milk" --due=fri') == ["todo", "add", "buy milk", "--due=fri"]
assert split_args("echo 'it is'   fine") == ["echo", "it is", "fine"]
assert split_args(r"rm my\ file.txt") == ["rm", "my file.txt"]
assert split_args('say "" ok') == ["say", "", "ok"]
assert split_args('a"b c"d') == ["ab cd"], "quotes can sit inside a token"
try:
    split_args('echo "oops')
    assert False, "an unclosed quote should raise ValueError"
except ValueError:
    pass
hints: str.split knows nothing about quotes. Walk the characters with a flag for "inside quotes".
Keep started separately from cur, so "" still produces an empty token, and only end a token at a space outside quotes.
blocks.starter:
def split_args(line):
    return line.split()

blocks.code:
import shlex
print(shlex.split('grep -n "two words" -- -file.txt'))

blocks.title: parse_args
blocks.prompt:
Write parse(argv, flags, options). flags is a set of names that are on/off; options is a set of names that take a value. Return (positionals, opts) where opts maps each name seen to True (flag) or its string value (option). Rules:

  • --name=value and --name value set an option. --name alone sets a flag.
  • -abc sets the short flags a, b and c. -o value sets a short option (its letter is in options).
  • -- ends options; everything after is positional.
  • An unknown name, or an option with no value, raises ValueError.
hints: The starter treats every dash as a flag and never looks at the next token. Use an index loop, so an option can take argv[i + 1] and skip it.
t[2:].partition("=") splits due=fri into name, "=", value in one go, and still works when there's no "=".

blocks.title: equals_in_value
blocks.prompt: This parser splits --name=value with split("="), so a value containing "=" (like --filter=size=big) crashes or loses its end. Only the first "=" separates the name. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
assert long_option("--due=fri") == ("due", "fri")
assert long_option("--filter=size=big") == ("filter", "size=big")
assert long_option("--empty=") == ("empty", "")
hints: partition("=") (or split("=", 1)) stops at the first "=".

blocks.title: Subcommands with a dispatch table
blocks.tests:
assert main(["add", "milk"]) == 0 and main(["add"]) == 1 and main(["list"]) == 0

blocks.q: Explain what happens between typing a command and the program acting on it: the shell's job, the parser's job, the option conventions, and why exit codes matter.
blocks.a: The shell splits the typed line into tokens: spaces separate, quotes group words and are removed, a backslash escapes the next character. The program receives that list (argv) and doesn't see the quotes. Its parser reads the tokens left to right with a spec of which names are on/off flags and which options take a value. Conventions: --name=value or --name value for long options, -v for a short flag, -vq for several at once, -o value for a short option, and -- to end options so later tokens are plain text even if they start with a dash. Subcommands are dispatched with a table from name to function. -h prints usage built from the spec. Exit codes tell other programs what happened: 0 is success, non-zero is failure (argparse uses 2 for usage errors), and shells use them for &&, || and if, so a tool that prints an error but exits 0 breaks scripts.

chapters.title: A shell (like bash)
chapters.tagline: Parse a command line into a pipeline, expand variables, and stream data between programs
goals: Parse pipes, redirects and a trailing & into a list of commands
Expand $VAR and ${VAR}, and know why single quotes stop it
Explain what a pipe is, and why yes | head -3 finishes
Build a mini-shell with built-ins, pipes and redirects over a pretend file system

sections.title: The loop at the heart of a shell

blocks.html:
A shell is a loop: read a line, parse it, run it, wait, repeat. Running a program on Unix takes two system calls: fork() copies the shell process, and in the copy exec() replaces it with the program. The parent wait()s for the child to exit and reads its exit code.

Everything interesting happens around that:

  • cmd > out.txt opens the file and points the child's standard output (file descriptor 1) at it before exec. >> appends; < points standard input (descriptor 0) at a file.
  • a | b creates a pipe, a small kernel buffer with a write end and a read end, and runs both programs at the same time: a's output goes into the pipe and b reads it out.
  • cmd & runs in the background: the shell doesn't wait.
  • cd and export must be built-ins: a child process changing its own directory wouldn't change the shell's.

blocks.name: bx-shell
blocks.title: seq | grep | head
blocks.goal: Run one at a time, through files to the end, then run pipes, all at once and compare.
blocks.intro: Three programs joined into a pipeline.

blocks.title: parse_line
blocks.prompt: Write parse_line(line). Split into tokens with shlex.split (imported for you in the starter). Return (commands, background): commands is a list of dicts, one per stage of the pipeline, each {"argv": [...], "stdin": None, "stdout": None, "append": False}. | starts a new stage, < file sets stdin, > file sets stdout, >> file sets stdout with append True, and a final & sets background. A redirect with no file name, or an empty stage, raises ValueError.
hints: The starter treats everything as one command. Walk the tokens: | closes the current stage, a redirect consumes the next token.
Strip a final & first. Keep a cur dict; when you see | or reach the end, check it has an argv and append it.

blocks.title: expand_vars
blocks.prompt: Write expand(line, env): replace $NAME and ${NAME} with env.get(NAME, ""). A name is letters, digits and underscores. Text inside single quotes is left exactly as is (that's why echo '$HOME' prints $HOME). Double quotes don't stop expansion. Keep all quote characters in the output; tokenizing comes later. A $ not followed by a name stays a $.
blocks.tests:
env = {"HOME": "/home/sam", "USER": "sam", "USERNAME": "sammy"}
assert expand("cd $HOME/docs", env) == "cd /home/sam/docs"
assert expand("echo $USERNAME ${USER}NAME", env) == "echo sammy samNAME", "longest name wins; braces end it"
assert expand("echo '$HOME' \"$USER\"", env) == "echo '$HOME' \"sam\""
assert expand("echo $MISSING.", env) == "echo ."
assert expand("cost: 5$ or $", env) == "cost: 5$ or $"

Track whether you're inside single quotes. At a $, either read up to } or read the longest run of letters, digits and underscores.

blocks.html: Python generators behave like pipes: each stage pulls one item at a time from the one before, and nothing runs ahead. head that stops pulling stops the whole chain, so it works even on an endless source.

blocks.title: lazy_pipeline
blocks.prompt: Write the stages as generator functions that take an iterator of lines and yield lines: grep(pattern) keeps lines containing pattern, head(n) passes the first n and stops, upper() upper-cases. Each returns a stage (a function from iterator to iterator). Then pipe(source, *stages) connects them and returns the final iterator. pipe(count(1), ...) on an endless source must still finish when head is last.
blocks.tests:
from itertools import count
words = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "grape", "pear"]
assert list(pipe(words, grep("an"), upper())) == ["BANANA"]
assert list(pipe(words, head(2))) == ["apple", "banana"]
assert list(pipe(words, head(0))) == []
nums = (str(i) for i in count(1))
assert list(pipe(nums, grep("7"), head(3))) == ["7", "17", "27"], "must stop on an endless source"
pulled = []
def spy(lines):
    for l in lines:
        pulled.append(l)
        yield l
list(pipe((str(i) for i in count(1)), spy, head(5)))
assert len(pulled) == 5, f"head(5) should pull only 5 lines, pulled {len(pulled)}"
hints: The starter's list comprehensions read everything first. With yield, nothing runs until someone asks for the next item.
In head, return as soon as you've yielded n lines, without asking for the next. pipe is just it = stage(it) in a loop.

blocks.q: yes prints "y" forever. Why does yes | head -3 finish?

head exits after 3 lines and closes the pipe's read end; yes's next write fails with SIGPIPE, which stops it
The shell kills yes after one second
The pipe holds only 3 lines

blocks.why: The pipe also stops yes running ahead: once its buffer is full, yes waits until head reads.

blocks.q: Explain how a shell runs cat in.txt | grep x > out.txt &: parsing, the system calls involved, what a pipe is, why some commands are built-ins, and how variables are expanded.
blocks.a: The shell reads a line, expands variables ($NAME and ${NAME}, but not inside single quotes), splits it into tokens with quotes grouping words, then parses: | separates pipeline stages, < > >> attach redirects to a stage, and a final & means background. To run it, the shell creates a pipe (a small kernel buffer with a read end and a write end), then forks a child for each stage. In each child it uses dup2 to point standard output (fd 1) at the pipe's write end or the output file, and standard input (fd 0) at the pipe's read end or input file, then exec replaces the child with the program. Both programs run at once; a full pipe makes the writer wait, an empty one makes the reader wait, and when the reader exits the writer gets SIGPIPE. Without &, the shell waits for the children and keeps the last exit code in $?. cd, export and exit are built-ins because they must change the shell's own process; a child changing its directory would leave the shell where it was.

chapters.title: An async runtime (like asyncio and Node)
chapters.tagline: One thread, a queue of ready tasks and a heap of timers, so waits overlap instead of adding up
goals: Explain why waiting on the network wastes a blocking program's time, and what an event loop does instead
Write an event loop that runs generator tasks with timers on a virtual clock
Build a future (a promise) with callbacks, and gather results in order
Limit how many requests are in flight at once

sections.title: Waiting is most of the work

blocks.html:
A web server spends most of its life waiting: for the database, for another service, for the network. With blocking calls, a program that sends a request sits idle until the answer arrives, and only then starts the next request. Ten requests of 100 ms each take a second.

An event loop keeps one thread busy differently. Each task runs until it has to wait, then gives control back (that's what await does). The loop parks it with a timer or an I/O watch and runs some other task that's ready. When the wait is over, the parked task becomes ready again. Waits overlap, so ten requests take about 100 ms.

The parts are small:

  • a ready queue of tasks that can run now,
  • a heap of timers ordered by wake-up time,
  • futures (promises in JavaScript): a box for a result that isn't there yet, with callbacks to run when it arrives,
  • a loop: run everything ready, then sleep until the next timer.

blocks.name: bx-async
blocks.title: Three jobs, one CPU
blocks.goal: Run blocking calls to the end, then run event loop and compare.
blocks.intro: Each job computes a little and waits on the network a lot.

blocks.html:
There's still only one thread, so CPU work never overlaps. Async helps with waiting, not with heavy computing; and one blocking call inside a task (like time.sleep instead of await asyncio.sleep) freezes every other task too.

Python generators are enough to build it: a task yields how long it wants to sleep, and the loop decides when to resume it. That's how asyncio started.

blocks.code:
def task():
    print("start")
    yield 3
    print("after 3")
    yield 1
    print("done")

t = task()
print(next(t))
print(next(t))

blocks.title: event_loop
blocks.prompt: Write run(tasks). tasks is a dict of name → generator; each generator yields a number of seconds to sleep. Use a virtual clock starting at 0 (no real sleeping) and a heap of (wake_time, seq, name, gen), where seq is a counter so ties go first-come first-served. Every task starts at time 0. Pop the earliest, set the clock to its time, resume it; if it yields d, push it back for clock + d; if it finishes, record (name, clock). Return the finish records in order.
blocks.tests:
def job(*waits):
    for w in waits:
        yield w
assert run({"a": job(3), "b": job(1, 1), "c": job(2)}) == [("c", 2), ("b", 2), ("a", 3)], "c set its timer for 2 before b did"
assert run({"x": job()}) == [("x", 0)]
assert run({"p": job(5), "q": job(5)}) == [("p", 5), ("q", 5)], "ties: first come, first served"
r = run({f"t{i}": job(1, 2, 3) for i in range(1000)})
assert r[-1] == ("t999", 6) and len(r) == 1000, "1000 tasks of 6 seconds each still finish at 6"
hints: The starter runs each task to the end before the next, like blocking code: 1000 tasks would take 6000 seconds.
heapq pops the smallest tuple. Put the wake time first and a counter second, so equal times never compare the generators.
blocks.solution:
import heapq

def run(tasks):
    heap, seq, clock, out = [], 0, 0, []
    for name, gen in tasks.items():
        heap.append((0, seq, name, gen))
        seq += 1
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    while heap:
        clock, _, name, gen = heapq.heappop(heap)
        try:
            d = next(gen)
        except StopIteration:
            out.append((name, clock))
            continue
        heapq.heappush(heap, (clock + d, seq, name, gen))
        seq += 1
    return out

blocks.title: tie_breaker
blocks.prompt: This timer heap stores (when, callback). When two timers are due at the same moment, Python compares the callbacks to break the tie and raises TypeError (functions can't be compared with <). Add a sequence number so ties keep the order they were scheduled in.
blocks.tests:
log = []
t = Timers()
t.call_later(2, lambda: log.append("b"))
t.call_later(1, lambda: log.append("a"))
t.call_later(2, lambda: log.append("c"))
t.call_later(2, lambda: log.append("d"))
t.run()
assert log == ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
hints: Make the tuple (when, seq, fn) with a counter that only goes up. Tuples compare left to right and stop at the first difference.

import heapq
from itertools import count
seq = count()
def g(*w):
    yield from w
heap = [(0, next(seq), "slow", g(5)), (0, next(seq), "fast", g(1, 1))]
heapq.heapify(heap)
done = []
blocks.tests: assert done == ["fast", "slow"]

blocks.title: future
blocks.prompt: Write a class Future (a promise): done(), result() (raises RuntimeError if not done yet), set_result(v) (raises RuntimeError if already set; otherwise stores v and calls every registered callback with the future, in order), and add_done_callback(fn) (if already done, call fn(self) straight away; otherwise remember it).
blocks.tests:
seen = []
f = Future()
assert not f.done()
try:
    f.result()
    assert False, "result() before set_result should raise"
except RuntimeError:
    pass
f.add_done_callback(lambda fut: seen.append(("first", fut.result())))
f.add_done_callback(lambda fut: seen.append(("second", fut.result())))
f.set_result(None)
assert f.done() and f.result() is None, "None is a valid result"
assert seen == [("first", None), ("second", None)]
f.add_done_callback(lambda fut: seen.append("late"))
assert seen[-1] == "late", "a callback added after completion runs immediately"
try:
    f.set_result(1)
    assert False, "setting twice should raise"
except RuntimeError:
    pass
hints: The starter uses None to mean "not done", which breaks when the result really is None. Keep a separate _done flag.
set_result stores the value and then runs the saved callbacks; add_done_callback runs the callback at once if the future is already done.

blocks.title: gather
blocks.prompt: Write gather(gens): run a list of generator tasks concurrently on a virtual clock (they yield sleep times, as in run) and collect each task's return value (a generator's return x arrives as StopIteration.value). Return (results, finish_time) with results in the same order as the input, not the order they finished.
blocks.tests:
def fetch(name, latency):
    yield latency
    return f"{name}:{latency}"
r, t = gather([fetch("a", 3), fetch("b", 1), fetch("c", 2)])
assert r == ["a:3", "b:1", "c:2"], "results in input order"
assert t == 3, "the slowest request decides the total"
r, t = gather([fetch(str(i), 1 + i % 5) for i in range(500)])
assert t == 5 and r[7] == "7:3"
assert gather([]) == ([], 0)
hints: The starter runs the tasks one after another, so the times add up. Use a heap, as in run.
Keep each task's input index with it in the heap, so its return value goes into the right slot of results.
blocks.solution:
import heapq

def gather(gens):
    heap = [(0, i, i, g) for i, g in enumerate(gens)]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    results, clock, seq = [None] * len(gens), 0, len(gens)
    while heap:
        clock, _, i, g = heapq.heappop(heap)
        try:
            d = next(g)
        except StopIteration as e:
            results[i] = e.value
            continue
        heapq.heappush(heap, (clock + d, seq, i, g))
        seq += 1
    return results, clock

blocks.q: Inside an async task you call time.sleep(2) instead of await asyncio.sleep(2). What happens?

opts.t: Only that task pauses
The whole event loop stops for 2 seconds: no other task can run, because the one thread is stuck
Python converts it automatically
It raises an error

blocks.why: await hands control back to the loop. A blocking call never does.

blocks.q: You have 8 CPU-heavy image resizes. Will asyncio make them faster?

opts.t: Yes, about 8 times faster
No: they don't wait on anything, and one thread still does them one at a time. Use processes for CPU work
Yes, if you add more awaits
Only on Linux

blocks.why: Async overlaps waiting. It can't overlap computing on one thread.

blocks.q: What does await fut do inside a task?

opts.t: Busy-waits until the future is done
Registers a callback on the future to resume this task, then gives control back to the loop
Starts a new thread
Cancels the future

blocks.why: When the future gets its result, the callback puts the task back in the ready queue.

blocks.solution:
import heapq

def run(tasks):
    heap, seq, out = [], 0, []
    for name, gen in tasks.items():
        heap.append((0, seq, name, gen))
        seq += 1
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    while heap:
        clock, _, name, gen = heapq.heappop(heap)
        try:
            d = next(gen)
        except StopIteration:
            out.append((name, clock))
            continue
        heapq.heappush(heap, (clock + d, seq, name, gen))
        seq += 1
    return out

blocks.q: Explain how an async runtime works: what problem it solves, the ready queue, timers, futures and await, why it uses one thread, and what it can't speed up.
blocks.a: Programs that talk to networks and disks spend most of their time waiting. Blocking calls leave the thread idle during each wait, so total time is the sum of all waits. An event loop runs many tasks on one thread. Each task runs until it needs to wait, then awaits: it registers interest in a future (a placeholder for a result not yet available) and hands control back. The loop keeps a queue of ready tasks and a heap of timers ordered by wake time (with a sequence number to break ties); it runs the ready tasks, then sleeps until the next timer or I/O event, and callbacks on completed futures put the waiting tasks back in the ready queue. Waits overlap, so ten 100 ms requests take about 100 ms. One thread means no locks are needed between awaits, but also that CPU work never overlaps, and a single blocking call (time.sleep, a slow loop) freezes every task. CPU-heavy work needs processes or threads instead. A semaphore limits how many operations are in flight at once.

chapters.title: A container runtime (like Docker)
chapters.tagline: Stack read-only layers, write on top with copy-on-write, and fence processes in with namespaces and limits
goals: Explain what a container is: an ordinary process with its own view (namespaces) and its own limits (cgroups)
Resolve a file through a stack of layers, including deletions (whiteouts)
Write copy-on-write: copy a file up before changing it
Cache image layers by hashing each build step on top of its parent

sections.title: A container is a process wearing blinkers

blocks.html:
A container isn't a small virtual machine. It's an ordinary process on the same kernel, started with three kinds of fence:

  • Namespaces change what it can see: its own process list (it believes it's PID 1), its own hostname, network interfaces, mount points and user IDs.
  • cgroups limit what it can use: CPU share, memory (go over and it's killed), number of processes, disk bandwidth.
  • A layered filesystem gives it its own root directory, built from an image.

The image part is what makes containers cheap. An image is a stack of read-only layers, each the changes made by one build step (FROM python, COPY app/, RUN pip install). A running container adds one thin writable layer on top. Reading a file looks down the stack from the top and takes the first match. Writing a file that lives in a lower layer first copies it up into the writable layer (copy-on-write). Deleting one writes a whiteout, a marker that hides it.

blocks.title: overlay_read
blocks.prompt: Layers are dicts from path to file contents, listed top first. A value of None is a whiteout: the file was deleted at that layer. Write read(layers, path): return the contents from the topmost layer that mentions the path, or raise FileNotFoundError if no layer has it or the topmost mention is a whiteout.

blocks.title: copy_on_write
blocks.prompt:
Write a class Container(image_layers) where image_layers is a list of read-only dicts, top first. The container has its own empty upper dict on top. Methods:

  • read(path): as before, looking in upper first.
  • write(path, text): store in upper (the image layers must never change).
  • append(path, text): copy-on-write: read the current contents (through the layers), add text, and write the result to upper.
  • delete(path): raise FileNotFoundError if it doesn't exist; otherwise put a whiteout (None) in upper.
  • upper_size(): total length of the strings in upper.
blocks.tests:
image = [{"/app/config": "debug=0\n"}, {"/etc/os": "debian\n", "/app/config": "old\n"}]
snapshot = [dict(l) for l in image]
a, b = Container(image), Container(image)
a.append("/app/config", "port=80\n")
assert a.read("/app/config") == "debug=0\nport=80\n"
assert b.read("/app/config") == "debug=0\n", "other containers see the original"
b.delete("/etc/os")
try:
    b.read("/etc/os")
    assert False
except FileNotFoundError:
    pass
assert a.read("/etc/os") == "debian\n"
a.write("/tmp/log", "hello")
assert a.upper_size() == len("debug=0\nport=80\n") + 5 and b.upper_size() == 0
assert image == snapshot, "the image layers must not change"
try:
    a.delete("/missing")
    assert False
except FileNotFoundError:
    pass
hints: The starter writes straight into the top image layer, so every container sharing the image sees the change. Give each container its own upper dict.
Make self.layers = [self.upper] + image_layers so read checks the upper layer first. append reads through the stack and writes the result to upper.

blocks.title: layer_cache
blocks.prompt: Docker caches build steps: each layer's ID is a hash of its parent's ID plus the step's text, so a step is reused only if it and every step before it are unchanged. Write layer_ids(steps): start with parent "", and for each step compute sha256((parent + "\n" + step).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]. Then write cache_hits(old_steps, new_steps): how many of the new build's layer IDs already existed in the old build.
blocks.tests:
v1 = ["FROM python:3.12", "COPY requirements.txt .", "RUN pip install -r requirements.txt", "COPY . ."]
v2 = ["FROM python:3.12", "COPY requirements.txt .", "RUN pip install -r requirements.txt", "COPY . .", "CMD python app.py"]
v3 = ["FROM python:3.13", "COPY requirements.txt .", "RUN pip install -r requirements.txt", "COPY . ."]
assert len(layer_ids(v1)) == 4 and len(set(layer_ids(v1))) == 4
assert cache_hits(v1, v2) == 4, "adding a step at the end reuses everything before it"
assert cache_hits(v1, v3) == 0, "changing the base invalidates every layer after it"
assert cache_hits(v1, list(reversed(v1))) == 0, "same steps in another order are different layers"
assert layer_ids(["A"]) == [hashlib.sha256(b"\nA").hexdigest()[:12]]
hints: The starter hashes each step on its own, so a step looks cached even if something before it changed. Chain the hashes: each ID depends on the previous one.

blocks.title: memory_limit
blocks.prompt: cgroups kill a container that goes over its memory limit (the OOM killer). Write oom_step(events, limit): events is a list of numbers, positive for allocating that many MB and negative for freeing. Return the index of the event that pushes usage over limit, or None if it never does. Usage can't go below 0.
blocks.tests:
assert oom_step([100, 200, -150, 300], 400) == 3
assert oom_step([100, 400, -400], 400) == 1, "the peak matters, not the final total"
assert oom_step([500, -500], 600) is None
assert oom_step([-50, 100], 60) == 1, "freeing more than you have doesn't give credit"
assert oom_step([], 1) is None
hints: The starter only checks the final total. The kernel checks at every allocation: keep a running total.
blocks.starter:
def oom_step(events, limit):
    return None if sum(events) <= limit else len(events) - 1

blocks.q: Inside a container, ps shows your app as PID 1 and nothing else. On the host, it's PID 48213. Why?

opts.t: The container runs its own kernel
A PID namespace gives the container its own numbering and only shows its own processes
Docker renames processes
PID 1 is reserved for containers

blocks.why: Same kernel, different view. That's what namespaces are.

blocks.q: Why are image layers read-only?

opts.t: So many containers (and images) can share them safely; all changes go to each container's own writable layer
To save CPU
Because disks are read-only
To make builds slower

blocks.why: Sharing is only safe if nobody can change what's shared.

blocks.q: A Dockerfile copies the whole project before installing dependencies. You change one line of code. What gets rebuilt?

opts.t: Nothing
Only the code layer
The copy step and every step after it, including the slow dependency install
Only the base image

blocks.why: Copy the requirements file and install first, then copy the rest, so code changes don't invalidate the install layer.

blocks.q: Explain what a container is and how its filesystem works: namespaces, cgroups, image layers, the writable layer, copy-on-write, whiteouts, and how build caching decides what to rebuild.
blocks.a: A container is an ordinary process on the host kernel with fences around it. Namespaces change what it sees: its own process IDs (it can be PID 1), hostname, network, mounts and users. cgroups limit what it uses: CPU share, memory (going over gets it killed by the OOM killer), and number of processes. Its root filesystem comes from an image, a stack of read-only layers, each holding the changes from one build step. A running container adds a thin writable layer on top. Reading a file looks down the stack and takes the topmost match. Writing a file from a lower layer first copies it up into the writable layer (copy-on-write), so the shared layers never change and every other container still sees the original. Deleting writes a whiteout that hides the file. Because layers are shared, many containers cost one image plus their small changes, and starting one copies nothing. Each layer's ID is a hash of its parent's ID and its step, so a cached layer is reused only if it and every earlier step are unchanged; that's why dependency installs should come before copying code that changes often.
